### 3.2. Court Calibration

[Figure 2](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f002) shows the process of court calibration. To calibrate the court, the whole information about the court is required. Our study developed the model to generate a bird’s-eye view of global court images with the following method. First, generate panoramic images from the clips that contain the court region in a video. Second, shift the channel of the image into a YCrCb channel and generate a histogram of the image. Third, limit the color of the image based on the mode color of the image and shift it into a binary image. The region of the court is represented as the biggest contour in the middle of the binary image. The model calculates the convex hull of this region and clusters each degree of the convex hull clockwise. After that, PCA is applied to the clustered result to represent straight lines. The points where different lines cross represent the vertices of the court. Each coordinate of the vertices is used to calculate the homography between the result and the actual court. Through this method, homography can be obtained from a sports clip. Some unstable courts in clips are replaced with the most accurate homography among clips. Finally, the total homography is calculated for the whole video, which allows a bird’s-eye view of the court to be formed. After that, to detect the partial field of the court according to the movement of the screen, the YOLO8-seg model distinguishes the court region, three-point line, paint area, center circle, and outside of the court. Fine-tuning was applied for better performance. A total of 1362 pieces of image data were used for training from the segmentation dataset [[20](#B20-applsci-15-01543)], 1342 for the basketball court, 1296 for the three-point line, 776 for the paint area under the goal post, and 507 for the center circle, with each labeled. Fine-tuning was performed with 300 epochs with 16 batch sizes for the model update. Detailed areas of the court and its convex hull were calculated in order to detect each player’s position on the court and exclude off-court players.

![Applsci 15 01543 g002](/applsci/applsci-15-01543/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-15-01543-g002-550.jpg)

**Figure 2.**
Court segmentation in local view.

### 3.3. Player and Ball Tracking

In this work, we proposed a tracking algorithm for reliable tracking. In the proposed tracking algorithm, the get\_player\_positions function processes data obtained from the YOLOv8 object detection model to extract player and basketball center coordinates, bounding boxes, and attributes. To improve the accuracy of detecting players and the ball, a total of 14,425 image data, consisting of 53,320 player data, 13,527 referee data, 5591 net data, and 4938 ball data are used for training in fine-tuning, with 300 epochs and 16 batch sizes for the model update from the athlete recognition dataset [[21](#B21-applsci-15-01543)]. Only objects with a confidence score of 0.5 or higher are considered. The basketball is linked to the nearest player by calculating the Euclidean distance between the basketball’s center coordinates and the center coordinates of all detected players. The compute\_iou function calculates the Intersection over Union (IoU) between bounding boxes to serve as the basis for matching objects. Objects with an IoU of 0.3 or higher are considered the same entity, while objects with an IoU below this threshold are treated as unmatched. The match\_players function generates a cost matrix based on IoU values and employs the Hungarian algorithm to perform optimal matching between bounding boxes from consecutive frames. The track\_players function updates the state of tracked objects based on matching results, incrementing a missed frames counter for unmatched objects. Objects that remain unmatched for more than five frames are removed from tracking. Finally, the player\_tracking function performs object tracking across all frames, exporting results in the JSON format. The saved data include each object’s ID, position information, bounding boxes, and relationships with the basketball. Through these functions, the algorithm maintains consistent player tracking and object association throughout the video, ensuring robust detection and tracking of players and the basketball.

### 3.4. Sports Activity Recognition

[Figure 3](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f003) provides the whole process of Player tracking and action recognition. To distinguish teams with recognized players, training for uniform data is required. YOLO-cls is used with fine-tuning to update the model. A total 3738 image data have been used for training, containing uniforms with black, blue, green, purple, red, and white colors from the uniform color dataset [[22](#B22-applsci-15-01543)]. A total of 100 epochs are taken with 16 batch sizes. The colors are classified by the model from extracted bounding boxes per frames. The color with the highest confidence level has been selected.

![Applsci 15 01543 g003](/applsci/applsci-15-01543/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-15-01543-g003-550.jpg)

**Figure 3.**
Player tracking and action recognition.

After the recognition of players, the R(2+1)D model has been applied to detect certain actions related to basketball like block, pass, run, dribble, shoot, ball in hand, pick, no action, and walk. The R(2+1)D model is a convolutional model which shows a decent performance with only a few parameters. It consists of 3D CNN and ResNet, a type of 2D CNN, to decompose and recognize a video into 2-dimensional space information and single dimensional time information. To fine-tune the action recognition model, the SpaceJam dataset [[23](#B23-applsci-15-01543)] has been used with 25 epochs, a 0.001 learning rate, and eight batch sizes. The SpaceJam data consist of 2000 labeled gif images, containing actions like block, pass, run, dribble, shoot, ball in hand, defense, pick, no action, and walk. Data augmentation was also applied, leading a total 49,901 data for training. Through this process, the model can extract key events with player recognition, team recognition, player position, and action for broadcasting.

### 3.5. Commentary Generation

This study applied ChatGPT-4.0 Turbo API to generate according commentary for the event based on the player, team, position and action. For generation, a basic message based on player information, team information, position, and action information in Json form is generated and prompted, allowing it to be regenerated as a form of natural commentary. The example of the commentary is shown in the following [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f004). To analyze the naturalness of the generated commentary, the extracted examples were compared with actual broadcast commentary. It was confirmed that the generated sentences were created at a level similar to actual broadcast commentary.

![Applsci 15 01543 g004](/applsci/applsci-15-01543/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-15-01543-g004-550.jpg)

**Figure 4.**
Prompt example for game commentary generation.

## 4. Experimental Result

### 4.1. Implementation

The suggested system architecture is shown on [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f005). The system for providing AI-based broadcast commentary is structured as follows. Users upload videos, which are stored in an S3 bucket called Input Video, and view the generated commentary through a web page. The system includes another S3 bucket named Model Results for saving the results of model executions. Events triggered by storing or updating videos in the Input Video bucket or results in the Model Results bucket are detected by Model Execute Triggers, an AWS Lambda trigger, which initiates the execution of the subsequent model. Model Endpoints leverage a GPU endpoint to run the R2+1D and YOLO models, implemented using FastAPI, and are proxied through Nginx to manage access to each model’s endpoint. The Model Weights component consists of an S3 bucket that stores the fine-tuned model weights after training. When the weights are updated, Model Weight Triggers, implemented as an AWS Lambda function, automatically update the .pt file of the corresponding model locally. The system operates as follows. When a user uploads a video, it is stored in the S3 bucket, triggering a Lambda function to execute the next step in the model pipeline. Once a model completes its process, the results are stored in the S3 bucket, and the process repeats. Ultimately, the commentary results are stored in the S3 bucket and retrieved by the frontend page to display them to the user.

![Applsci 15 01543 g005](/applsci/applsci-15-01543/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-15-01543-g005-550.jpg)

**Figure 5.**
Overall system architecture.

[Figure 6](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f006) shows the screenshot of the system provided to the user. The broadcasting service has information about the teams playing in the current game on top along with the player and ball detection result on the right side of the screen. The commentaries generated with the detected team, players, ball, and player positions are located at the bottom part of the screen. The current performance indicates that processing a 20-s video, including the entire pipeline, takes approximately 1 min. To generate commentary, the system requires a minimum of 16 frames per second, which is sufficient to produce results.

![Applsci 15 01543 g006](/applsci/applsci-15-01543/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-15-01543-g006-550.jpg)

**Figure 6.**
Application screenshot.

### 4.2. Experimental Result

This study calculated the IoU to analyze the accuracy of the generated bird’s-eye view court image. Image labeling was performed with the LabelImg tool, consisting of the Left Court Paint Zone (Left box), Right Court Paint Zone (Right box), full court (Full Court), Left Court 3 Point Line (Left Semicircle), Right Court 3 Point Line (Right Semicircle), Left Half Court (Left Court), Right Half Court (Right Court), and Court Center Circle (Mid Circle). With the ROI (Region of Interest) coordinate, a polygon-shaped BitMask is generated, and the intersection and union of the BitMask is calculated, allowing derivation of the IoU by Function 1. The calibrated result of the court is shown on [Figure 7](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f007). The colored lines are the calibrated result of the model.

![Applsci 15 01543 g007](/applsci/applsci-15-01543/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-15-01543-g007-550.jpg)

**Figure 7.**
Calibrated result of court.

At the calibration stage, the target value and the outcome value have been compared. As a result, the IoU value for recognizing the whole court showed about 97%, the left court 3 point line showed 96%, the left court paint zone showed about 94%, the left court half line showed about 95%, the right court half line showed about 95%, the court center circle showed about 95%, the right court 3 point line showed 94%, and the right court paint zone showed about 94% accordant accuracies each. The average court accordant IoU showed about 95.4%. The whole result is shown on [Table 1](#table_body_display_applsci-15-01543-t001). Partial IoU Ranges represent the area of courts and IoUpart represents its accuracy. This result outperformed the previous study of Wen et al. which showed an accuracy of 80.5% [[8](#B8-applsci-15-01543)]. It also outperformed the previous study of Long Sha et al., which had been studied with End-to-End process and showed an accuracy of 83.2% [[9](#B9-applsci-15-01543)]. Overall, our model improved the result compared to the previous studies from about 12.2% to 14.9%.

**Table 1.**
Partial IoU ranges and IoUpart (mean, %).

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

For the action recognition model, 10% of the dataset was randomly allocated as test data. The models trained with YOLO used split data from each Roboflow dataset. Specifically, for athlete recognition, 87%/6%/6% of the data were allocated for training, validation, and testing, respectively. For court segmentation, 87%/9%/4% of the data were used, and for uniform classification, 80%/13%/7% of the data were applied. The results were analyzed based on these allocations. The segmentation result is shown in [Figure 8](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f008). The center circle, paint zone, basketball court, and 3-point line showed an average of 92.5% accuracy and, in particular, the segmentation result for the paint zone and 3-point line showed a high 98% accuracy, which indicates that the model showed a significant impact. For the background, our study applied an additional algorithm to recognize the non-court part as a background, so no additional accuracy calculation has been taken. Overall, excluding the background, the model performed with an average of 92.46% accuracy of court segmentation.

![Applsci 15 01543 g008](/applsci/applsci-15-01543/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-15-01543-g008-550.jpg)

**Figure 8.**
Confusion matrix for court segmentation.

The detection and classification for player uniforms, teams, and actions are shown in [Figure 9](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f009) and [Figure 10](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f010). [Figure 9](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f009) shows the confusion matrix result for player actions and results in about an 85.04% average accuracy for detecting the actions. In particular, the model shows a high classification result for specific important actions in games, such as blocking or shooting. The cases with the lowest accuracy in the analysis results are ’Ball in Hand’, ’Defense’, and ’No Action’. For ’Ball in Hand,’ the low accuracy might be attributed to the fact that this action often overlaps with dribbling or passing, as players tend to hold the ball momentarily during these actions. Therefore, it is anticipated that accuracy can be improved by further analyzing the action recognition results in conjunction with temporal information, specifically by considering the duration of ball possession to more accurately distinguish simple ball-holding actions. [Figure 10](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f010) shows the confusion matrix result for team classification with their uniform colors. While most of the uniforms are classified well, the purple-colored uniform shows the least accuracy with 67% and 57.14%. The low recognition rate for the purple color is likely due to the limited data available for purple uniforms. This issue can be addressed by improving the dataset through data augmentation techniques.

![Applsci 15 01543 g009](/applsci/applsci-15-01543/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-15-01543-g009-550.jpg)

**Figure 9.**
Confusion matrix for R(2+1)D action recognition.

![Applsci 15 01543 g010](/applsci/applsci-15-01543/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-15-01543-g010-550.jpg)

**Figure 10.**
Confusion matrix for YOLO results.

The generated commentary results are shown in [Figure 11](#fig_body_display_applsci-15-01543-f011). The positions and actions of all players, as well as the ball’s location in the video, are extracted in JSON format as keywords. Based on this extracted information, commentary is generated using the ChatGPT-4.0 Turbo API. Currently, the generated commentary has been analyzed subjectively. Three individuals were surveyed to assess whether the extracted sentences accurately described the scenes, and in most cases, the explanations were deemed appropriate for the given video.

![Applsci 15 01543 g011](/applsci/applsci-15-01543/article_deploy/html/images/applsci-15-01543-g011-550.jpg)

**Figure 11.**
AI commentary generation result.

In Example 1, however, the location of the shooting action is incorrectly recognized as being in the paint zone, although it is not. This issue seems to arise because the YOLO-based model recognizes individuals using bounding boxes but fails to accurately determine the precise standing position of the player. To address this, future improvements should focus on stabilizing the recognition of foot positions by using the lowest point of the bounding box as the reference. In the example, there were no errors in the scene description, but the commentary followed a similar pattern to Example 1. This seems to be a result of the limited input format, which makes it challenging to generate a diverse understanding of the situation. Therefore, prompt engineering should be utilized in the future to add more context to the descriptions, or methods like the Chain of Thought approach should be explored to enable a more varied commentary for different situations. Additionally, in future studies, we aim to complement the subjective analysis by objectively evaluating the generated commentary through comparisons with existing professional commentaries.

## 5. Discussion

This paper proposes a study on generating sports commentary by analyzing and tracking broadcast videos using deep learning technologies and generating commentary based on generative AI techniques. To generate sports broadcasts, the integration of court recognition, player behavior recognition and tracking, game event recognition, and generative AI-based commentary generation is essential. This study presents a complete process for commentary generation through the integration of these individual technologies. Analyzing sports videos requires stable recognition and tracking technologies, considering domain knowledge about the game, complex backgrounds, occluded movements, and irregular lighting conditions. Additionally, the rapid pace of the game results in frequent movements of the camera and players, making detection challenging. Pre-existing knowledge of teams, referees, and players is also necessary to differentiate between them accurately. In this study, domain knowledge is utilized, including information on team colors, the number of players and referees, team associations, and court layout, to support player recognition. **Integrated AI System for Real-Time Sports Broadcasting: Player Behavior, Game Event Recognition, and Generative AI Commentary in Basketball Games**

This open-access study (published in *Applied Sciences*, Vol. 15, Issue 3, February 2025) presents an AI-based sports broadcasting system capable of real-time game analysis and automated commentary for basketball games. The system was developed by researchers Sunghoon Jung, Hanmoe Kim, Hyunseo Park, and Ahyoung Choi from the Department of AI and Software, Gachon University, Republic of Korea.

**Methodology:**
- The system first acquires background knowledge (court layout, game rules, team/player info).
- YOLO model-based segmentation is applied for local camera view court recognition.
- Player actions and ball tracking are performed via YOLO algorithms; a proposed tracking algorithm computes IoU from previous frames to link bounding boxes and track player movement paths.
- Player behavior is detected using the R(2+1)D action recognition model (actions: running, dribbling, shooting, blocking).
- Key game events are identified from positional and action data; broadcast lines are generated using GPT-4.0 Turbo API and converted to audio via Text-to-Speech (TTS).

**Performance Results:**
- Court calibration: 97% average accuracy
- Player and object detection: 92.5% average accuracy
- Action recognition: 85.04% average accuracy
- Court segmentation (IoU): ~95.4% average, outperforming prior studies (Wen et al.: 80.5%; Sha et al.: 83.2%)

**Training Data:**
- Court segmentation: 1,362 images
- Athlete recognition: 14,425 images (53,320 player data, 13,527 referee, 5,591 net, 4,938 ball)
- Uniform color classification: 3,738 images
- Action recognition: SpaceJam dataset (49,901 augmented data points)

**System Architecture:**
- Uses AWS S3 for video storage, Lambda triggers for model execution, GPU endpoints (FastAPI) for model inference.
- Processes a 20-second video in approximately 1 minute; requires minimum 16 fps for commentary generation.

**Key Contributions:**
1. Advances beyond mere object recognition to encompass tracking, key event extraction, and commentary generation.
2. Incorporates domain-specific basketball knowledge to distinguish teams, players, referees, and in-bounds/out-of-bounds events.
3. Demonstrates feasibility of high-quality automated sports broadcasting using fine-tuned existing models.
4. Expected to be applicable to less popular sports not currently broadcast.

**Limitations noted:**
- Purple uniform color recognition showed lower accuracy (67%/57.14%) due to limited data.
- "Ball in Hand," "Defense," and "No Action" had lower recognition accuracy; ball-holding actions overlap with dribbling/passing.
- Commentary generated using GPT-4.0 Turbo followed similar patterns; prompt engineering improvements needed for more diverse descriptions.
- Shoot location inaccuracies due to bounding box-based position estimation (foot position not accurately determined).
- Study is limited to basketball games and rules.

## Abstract

The recent rise in the popularity of digital sports training tools has brought into focus the need to have intelligent, real-time, and personalized performance analysis. The traditional methods of coaching are not very scalable, flexible, or correct, particularly in remote or resource-constrained locations. The combination of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT) can be used to overcome these weaknesses by providing continuous surveillance and feedback. However, the challenges of low-latency data processing, scalable deployment, and personalization to an athlete are yet to be addressed. The paper suggests and analyzes a proposal of an AI-IoT integrated system, CoachXNet, which is proposed to deliver personalized digital training and instant corrective feedback in sports. It leverages deep learning algorithms based on hybrid algorithms to predict the pose and produce suggestions, and takes advantage of edge-cloud cooperation to balance the latency, scalability, and resource usage. In order to test the system, the SportsPose and AthletePose3D datasets were incorporated into the experiments. Motion capture was carried out through IoT-based wearable and vision-based sensors, and preprocessing and augmentation were applied to enhance model generalization. The low-latency inference was done via a server on the edge, but the model updates were done on the cloud resources on a large scale. The metrics used to evaluate were the accuracy of the action recognition, Mean Per Joint Position Error (MPJPE), the latency, and the efficiency of providing the feedback. CoachXNet performed better than the baseline frameworks with an accuracy of 94.1%, an MPJPE of 35.2 mm, and an average end-to-end latency of 32 ms. Individualized training recommendations resulted in better outcomes of athlete performance by 18–23% than non-individualized training recommendations. CoachXNet shows that it is possible to implement an AI-IoT integrated feedback loop in sports training and increase accuracy, responsiveness, and personalization of the system significantly. The results indicate its capabilities in developing scalable athlete-centered digital coaching systems for the future generation of sports ecosystems.

## 1 Introduction

The fast growth of digital technologies has reshaped how the performance of sports is analyzed, tracked, and optimized. Traditional coaching is still based on subjective observation and video analysis after the training, which often results in delayed feedback that is not personalized [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR1 "Ingwersen, C.K., Mikkelstrup, C.M., Jensen, J.N., Hannemose, M.R., Dahl, A.B.: Sportspose-a dynamic 3d sportspose dataset. In: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pp. 5219–5228 (2023) ")]. Conversely, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT) are offering new capabilities that will provide continuous, real-time, and data-driven athlete performance insights [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR2 "Yeung, C., Suzuki, T., Tanaka, R., Yin, Z., Fujii, K.: AthletePose3D: a benchmark dataset for 3D human pose estimation and kinematic validation in athletic movements. In: Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference, pp. 5945–5956 (2025) "), [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR3 "Chao, Z., Yi, L., Min, L., Long, Y.Y.: IoT-enabled prediction model for health monitoring of college students in sports using big data analytics and convolutional neural network. Mob. Netw. Appl. 29, 1–18 (2024). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11036-024-02370-4
                  
                ")]. This paradigm shift in assessment from qualitative to quantitative monitoring has far-reaching effects in the area of training personalization, injury prevention, and performance enhancement [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR4 "Alzahrani, A., Ullah, A.: Advanced biomechanical analytics: wearable technologies for precision health monitoring in sports performance. Digit. Health. 10, 20552076241256745 (2024)")]. Despite some research on the combination of AI and IoT in several fields, including healthcare [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR5 "Badidi, E., Moumane, K., Ghazi, F.E.: Opportunities, applications, and challenges of edge-AI enabled video analytics in smart cities: a systematic review. IEEE Access. 11, 80543–80572 (2023)")] and smart cities [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR6 "Musat, C.L., Mereuta, C., Nechita, A., Tutunaru, D., Voipan, A.E., Voipan, D., et al.: Diagnostic applications of AI in sports: a comprehensive review of injury risk prediction methods. Diagnostics. 14, 2516 (2024) ")], their potential in digital sports is uninvestigated. Available sports analytics engines are dominated by wearable IoT-based sensing [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR7 "Passos, J., Lopes, S.I., Clemente, F.M., Moreira, P.M., Rico-González, M., Bezerra, P., et al.: Wearables and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies for fitness assessment: a systematic review. Sensors. 21, 5418 (2021) ")] or AI-based pose recognition [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR8 "Huang, R., Zhang, B., Yao, Z., Xie, B., Guo, J.: DESNet: Real-time human pose Estimation for sports applications combining IoT and deep learning. Alexandria Eng. J. 112, 293–306 (2025)")], but seldom do they offer a closed-loop system that links data collection and analysis, personalization, and immediate feedback provision. Such a limitation inspires the creation of a new AI-IoT integrated system, CoachXNet, that will be able to support personalized training and feedback in digital sports. Biomechanical, physiological, and contextual factors have a wide variety of influences on the performance of an athlete [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR9 "Mishra, N., Habal, B.G.M., Garcia, P.S., Garcia, M.B.: Harnessing an AI-driven analytics model to optimize training and treatment in physical education for sports injury prevention. In: Proceedings of the 2024 8th International Conference on Education and Multimedia Technology, pp. 309–315 (2024) ")]. The available methods are usually generic. Thus, they do not take into consideration the individual needs of sports subjects who have varying physiological conditions, previous injury history, and training objectives [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR10 "Wu, X., Liu, C., Wang, L., Bilal, M.: Internet of things-enabled real-time health monitoring system using deep learning. Neural Comput. Appl. 35, 14565–14576 (2023)")]. Furthermore, the ability to interpret feedback and analyze in real-time is a considerable issue because of the computational time demands, network delay, and the incompatibility between sensor and AI systems [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR11 "Ma, Z., Xiao, M., Xiao, Y., Pang, Z., Poor, H.V., Vucetic, B.: High-reliability and low-latency wireless communication for internet of things: challenges, fundamentals, and enabling technologies. IEEE Internet Things J. 6, 7946–7970 (2019)")]. More recent research indicates that it is not only necessary to have systems that analyze the data gathered by sensors in real-time, but that they need to be able to personalize training recommendations [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR12 "Shen, D.: AI-based Fatigue Assessment System for Athletes Using Smart Textile Wearables. Université de Lille; Donghua University (Shanghai, China) (2024)")]. For example, SportsPose [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR1 "Ingwersen, C.K., Mikkelstrup, C.M., Jensen, J.N., Hannemose, M.R., Dahl, A.B.: Sportspose-a dynamic 3d sportspose dataset. In: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pp. 5219–5228 (2023) ")] and AthletePose3D [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR2 "Yeung, C., Suzuki, T., Tanaka, R., Yin, Z., Fujii, K.: AthletePose3D: a benchmark dataset for 3D human pose estimation and kinematic validation in athletic movements. In: Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference, pp. 5945–5956 (2025) ")] datasets show the promise of deep learning models in understanding complex sports movements. Nevertheless, in practice, they will need to be tightly coupled with IoT sensing systems and low-latency AI inference engines. It is due to these deficiencies that we are developing a scalable and athlete-focused platform, CoachXNet, that will address that gap. IoT sensors such as an inertial measurement unit (IMU), a smartwatch, a GPS tracker, and a pressure sensor can be used to monitor multimodal data during training sessions [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR13 "Molavian, R., Fatahi, A., Abbasi, H., Khezri, D.: Artificial intelligence approach in biomechanics of gait and sport: a systematic literature review. J. Biomed. Phys. Eng. 13, 383 (2023)")] continuously. The data provides a clear view of the movement of an athlete, his/her physiology, and workload. This data is relayable in near-real time together with low-latency wireless protocols (e.g., 5G, Wi-Fi 6) to be processed further [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR14 "Guo, L.: Intelligent optimization and recommendation system design for personalized training programs for marathon athletes based on machine learning. Scalable Comput. Pract. Exp. 26, 864–870 (2025)")]. Raw IoT data are processed by the AI methods of deep neural networks, TCNs, and transformers, and converted into high-level features such as action classification, pose estimation, fatigue, and injury risk prediction [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR15 "Pan, H., Song, H., Zhang, Q., Mi, W.: Review of closed-loop brain–machine interface systems from a control perspective. IEEE Trans. Hum.-Mach. Syst. 52, 877–893 (2022)"), [16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR16 "Shaikh, M.B., Chai, D., Islam, S.M.S., Akhtar, N.: From CNNs to Transformers in multimodal human action recognition: a survey. ACM Trans. Multimedia Comput. Commun. Appl. 20, 1–24 (2024)")]. Along with recognition, personalized recommendation systems also use AI to be varied in intensity, repetitions, or recovery to athletes based on their profiles [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR17 "Hao, Y., Qiu, Z., Meng, L., Du, Y., Wu, M., Wang, C.: The Development Trend of Sports Industry under the Vision of Internet of Things and Intelligent Edge Model (2022)")]. This point of intersection between AI and IoT, then, generates a closed-loop digital sports experience: the IoT sensors record the motion and physiological data; the AI models process the data to detect deviations or dangers; and the feedback is sent back to the athlete and coach in real-time via the visual, auditory, or haptic interfaces [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR18 "Ren, G., Huang, Z., You, S., Lin, W., Huang, T., Wang, G., et al.: Enhancing motor skills and coordination with Visual-Haptic feedback in ball sport training. IEEE Access. 13, 49214–49231 (2025)")]. The cycle transforms training into an adaptive, feedback, and personalized process, which is a weakness of the traditional coaching process. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

*   We propose CoachXNet, a novel AI–IoT integrated platform for personalized training and feedback in digital sports. Unlike prior approaches, CoachXNet provides an end-to-end architecture unifying IoT sensing, AI personalization, and real-time feedback delivery.

*   We design and implement a scalable IoT framework that supports real-time multimodal data acquisition, efficient edge–cloud collaboration, and low-latency feedback generation for athletes.

*   We conduct comprehensive experiments using the SportsPose and AthletePose3D datasets to evaluate the accuracy, latency, and personalization effectiveness of CoachXNet.

*   The results show that CoachXNet achieves higher accuracy (94.6% on SportsPose, 92.8% on AthletePose3D) and lower feedback latency (27.8 ms average) than existing solutions, enabling practical deployment in real-time sports environments.

CoachXNet also proposes a single AI-IoT architecture, as opposed to current frameworks that only identify poses or analytics, including (i) adaptive edge-cloud cooperation to incur latency-conscious inference, (ii) a personalized training proposal model that learns individual performance patterns, and (iii) a real-time feedback engine taking into account multimodal sensor data. All of these innovations together make intelligent, context-friendly digital sports coaching possible, which was not possible in other existing systems. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#Sec3) provides background and motivation, while Sect.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#Sec3) details the proposed CoachXNet platform, datasets, and preprocessing steps. Section[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#Sec14) describes the experimental setup. Section[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#Sec15) presents results and analysis, followed by discussion in Sect.[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#Sec16) and the conclusion in Sect.[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#Sec16).

## 3 Proposed Platform: CoachXNet

The proposed CoachXNet solution is an AI-based IoT integrated system that will allow delivery of real-time feedback and provide personal training recommendations in the digital sport setting. Unlike traditional sports analytics systems, CoachXNet offers a closed-loop data pipeline that seamlessly integrates IoT-based sensing, AI-driven personalization, and feedback, all with low-latency edge-cloud processing.

Figure [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#Fig1) outlines the IoT devices used, such as wearable, vision, and environmental sensors, to capture multimodal motion and physiological data. The preprocessing pipeline provides synchronization, noise removal, pose estimation, and feature engineering to generate low-level kinematic features and high-level embeddings. The DPMS AI model uses two paths in parallel: data processing on the edge (CNN, RNN on low-latency inference) and in the cloud (GCN, Transformer on rich contextual modeling on the temporal axis). A fusion module based on attention combines the outputs into a vector representation of an athlete. Individualized training modules provide real-time corrective training (voice, augmented reality, haptic), and long-term adaptive schedules (injury risk prediction, workload balancing). Edge-cloud collaboration provides scalability and low latency, and a closed feedback loop enables constant improvement of athlete performance.

### 3.1 Datasets

#### 3.1.1 SportsPose Dynamic 3D Sports Movement Dataset

The SportsPose dataset [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR30 "Christian Keilstrup Ingwersen*, C. M., Jensen, J.N., Hannemose, M.R., Dahl, A.B.: SportsPose—A Dynamic 3D SportsPose dataset, GitHub (2023). [Online] Available at: 
                  https://christianingwersen.github.io/SportsPose/
                  
                ")] is a large-scale archive of 3D movements in sports activities recorded in a wide variety of athletic actions. It covers different forms of sports such as football, basketball, tennis, volleyball, gymnastics, and martial arts. The information is centered on moving on full-body exercises, which are performed in a natural training setting. Every sequence is labeled with three-dimensional skeletal joint positions, body features, and action tags. A wide range of athletes who participate in recreational training to semi-professional sports is covered, which will assist in testing the generalization capability of CoachXNet to different body types, skill levels, and the intensity of movement.

#### 3.1.2 AthletePose3D High-Speed Athletic Motion Dataset

The AthletePose3D dataset [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR31 "Yeung, C.: AthletePose3D: A Benchmark Dataset for 3D Human Pose Estimation and Kinematic Validation in Athletic Movements, Github, [Online] (2025). Available at: 
                  https://github.com/calvinyeungck/AthletePose3D
                  
                ")] is specifically gathered to capture high-speed elite-level athletic motions. It centers on the performance-based actions like sprinting, hurdles, long jump, and sharp changes of direction. Unlike SportsPose, which focuses on variety, AthletePose3D will focus on temporal accuracy at a higher frame rate (240 Hz) to capture subtle aspects of acceleration, explosive take-off, and landing mechanics. Every motion sequence is marked with a phase label (e.g., acceleration, peak velocity, recovery) as well as with detailed 3D skeletal data. This is why AthletePose3D is especially applicable to the task of testing CoachXNet efficiency to provide the corrective feedback in real-time in a situation that requires precise actions on a millisecond level.

#### 3.1.3 Dataset Preprocessing and Augmentation

The two datasets were first processed in a preprocessing pipeline before training. Raw skeleton data were scaled to a standard body frame to eliminate the variation between the different heights and builds of the athletes. Temporal alignment methods were used to normalize all the sequence lengths, to provide equal comparison of other actions of various lengths. Gaps or erroneous data values were adjusted by smoothing and interpolation.

Data augmentation methods enhanced robustness. These involved introducing minor random noise to emulate sensor noise, introducing minor temporal distortions to emulate recording irregularities, and introducing spatial transformations to emulate differences in recording perspective. Collectively, these preprocessing procedures improved the quality and diversity of training data. Figure[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#Fig2) depicts the entire preprocessing pipeline where raw skeletal data are converted into standardized pose data.

#### 3.1.4 Justification for Dataset Selection

The chosen SportsPose and AthletePose3D offer a supplementary assessment system of CoachXNet. SportsPose provides coverage of wide-ranging and varied sporting movements, which represent real-life conditions of deployment in various forms of athletes and activities. Compared to AthletePose3D, it is more focused on precision and high-speed dynamics, and it simulates conditions that are found in professional training settings. This combination of datasets will guarantee that the data on CoachXNet is tested in generalized situations with sports applications and in high-performance athletic scenarios, which makes the platform adaptable, scalable, and real-world applicable when it is used in digital sports training.

### 3.2 IoT Integration for Data Acquisition and Monitoring

The IoT implementation in CoachXNet is meant to deliver the continuous, multimodal data streams covering both biomechanical and physiological performance of athletes. This system also uses wearable sensors that are the inertial measurement units (IMUs), GPS trackers, and heart rate sensors, and the environmental sensors where this system is implemented in the field. Let the IoT sensing layer consist of \(\:N\) devices,

$$\:S=\left\{{s}_{1},{s}_{2},\dots\:,{s}_{N}\right\},\:\:\:\:\:\:\:{x}_{i}\left(t\right)\in\:{\mathbb{R}}^{{d}_{i}}$$

 (1) 

where \(\:{x}_{i}\left(t\right)\) is the data stream of sensor \(\:{s}_{i}\)​ at time \(\:t\). The aggregated multimodal feature vector is

$$\:X\left(t\right)={\left[{x}_{1}\left(t\right),{x}_{2}\left(t\right),\dots\:,{x}_{N}\left(t\right)\right]}^{T}\in\:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}$$

 (2) 

with \(\:d=\sum_{i=1}^{N}{d}_{i}\)​. Synchronization across heterogeneous sensors is guaranteed by aligning all signals to the effective frequency

$$\:{f}_{eff}=\underset{i\in\:\{1,\dots\:,N\}}{\text{min}}{f}_{i}$$

 (3) 

which ensures uniform temporal resolution. The end-to-end latency of data acquisition and transfer is expressed as

$$\:\tau\:={\tau}_{p}+{\tau}_{q}+{\tau}_{t}$$

 (4) 

where \(\:{\tau}_{p}\)​ denotes preprocessing delay, \(\:{\tau}_{q}\)​ queuing delay, and \(\:{\tau}_{t}\)​ wireless transmission delay. Real-time constraints require

$$\:\tau\:\le\:{\tau}_{max},\:\:{\tau}_{max}\in\:\left[\text{30,50}\right]\:ms$$

 (5) 

Since wearables are battery-limited, energy efficiency is modeled as

$$\:{E}_{total}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\int_{0}^{T}{P}_{i}\left(t\right)\hspace{0.17em}{d}_{t}$$

 (6) 

where \(\:{P}_{i}\left(t\right)\) is the instantaneous power consumption of device sis_isi​ during a session of duration \(\:T\). The optimization problem is formulated as

$$\mathop {{\text{min}}}\limits_{{s_{i} \in S}} \;E_{{total}} \:\:\:\:\:\:\:s.t.\:\:\:\:\:\:\tau \: \le \:\tau \:_{{max}}$$

 (7) 

Finally, the acquired multimodal data streams are preprocessed at the edge to obtain

$$\:Z\left(t\right)=\phi\:\left(X\left(t\right)\right)$$

 (8) 

where \(\:\phi\:(\cdot\:)\) represents denoising, normalization, and feature extraction operators. The resulting representation \(\:Z\left(t\right)\) is forwarded to the AI personalization module for higher-level inference.

### 3.3 CoachXNet Models

The core of CoachXNet is its AI-driven personalization engine, which adapts training recommendations to individual athletes by learning from multimodal IoT sensor data. Unlike conventional edge-only systems [[34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#ref-CR34 "Alabdeli, H., Kumar, P.P.: IoT sensors and data analytics for analyzing game patterns and optimizing strategies for coaches. In: Prasanna Balaji, D., Kalayci, P.D., Ramkumar SS (eds.) Advances in Sports Science and Technology, pp. 84–88. ed: CRC (2025)")], CoachXNet dynamically partitions inference between edge and cloud nodes based on latency and network state. Let \(\:Z\left(t\right)\in\:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\) denote the fused representation of sensor streams at time ttt. A personalization model \(\:{f}_{\theta\:}(\cdot\:)\), parameterized by \(\:\theta\:\), maps \(\:Z\left(t\right)\) to a prediction of the athlete’s performance state \(\:\widehat{y}\left(t\right)\):

$$\:\widehat{y}\left(t\right)={f}_{\theta\:}\left(Z\right(t\left)\right)$$

 (9) 

This prediction is compared against an optimal state \(\:{y}^{*}\left(t\right)\), obtained from expert annotations or historical best performances, to compute the deviation:

$$\:\varDelta\:\left(t\right)={y}^{*}\left(t\right)-\widehat{y}\left(t\right)$$

 (10) 

The deviation signal is used to generate personalized recommendations, such as corrective movement cues, intensity adjustment, or recovery alerts.

Personalization is achieved by incorporating athlete-specific embeddings \(\:{e}_{a}\in\:{\mathbb{R}}^{k}\), where each athlete \(\:a\) has a unique profile embedding capturing physiological characteristics, training history, and injury risk. The recommendation model is thus defined as:

$$\:{r}_{a}\left(t\right)={g}_{\phi\:}\left(Z\left(t\right),\:{e}_{a},\varDelta\:\left(t\right)\right)$$

 (11) 

where \(\:{g}_{\phi\:}(\cdot\:)\) is a recommendation generator with parameters \(\:\phi\:\). The training objective minimizes a weighted sum of prediction error and personalization loss:

$$\:L=\alpha\:\cdot\:{||{y}^{*}\left(t\right)-\widehat{y}\left(t\right)||}^{2}+\beta\:\cdot\:{||{r}_{a}\left(t\right)-{r}_{a}^{*}\left(t\right)||}^{2}$$

 (12) 

where \(\:{r}_{a}^{*}\left(t\right)\) denotes expert recommendations and \(\:\alpha\:,\beta\:\) are trade-off coefficients. This enables CoachXNet to provide athlete-centered, adaptive training strategies presented in Algorithm 1.

### 3.4 Real-Time Feedback Generation and Delivery Mechanisms

The feedback module in CoachXNet ensures that corrective recommendations are generated, transmitted, and delivered to athletes with strict real-time guarantees. Let the end-to-end latency of the pipeline be

$$\:{\tau}_{fb}={\tau}_{inf}+{\tau}_{tx}+{\tau}_{rd}$$

 (13) 

where \(\:{\tau}_{inf}\)​ is inference delay of the personalization model, \(\:{\tau}_{tx}\) is wireless transmission delay, and \(\:{\tau}_{rd}\)​ is rendering delay of the feedback interface. To guarantee practical responsiveness,

$$\:{\tau}_{fb}\le\:{\tau}_{max},{\tau}_{max}\in\:\left[\text{30,50}\right]\:ms$$

 (14) 

Let \(\:\varDelta\:\left(t\right)={y}^{*}\left(t\right)-\widehat{y}\left(t\right)\) denote the deviation between target and predicted performance, and let \(\:{f}_{motion}\) be the fundamental frequency of athlete motion. If the end-to-end latency satisfies

$$\:{\tau}_{fb}\le\:\frac{1}{2{f}_{motion}}$$

 (15) 

then CoachXNet guarantees stable feedback convergence, i.e., corrections arrive within the same motion cycle and reduce deviation \(\:\varDelta\:\left(t\right)\). A motion cycle has period \(\:{T}_{motion}=\frac{1}{{f}_{motion}}\)​. For feedback to be effective, it must arrive before the same cycle completes, requiring \(\:{\tau}_{fb}\le\:Tmotion\). To prevent oscillatory corrections across cycles, feedback must arrive within half a cycle, giving the bound \(\:{\tau}_{fb}\le\:{T}_{motion}/2\).

If CoachXNet employs multimodal rendering with \(\:M\) feedback modalities executed in parallel (e.g., visual, auditory, haptic), then the effective rendering delay is:

$$\:{\tau}_{rd}^{eff}=\underset{m\in\:\{1,\dots\:,M\}}{\text{max}}{\tau}_{rd}^{\left(m\right)}$$

 (16) 

and the stability condition becomes

$$\:{\tau}_{inf}+{\tau}_{tx}+\underset{m}{\text{max}}\,{\tau}_{rd}^{\left(m\right)}\le\:\frac{1}{2{f}_{motion}}$$

 (17) 

This result shows that multimodal rendering does not add delays additively but is bounded by the slowest feedback channel, thus preserving the stability condition if at least one modality satisfies the inequality. Feedback recommendations are mapped to athlete-perceivable signals:

$$\:{u}_{a}\left(t\right)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}{w}_{m}\cdot\:h\left({r}_{a}\left(t\right),m\right)$$

 (18) 

where \(\:h(\cdot\:)\) is the rendering function for modality \(\:m\) (visual, auditory, haptic) and \(\:{w}_{m}\ge\:0\), \(\:\sum_{m}{w}_{m}=1\). The weights are adapted to context, e.g., \(\:{w}_{haptic}\approx\:1\) in noisy environments. The joint optimization of recommendation accuracy and feedback efficiency is formulated as

$$\:\underset{\theta\:,\phi\:}{\text{min}}E\left[{||{y}^{*}\left(t\right)-\widehat{y}\left(t\right)||}^{2}+\lambda\:{||{r}_{a}\left(t\right)-{r}_{a}^{*}\left(t\right)||}^{2}\right]$$

 (19) 

subject to

$$\:{\tau}_{fb}\le\:\frac{1}{2{f}_{motion}},\:\:{E}_{total}\le\:{E}_{max}$$

 (20) 

This formulation ensures that CoachXNet delivers personalized, real-time, and energy-aware feedback while maintaining stability across athlete motion cycles. As shown in Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-025-01146-2#Fig3) CoachXNet integrates edge and cloud inference with feedback.

In the PAL framework, each athlete \(\:{a}_{i}\) is represented by a learnable embedding vector \(\:{\text{e}}_{{a}_{i}}\in\:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\), which captures individualized performance characteristics (e.g., motion smoothness, response latency, stability index). During training, these embeddings are jointly optimized with the global model parameters \(\:{\Theta\:}\)according to the objective:

$$\mathcal{L}_{total}=\mathcal{L}_{recog}+{\lambda}_{1}\mathcal{L}_{pose}+{\lambda}_{2}\parallel\:{e}_{{a}_{i}}-f\left({h}_{{a}_{i}}\right){\parallel}_{2}^{2}$$

 (21) 

where \(\:{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{recog}}\) denotes the action recognition loss, \(\:{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{pose}}\) represents the pose estimation error, and the final term enforces adaptive consistency between the athlete embedding and intermediate latent representation \(\:{\text{h}}_{{a}_{i}}\). During online operation, PAL performs incremental adaptation through a gradient-weighted update.

$$\:{e}_{{a}_{i}}^{t+1}={e}_{{a}_{i}}^{t}-\eta\:{\nabla}_{{e}_{{a}_{i}}}{\mathcal{L}}_{total}$$

 (22) 

allowing the model to refine each athlete’s representation in real time as new performance data are received. This adaptive embedding mechanism enhances the system’s responsiveness to individual progress and variability, providing more precise, personalized feedback than fixed-parameter approaches.

### 3.5 Edge–Cloud Collaboration for Low Latency and Scalability

Let a task at time \(\:t\) be characterized by input size \(\:{B}_{t}\) (bits), result size \(\:{b}_{t}\ll\:{B}_{t}\), required compute cycles \(\:{C}_{t}\)(FLOPs), and compute–intensity \(\:{\kappa}_{t}={C}_{t}/{B}_{t}\)​ (FLOPs per bit). The edge and cloud deliver effective compute rates \(\:{f}_{e}\)​ and \(\:{f}_{c}\) (FLOPs/s) with \(\:{f}_{c}>{f}_{e}\). The uplink/downlink rates are \(\:{R}_{u},{R}_{d}\) (bit/s). The end–to–end latency if executed at the edge is

$$\:{T}_{e}\left(t\right)=\frac{{C}_{t}}{{f}_{e}}+{D}_{e}$$

 (23) 

where \(\:{D}_{e}\) denotes queueing/OS overhead at the edge. If offloaded to the cloud,

$$\:{T}_{c}\left(t\right)=\frac{{B}_{t}}{{R}_{u}}+\frac{{C}_{t}}{{f}_{v}}+\frac{{b}_{t}}{{R}_{d}}+{D}_{c}+\delta\:$$

Latency–optimal offloading rule. Offload task \(\:t\) iff \(\:{T}_{c}\left(t\right)<{T}_{e}\left(t\right)\). Rearranging with \(\:{r}_{t}={b}_{t}/{B}_{t}\)​ gives the threshold inequality

Energy on the device (radio + local compute) is modeled as

 (27)

args.summary: This is a research article published in the International Journal of Computational Intelligence Systems (Volume 19, article number 49, 2026) titled "CoachXNet: An Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things Integrated Platform for Personalized Training and Feedback in Digital Sports." The paper proposes CoachXNet, an AI-IoT integrated platform that delivers personalized digital training and real-time corrective feedback in sports. It uses deep learning (hybrid algorithms) for pose prediction and recommendations, with edge-cloud collaboration to balance latency, scalability, and resource usage. The system was tested on SportsPose and AthletePose3D datasets, using IoT-based wearable and vision-based sensors. Key performance metrics: action recognition accuracy of 94.1%, Mean Per Joint Position Error (MPJPE) of 35.2 mm, average end-to-end latency of 32 ms. Individualized training improved athlete performance by 18–23% compared to non-individualized recommendations. The architecture includes: (1) adaptive edge-cloud cooperation, (2) a personalized training recommendation model, and (3) a real-time feedback engine using multimodal sensor data. The authors are Yongkang Wang, Xuehan Feng, Yujia Wu, Xi Zhang, and Jian Wu. The paper is open access, published January 19, 2026, with 5 citations and 2203 accesses.
