## 1 Introduction

Pose estimation and tracking have become essential tools in modern sports (Bartlett [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR29 "Bartlett R (2014) Introduction to sports biomechanics: Analysing human movement patterns. Routledge, Abingdon-on-Thames"); Petrigna and Musumeci [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR240 "Petrigna L, Musumeci G (2023) 3d analysis of human movement, sport, and health promotion")) due to their transformative potential in performance analysis (Aderinola et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR2 "Aderinola TB, Younesian H, Goulding C, et al (2023) Machine vision-enabled sports performance analysis. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2312.11340
                  
                "); Li et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR163 "Li J, Mo S, Shen Y (2023) Taichi action capture and performance analysis with multi-view rgb cameras. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2306.14490
                  
                "); Xi et al [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR327 "Xi X, Zhang C, Jia W et al (2024) Enhancing human pose estimation in sports training: integrating spatiotemporal transformer for improved accuracy and real-time performance. Alex Eng J 109:144–156"); Panconi et al [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR233 "Panconi G, Grasso S, Guarducci S, et al (2024) Deep-learning-based markerless pose estimation systems in gait analysis: Deeplabcut custom training and the refinement function. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2407.10590
                  
                ")), injury prevention (Demircan et al [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR68 "Demircan E, Khatib O, Wheeler J, et al (2009) Reconstruction and emg-informed control, simulation and analysis of human movement for athletics: Performance improvement and injury prevention. In: 2009 Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society, IEEE, pp 6534–6537"); Moustridi et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR217 "Moustridi E, Risvas K, Moustakas K (2023) Predictive simulation of single-leg landing scenarios for acl injury risk factors evaluation. PLoS ONE 18(3):e0282186"); Johnson et al [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR137 "Johnson WR, Mian A, Lloyd DG et al (2019) On-field player workload exposure and knee injury risk monitoring via deep learning. J Biomech 93:185–193")), rehabilitation, strategic decision-making, and enhanced audience experience. By capturing detailed motion data, these systems allow coaches and athletes to identify inefficiencies in technique, refine training methods (Frangoudes et al [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR95 "Frangoudes F, Matsangidou M, Schiza EC et al (2022) Assessing human motion during exercise using machine learning: a literature review. IEEE Access 10:86874–86903"); Karg et al [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR141 "Karg M, Venture G, Hoey J et al (2014) Human movement analysis as a measure for fatigue: a hidden markov-based approach. IEEE Trans Neural Syst Rehabil Eng 22(3):470–481")), and optimize athletic performance. Biomechanics-based evaluation helps perfect a sprinter’s stride and improve a gymnast’s posture. It also offers valuable insights into movement patterns (Liu and Yuan [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR182 "Liu M, Yuan J (2018) Recognizing human actions as the evolution of pose estimation maps. In: Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition, pp 1159–1168"); Fang et al [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR85 "Fang HS, Li J, Tang H et al (2022) Alphapose: whole-body regional multi-person pose estimation and tracking in real-time. IEEE Trans Pattern Anal Mach Intell 45(6):7157–7173"); Raza et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR250 "Raza A, Qadri AM, Akhtar I et al (2023) Logrf: an approach to human pose estimation using skeleton landmarks for physiotherapy fitness exercise correction. IEEE Access, New York"); Gozlan et al [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR109 "Gozlan Y, Falisse A, Uhlrich S, et al (2024) Opencapbench: A benchmark to bridge pose estimation and biomechanics. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2406.09788
                  
                ")), posture (Elforaici et al [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR80 "Elforaici MEA, Chaaraoui I, Bouachir W, et al (2018) Posture recognition using an rgb-d camera: exploring 3d body modeling and deep learning approaches. In: 2018 IEEE life sciences conference (LSC), IEEE, pp 69–72"); Mehdi et al [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR206 "Mehdi N, Thomas V, Ivaldi S, et al (2022) Simultaneous pose and posture estimation with a two-stage particle filter for visuo-inertial fusion. In: 2022 International Conference on Advanced Robotics and Mechatronics (ICARM), IEEE, pp 132–137"); Raza et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR250 "Raza A, Qadri AM, Akhtar I et al (2023) Logrf: an approach to human pose estimation using skeleton landmarks for physiotherapy fitness exercise correction. IEEE Access, New York")), and alignment (Mohammed et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR212 "Mohammed S, Siebers H, Preuß T (2023) Strengths and weaknesses of 3d pose estimation and inertial motion capture system for movement therapy. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2306.06117
                  
                ")). Furthermore, these technologies aid in injury prevention by detecting biomechanical irregularities and high-risk movements, thereby reducing long-term damage and enabling evidence-based rehabilitation protocols. Pose estimation technologies also play a pivotal role in sports broadcasting by delivering real-time visual analytics–such as motion trails and heatmaps–that illuminate player movements and strategies, enhancing viewer engagement and democratizing access to expert-level game analysis (Guo et al [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR117 "Guo W, Pan Z, Xi Z, et al (2024) Sports analysis and vr viewing system based on player tracking and pose estimation with multimodal and multiview sensors. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2405.01112
                  
                "); Liu et al [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR180 "Liu J, Liu X, Qu M et al (2025) Eitnet: an iot-enhanced framework for real-time basketball action recognition. Alex Eng J 110:567–578"); Baumgartner et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR33 "Baumgartner T, Paassen B, Klatt S (2023) Extracting spatial knowledge from track and field broadcasts for monocular 3d human pose estimation. Sci Rep 13(1):14031"); An [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR12 "An PY (2024) Sports broadcasting: how big data technology impacts the viewer experience in baseball broadcasting. Eng Proceed 74(1):60")). These capabilities enrich the overall spectator experience and support a broader audience in understanding complex in-game dynamics. Through the integration of machine learning and artificial intelligence, pose estimation systems now offer accurate, real-time feedback even in dynamic and unconstrained sports environments (Moran et al [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR216 "Moran A, Gebka B, Goldshteyn J, et al (2022) Muscle vision: Real time keypoint based pose classification of physical exercises. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2203.12111
                  
                "); Yeung et al [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR337 "Yeung C, Ide K, Fujii K (2024) Autosoccerpose: Automated 3d posture analysis of soccer shot movements. In: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pp 3214–3224"); Riccio [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR256 "Riccio R (2024) Real-time fitness exercise classification and counting from video frames. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2411.11548
                  
                "); Ajay et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR5 "Ajay L, Biradar VG, Chandu M, et al (2023) Ai tool as a fitness trainer using human pose estimation. In: 2023 International Conference on Network, Multimedia and Information Technology (NMITCON), IEEE, pp 1–12")). As the demand for precision and data-driven insights grows, pose estimation has emerged as a cornerstone technology–bridging traditional coaching methodologies with advanced performance analytics.

Pose estimation and tracking, the process of identifying and analyzing human body positions and movements, has witnessed remarkable advancements in recent years, driven by innovations in computer vision and artificial intelligence (Ngali and An [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR224 "Ngali MZ, An WC (2023) Artificial intelligence in biomechanics pose estimation and the applications in human-related engineering. In: AIP Conference Proceedings, AIP Publishing"); Sharma et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR274 "Sharma H, Tickoo A, Shrivastava AK, et al (2023) Human pose estimation using artificial intelligence. In: Applications in Reliability and Statistical Computing. Springer, p 245–270"); Chamola et al [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR45 "Chamola V, Gummana EP, Madan A et al (2024) Advancements in yoga pose estimation using artificial intelligence: A survey. Curr Bioinform 19(3):264–280"); Chen et al [2020a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR52 "Chen W, Yu C, Tu C et al (2020) A survey on hand pose estimation with wearable sensors and computer-vision-based methods. Sensors 20(4):1074"); Algabri et al [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR8 "Algabri R, Abdu A, Lee S (2024) Deep learning and machine learning techniques for head pose estimation: a survey. Artif Intell Rev 57(10):1–66"); Roggio et al [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR257 "Roggio F, Trovato B, Sortino M et al (2024) A comprehensive analysis of the machine learning pose estimation models used in human movement and posture analyses: a narrative review. Heliyon 10:21")). In the context of sports, these technologies offer transformative potential by providing precise insights into athletes’ biomechanics, facilitating performance optimization, and enhancing the overall sports experience (Sharma [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR273 "Sharma D (2024) Review of application of gesture and poses for reducing injury in sports. Int J Conver Healthc 4(1):31–35"); Mundt et al [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR218 "Mundt M, Born Z, Goldacre M et al (2022) Estimating ground reaction forces from two-dimensional pose data: a biomechanics-based comparison of alphapose, blazepose, and openpose. Sensors 23(1):78"); Badiola-Bengoa and Mendez-Zorrilla [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR21 "Badiola-Bengoa A, Mendez-Zorrilla A (2021) A systematic review of the application of camera-based human pose estimation in the field of sport and physical exercise. Sensors 21(18):5996"); Stenum et al [2021a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR288 "Stenum J, Cherry-Allen KM, Pyles CO et al (2021) Applications of pose estimation in human health and performance across the lifespan. Sensors 21(21):7315")). Pose estimation is the computational process of detecting and predicting the spatial locations of specific key points (e.g., joints, body landmarks) on a human body within an image (Maji et al [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR198 "Maji D, Nagori S, Mathew M, et al (2022) Yolo-pose: Enhancing yolo for multi person pose estimation using object keypoint similarity loss. In: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pp 2637–2646"); Zimmermann et al [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR366 "Zimmermann C, Welschehold T, Dornhege C, et al (2018) 3d human pose estimation in rgbd images for robotic task learning. In: 2018 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), IEEE, pp 1986–1992"); Zheng et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR355 "Zheng C, Wu W, Chen C et al (2023) Deep learning-based human pose estimation: a survey. ACM Comput Surv 56(1):1–37"); Dang et al [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR65 "Dang Q, Yin J, Wang B et al (2019) Deep learning based 2d human pose estimation: a survey. Tsinghua Sci Technol 24(6):663–676"); Lan et al [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR154 "Lan G, Wu Y, Hu F et al (2022) Vision-based human pose estimation via deep learning: a survey. IEEE Trans Human Mach Syst 53(1):253–268"); Fang and López [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR87 "Fang Z, López AM (2019) Intention recognition of pedestrians and cyclists by 2d pose estimation. IEEE Trans Intell Transp Syst 21(11):4773–4783")) or video (Kocabas et al [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR148 "Kocabas M, Athanasiou N, Black MJ (2020) Vibe: Video inference for human body pose and shape estimation. In: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition, pp 5253–5263"); Zhou et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR362 "Zhou L, Meng X, Liu Z, et al (2023) Human pose-based estimation, tracking and action recognition with deep learning: a survey. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2310.13039
                  
                "); Zheng et al [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR355 "Zheng C, Wu W, Chen C et al (2023) Deep learning-based human pose estimation: a survey. ACM Comput Surv 56(1):1–37"); Dang et al [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR66 "Dang Y, Yin J, Zhang S et al (2024) Kinematics modeling network for video-based human pose estimation. Pattern Recogn 150:110287")). Pose estimation involves identifying the positions and relationships of various body parts, such as the head, shoulders, elbows, knees, and ankles, to reconstruct a representation of the person’s posture or movement (Sigal [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR278 "Sigal L (2021) Human pose estimation. In: Computer Vision: A Reference Guide. Springer, p 573–592"); Kulkarni et al [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR151 "Kulkarni A, Shivananda A, Sharma NR (2022) Computer vision projects with PyTorch: design and develop production-grade models. Springer, Cham")). Pose estimation can be broadly categorized into two types: 2D (Cao et al [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR44 "Cao Z, Simon T, Wei SE, et al (2017) Realtime multi-person 2d pose estimation using part affinity fields. In: Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition, pp 7291–7299"); Girdhar et al [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR103 "Girdhar R, Gkioxari G, Torresani L, et al (2018) Detect-and-track: Efficient pose estimation in videos. In: Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition, pp 350–359"); Papandreou et al [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR236 "Papandreou G, Zhu T, Kanazawa N, et al (2017) Towards accurate multi-person pose estimation in the wild. In: Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition, pp 4903–4911"); Liu et al [2022b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR187 "Liu W, Bao Q, Sun Y et al (2022) Recent advances of monocular 2d and 3d human pose estimation: a deep learning perspective. ACM Comput Surv 55(4):1–41")) and 3D (Liu et al [2022b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR187 "Liu W, Bao Q, Sun Y et al (2022) Recent advances of monocular 2d and 3d human pose estimation: a deep learning perspective. ACM Comput Surv 55(4):1–41"), [2020c](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR189 "Liu X, Jonschkowski R, Angelova A, et al (2020c) Keypose: Multi-view 3d labeling and keypoint estimation for transparent objects. In: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition, pp 11602–11610"); Zimmermann et al [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR366 "Zimmermann C, Welschehold T, Dornhege C, et al (2018) 3d human pose estimation in rgbd images for robotic task learning. In: 2018 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), IEEE, pp 1986–1992"); Moon et al [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11344-1#ref-CR215 "Moon G, Chang JY, Lee KM (2018) V2v-posenet: Voxel-to-voxel prediction network for accurate 3d hand and human pose estimation from a single depth map. This webpage is an open-access academic article published in Artificial Intelligence Review (Volume 59, article 54, 2026) titled 'A comprehensive survey on pose estimation and tracking in sports: methodologies, datasets, challenges, and future directions.' Authors include Mustafa Hikmet Bilgehan Uçar, Serdar Solak, Ali Olow Jimale, Hakan Ünal, and Süleyman Eken.

**Key Content:**
- **Scope:** Comprehensive survey of pose estimation and tracking technologies applied to sports, covering traditional approaches (geometric/statistical models) and the transformative impact of deep learning (CNNs, transformers, hybrid architectures).
- **Definition:** Pose estimation identifies spatial locations of key body points (joints/landmarks) from images or video, categorized into 2D (x,y coordinates) and 3D (x,y,z with depth). Pose tracking extends this by maintaining temporal consistency across video frames.
- **Applications:** Performance analysis, injury prevention (detecting biomechanical irregularities), rehabilitation, strategic decision-making, and enhanced audience experience (real-time visual analytics, motion trails, heatmaps).
- **Challenges Identified:** Occlusions (body parts obstructed), variable lighting conditions, rapid/unpredictable motion, dynamic backgrounds, and computational efficiency.
- **Technologies Covered:** CNNs, transformers, RNNs, multi-modal data fusion (depth maps, wearable sensors, multi-camera systems), and hybrid architectures.
- **Datasets & Ground-Truthing:** Discusses creation of sports-specific datasets emphasizing multimodal data, scalability, and representativeness.
- **Future Directions:** Integration of multimodal data, edge computing, ethical considerations, and improving accuracy, interpretability, and generalizability.
- **Metrics:** The article has 7883 Accesses, 4 Citations, and 1 Altmetric score as of publication.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739)Abstract

Kinematic and biomechanical analysis in monitoring human movement to assess athletes’ or patients’ motor control behaviors. Traditional motion capture systems provide high accuracy but are expensive and complex for the public. Recent advancements in markerless systems using videos captured with commercial RGB, depth, and infrared cameras, such as Microsoft Kinect, StereoLabs ZED Camera, and Intel RealSense, enable the acquisition of high-quality videos for 2D and 3D kinematic analyses. On the other hand, open-source frameworks like OpenPose, MediaPipe, AlphaPose, and DensePose are the new generation of 2D or 3D mesh-based markerless motion tools that utilize standard cameras in motion analysis through real-time and offline pose estimation models in sports, clinical, and gaming applications. The review examined studies that focused on the validity and reliability of these technologies compared to gold-standard systems, specifically in sports and exercise applications. Additionally, it discusses the optimal setup and perspectives for achieving accurate results in these studies. The findings suggest that 2D systems offer economic and straightforward solutions, but they still face limitations in capturing out-of-plane movements and environmental factors. Merging vision sensors with built-in artificial intelligence and machine learning software to create 2D-to-3D pose estimation is highlighted as a promising method to address these challenges, supporting the broader adoption of markerless motion analysis in future kinematic and biomechanical research.

**Keywords:**markerless motion capture, vision sensors, pose estimation, human movement analysis, sports biomechanics, kinematic analysis, artificial intelligence in sports, sports technology

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739)1 Introduction

Understanding musculoskeletal movement is an important approach in monitoring human movements and motor behaviors ([Schmidt and Lee, 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B67)). Kinematic and biomechanical analysis helps evaluate these parameters to measure and capture the degrees of freedom of joints and limbs independently, diagnose injuries, and analyze the performance of athletes and patients ([Dao and Tho, 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B13)). Numerous studies using motion capture systems (MoCap), wearable sensors, and technologies have become essential tools in laboratories and field tests for investigating specific biomechanical or kinematic issues. While these technologies serve as the gold standard for monitoring individuals in 3D simulations, their high costs and the setup complexity present significant limitations ([Edriss et al., 2024a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B18); [Patrizi et al., 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B57)).

In the recent decade, body simulation in 2D and 3D has undergone rapid evolution, driven by artificial intelligence (AI), and has combined with the sports, medicine, animation, and gaming industries ([Khan et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B40); [Dai and Li, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B12)). Kinematic monitoring and analysis represent a contemporary method for simulating human body motion, especially in 2D ([Seo et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B68)). Numerous studies have examined the validity of various devices and software designed to monitor specific motions. While 3D data offers more information than 2D data, the choice largely depends on the intended application. 2D information can be suitable for particular applications, especially concerning ease of use and cost. However, 2D simulation has limitations like restricted access to certain angles and the capturing of movements from specific perspectives. Despite these limitations, these systems provide significant advantages, including low costs for registering videos with one or a few cameras, quick and easy to setup and operate ([Caprioli et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B8)). Kinematics is valuable for characterizing changes in specific joint angles to monitor how motion performs and loads in land and water environments ([Cronin et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B10)). Markerless systems use RGB, depth, or infrared cameras, with Microsoft launching the successful commercial system supported by a pose estimation (PE) device in 2010 ([Holte et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B33)). Now, vision sensors, including depth RGB-D and stereo cameras, are being used. Depth RGB cameras capture actual 3D spatial information through active sensing methods such as infrared projection, stereo vision, or Time-of-Flight technology, and stereo cameras use two RGB lenses to estimate depth through disparity. Later, in 2017, OpenPose, as one of the first PE frameworks, was released to extract body pose from standard 2D videos ([Qiao et al., 2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B62)).

This review explores the development of commercial technologies in real-time and offline markerless MoCap, starting with earlier systems using vision sensors that enable direct 3D motion tracking, followed by newer PE frameworks that analyze standard videos with AI, emphasizing the importance of their integration. Each methodology has its exclusive capabilities, and familiarity with each tool is beneficial; however, recent research has increasingly combined both to enhance functionality and usability. Conversely, PE frameworks estimate joint positions from 2D RGB videos using machine learning (ML) algorithms. Consequently, studies since 2010 on kinematic hardware and software for 2D and 3D analysis have focused on their validity and reliability compared to gold-standard systems. The selected experimental validation and technical reports focused on body motion in English are sourced from IEEE, PubMed, and Google Scholar since 2012, with PE tools from 2018 onward. The following keywords and combinations were used: “markerless-MoCap”, “vision-sensors”, “pose-estimation”, “MediaPipe”, “OpenPose”, “RealSense”, “Kinect”, “ZED-camera”, and “sports-tracking-analysis.” The review also highlights the chosen gold-standards for these systems’ validation, optimal perspectives, and setups to achieve the best results in sports applications, emphasizing the practical benefits and uses of these technologies in human activity research and athletic performance, and emphasizing the need for future vision sensor generation to integrate AI-based PE frameworks for broader usability.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739)2 Hardware (vision sensors)

### 2.1 Kinect

Microsoft designed and released Kinect K1 (in 2010) and K2 (in 2014), which consist of one IR emitter, one IR camera, and one RGB camera, to gain depth and color images. To strongly enter the gaming industry and provide human connections as a part of Xbox consoles, targeted the companies that designed the Kinect, which has lately been used as a markerless, affordable, and portable MoCap sensor ([Bilesan et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B7)). Kinect can perform PE using its built-in depth sensor and the associated software development kits (SDKs). Many studies explored the accuracy of the two Kinects in real-time skeletal tracking during human movements ([Ganea et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B24); [Kurillo et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B41)). However, according to ([Wang et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B75)), regarding MoCap selection as a gold standard, the K2 generation is beneficial in terms of joint estimation accuracy and more robust in handling track occlusion and body rotation. In another study, a Vicon MoCap was compared with Kinect in gait analysis, as participants walked and jogged on a treadmill. The results show the validity of the Kinect in the sagittal plane for stride timing in kinematic analysis ([Pfister et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B59)).

Depending on the coaches’ purpose, estimated pose through the Kinect somatosensory camera can be sufficient in physical activity recognition, such as qigong movement detection ([Fan et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B20)). Or by requiring more complex analysis processes, their implementation with other codes or devices, such as 3DSMAX, can invent novel methods for monitoring the sports training seasons ([Shi, 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B70)). Additionally, regarding simulating and estimating the body joints and limbs, the skeletal body structure, Asteriadis et al. used Kinect in body estimation in 3D by minimizing the noise ([Asteriadis et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B4)).

The Kinect device alone lacks accuracy in defining orthogonal axes unrelated to joint centers, limiting its ability to measure internal or external angular rotations and displacement. Adding depth sensors, video cameras, or multiple devices to make a MoCap-based Kinect can improve the tracking process and angular measurement accuracy ([Clark et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B9); [Napoli et al., 2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B55)).

### 2.2 StereoLabs ZED camera

The ZED Camera by StereoLabs, released in 2015, was followed by the next-generation, including ZED2 (2019) and ZED2i (2021), which were enhanced with depth sensing and AI features ([Sarıalioğlu et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B66)). ZED cameras are equipped with two high-resolution lenses to capture in-depth information, making them suitable commercial vision hardware for integrating open pose libraries in kinematic and biomechanical studies ([Avogaro et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B5)). A comparative analysis of the ZED2 camera with other commercial vision systems, including Azure Kinect and RealSense D455, utilizing their respective SDKs, shows higher performance in human pose tracking at distances exceeding 3 m. This advantage aids PE in larger spaces or dynamic environments, such as field tests ([Ramasubramanian et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B63)). Another suggests that Nuitrack and MediaPipe software integrate with ZED2i to perform better in upper and lower extremity features for pose tracking ([Aharony et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B1)). Combining ZEDmini with a Virtual Reality (VR) headset and an augmented reality (AR) prototype resulted in a device capable of recognizing body formation and sports equipment such as a tennis racket and basketball hoop. This novelty aids players with low vision to enhance their ability to identify the players and objects ([Lee et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B43)). The advantages of ZED cameras as hardware for exercise monitoring, assessing gait impairment in Neurodegenerative disorders, and joint angle measurement include their ease of use, affordability, and ability to deliver reliable results in both 2D and 3D kinematic analyses of exercises, such as squats ([Aliprandi et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B2); [Zanela et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B83)).

### 2.3 Intel RealSense

Intel RealSense cameras combine high-resolution RGB imaging with depth perception, offering models like the D400 series for general depth sensing, the L515 for precise LiDAR tasks, and the T265 for motion tracking with simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) capabilities ([Moghari et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B52); [Tsykunov et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B74)). By capturing depth maps and RGB frames, they integrate seamlessly with pose-estimation software framework tools, mapping 2D keypoints to real-world coordinates. Their lightweight design, robust SDK, and real-time performance make them versatile for indoor and outdoor applications, outperforming infrared-based systems like Kinect in varied lighting conditions ([Maddipatla et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B48)).

An Intel RealSense camera is used in head motion tracking using custom software while participants walk indoors and outdoors. They walked in both slow and fast modes, and their head motion tracking was compared with that of a perambulator containing inertial measurement units (IMUs) and a distance counter, serving as the gold standard. The accurate results of this gait study showed that while the participants walked slowly ([Hausamann et al., 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B30)). Another study compared the Intel RealSense camera to the Kinect in slow walking gait analysis. The results indicated that while the Intel RealSense D435 is valid for measuring certain spatiotemporal variables, the Kinect proved more reliable for collecting skeletal data due to its more robust RGB-D camera ([Mejia-Trujillo et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B50)). MediaPipe landmarks and two Intel RealSense cameras were used to estimate angular parameters in five exercises, including squats, knee, ankle, hip extension, and shoulder elevation, compared with OptiTrack as the reference. The results showed an error of less than 20 degrees, demonstrating an adequate estimation quality. Still, further improvements in both software and hardware can enhance the system’s accuracy ([Pilla-Barroso et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B61)). These generations of cameras are increasingly being used in sports performance analysis through integration with AI-based markerless MoCap software. Intel RealSense depth cameras serve as sufficient registration tools in markerless PE, especially for closer range (under 3 m) ([Ramasubramanian et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B63); [Jacobsson et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B38)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739)3 Software (pose estimation models)

### 3.1 OpenPose

OpenPose is an open-source library developed by Carnegie Mellon University for 2D PE of the skeletal structure by detecting 25 keypoints on the body ([Hidalgo et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B32)). A real-time detection system may focus on specific angles between joints, the center of mass, or a point of displacement ([Cronin et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B11); [Needham et al., 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B56)). To analyze the running performance and timing, OpenPose evaluated it with the Coco dataset regarding human PE to recognize hurdles athletes’ wrists, ankles, hips, and knees ([Jafarzadeh et al., 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B39); [Sharma et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B69)). The Coco dataset recognizes 18 pre-trained landmarks with x, y, and v values, where x and y indicate coordinates, and v shows the visibility of the landmarks ([Duan et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B15)).

PE relies on video quality and frame rates, meaning that weather conditions and lighting impact the accuracy of ML systems. A study evaluating the AI accuracy of OpenPose as a PE model under various environmental and lighting conditions, while participants performed stretching exercises, found that the accuracy rates depend on the environment and setup context ([Song and Chen, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B71)).

In a study using 3D motion analysis as the reference standard, an OpenPose-based motion analysis was used to compare knee valgus angular data during the drop vertical jump test. The strong correlation among these data indicated a sufficient ML accuracy level of the PE models in measuring angular movements ([Ino et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B35)). In baseball, analyzing a hitter’s limb angles and hip distance aids in swing performance ([Li et al., 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B44)). AI-driven gesture recognition supports biomechanical analysis in training techniques and game strategy evaluation. This approach was a key objective in a study analyzing tennis player performance through skeletal PE ([Wu et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B79)).

Furthermore, PE models’ integration with wearable sensors or MoCap can facilitate more complex processes through Taekwondo kinematic analysis through a PE model, 8 body joint angles in players’ upper and lower body registered by Contemplas cameras, and the Vicon system. OpenPose was used to process recordings from Contemplas cameras to extract 2D human skeleton data, then triangulated to obtain 3D joint angles to compare world-class and master-class players’ kicking performance ([Fukushima et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B23)). Plus, optimal and kinetic analysis of fouling and shooting in basketball player performance was conducted using video-based (2D) methods with a lightweight deep learning (DL) architecture, where OpenPose was used as the PE model ([Xu, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B80)). This open-source framework is being used in athletes’ 3D estimating with integration with sensors or the Internet of Things (IoT) in various sports such as gymnastics ([Ren et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B64)).

### 3.2 MediaPipe

MediaPipe is an open-source framework developed by Google for 2D human PE ([Pham et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B60)). It enhances AI applications by detecting keypoints on the body, face, and hands in images or live video streams to offer gesture recognition, motion analysis, and interactive systems ([Saini, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B65)). MediaPipe is a broader framework that includes BlazePose and other ML solutions, where BlazePose specializes in detecting 33 keypoints ([Wang, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B76)).

An important finding shows that when assessing PE quality using MediaPipe from a frontal and lateral view, an error margin of less than 25% of the range of motion is optimal, with specific tolerances: under 20 degrees for movements greater than 90°, around 10 degrees for movements up to 40°, and below 10° for static angles ([Pilla-Barroso et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B61)).

The validity of MediaPipe BlazePose in measuring joint angles compared with the IMU-based MoCap in 2D image analysis, and the results showed that the difference in accuracy is within 10% ([Pau et al., 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B58)). In addition, an ML tool using MediaPipe simulated kinematic points, assuming shoulder, knee, hip, and ankle joints for artistic swimming analysis. Regarding the 2D kinematic simulation frames, the leg deviation angles were measured during execution and body position in preparation to aid officiating systems and performance monitoring ([Edriss et al., 2024b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B16)).

In a video performance analysis using an ML tool with MediaPipe, the knee angles of advanced and beginner pickleball players were measured during dink shots. This kinematic analysis assessed the differences in knee bending and body flexion between the two groups, suggesting an appropriate positioning formation and preparation for dinking ([Edriss et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B19)).

An application using MediaPipe, compared with Kinect, was used to measure knee angles for athletes under a motion test. The results showed the higher capacity of the MediaPipe framework in analyzing ACL injury risk by calculating lower limb kinematics through a smartphone ([Babouras et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B6)). However, a limitation of the MediaPipe source is the lack of ability to recognize multiple people in a frame ([Dong and Yan, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B14)).

### 3.3 AlphaPose

AlphaPose is an open-source tool that provides PE by detecting 25 keypoints. It was developed by the Chinese University of Hong Kong ([Fang et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B21)). Like OpenPose, AlphaPose provides a high keypoint detection rate and is highly interchangeable with ML models for biomechanical PE parameters like ground reaction forces ([Mundt et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B54)).

This framework is used in various ways, including gait and player kinematic analyses. For example, in gait analysis, participants walked at different speeds, and their estimated poses were captured using AlphaPose ([Wei et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B77)). Additionally, AlphaPose captured accurate skeleton PE of badminton players to classify their movements. These results achieved an 80% prediction accuracy, effectively analyzing the sequential nature of badminton actions ([Liang and Nyamasvisva, 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B45)).

Several researchers are working on PE framework development through the DL tool, such as YOLO ([Yang et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B82); [Zhao et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B85)). Although the validity of AlphaPose is sufficient, its accuracy compared to the data of other frameworks is considered. For example, a study compared MediaPipe BlazePose and AlphaPose with Vicon MoCap as the reference standard in gait joint kinematics analysis. This study emphasized that MediaPipe shows a lower mean square error (RMSE), indicating more accurate joint kinematic measurements. However, AlphaPose showed greater variability with a higher range of motion and RMSE ([Hulleck et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B34)).

### 3.4 DensePose

DensePose is a PE model developed by Facebook AI Research that maps human pixels in an image to the body’s 3D surface ([Gu et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B26); [Lovanshi and Tiwari, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B47); [Mahajan et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B49)). The advantages of DensePose, compared to other frameworks, are its perfect ability for multi-person recognition and its capability to estimate the body by keypoints or mesh ([Güler et al., 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B28); [Guler and Kokkinos, 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B27); [Zhang et al., 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B84)). DensePose is effective for applications in augmented reality, virtual try-on, and immersive human-body interaction scenarios ([Islam et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B36); [Zhu and Song, 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B86)). Athletes’ biomechanical and kinematic analyses can be conducted by designing a 2D PE from videos using DensePose, which is pre-trained on the COCO keypoint dataset. For monocular 3D PE, MotionAGFormer, pre-trained on the Human3.6M dataset, can be utilized. DensePose requires more technical skills to set up due to its powerful GPU resources and custom code for mesh mapping. Studies indicate that joint angular measurements obtained through DensePose also provide reliable data ([Hellstén et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B31); [Suzuki et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B73)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739)4 Discussion

Many researchers believe future sports motion studies will rely on markerless motion analysis systems ([Ismail et al., 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B37)). Therefore, much research highlighted the accuracy and reliability of the body pose simulation device and software in the kinematic analysis procedures ([Clark et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B9)), particularly for motions within a single plane. Mainly, the articles validated body simulation tools by gold-standard IMUs or MoCaps such as Vicon or OptiTrack, comparing quantitative methods like RMSE in joint angles and joint position errors. Some studies applied qualitative validation, such as expert visual assessment or usability scoring. However, high limitations exist because 2D PE restricts their ability to capture out-of-plane movements, such as joint flexion or rotation, as they lack depth information ([Pfister et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B59); [Annino et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B3)). Additionally, proper setup requires careful camera or device setup procedures to reduce their limitation ([Yang and Park, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B81)). Plus, PE accuracy depends on video quality, frame rates, and environmental conditions (outdoor, indoor, or natural or artificial lights), with studies showing varying OpenPose performance across different scenarios ([Song and Chen, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B71)).

Despite these drawbacks, 2D PE methods are beneficial due to affordability, ease of use, and relatively simple setup compared to 3D systems such as Vicon ([Menychtas et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B51)). Regarding the investigation aims, the camera and device can be set preferably if the motions are in the same plane, and it is beneficial to use the 2D PE methods to assess clinical or physical kinematic or biomechanical aspects ([Gozlan et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B25); [Hamill et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B29); [Winter, 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B78)).

Regarding the articles, each hardware and software tool has limitations. Kinect and RealSense are constrained by lighting conditions, occlusions, and limited field of view, especially in dynamic environments. ZED cameras may require more computational resources. OpenPose and MediaPipe rely heavily on camera angles and lighting and may struggle with occlusions or out-of-plane movements. AlphaPose exhibits higher RMSE and variability in certain tasks, while DensePose requires significant computational resources. While these hardware and software tools can function independently, leveraging RGB video and PE software (for example, Kinect with OpenPose or ZED with MediaPipe) offers a simple way to obtain 3D body landmarks and points of interest for the upper and lower body analysis, with high accuracy ([Ramasubramanian et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B63); [Liu and Chang, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B46)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739)5 Conclusion

PE software has strengths compared to others; thus, selecting the best framework is not straightforward. For instance, some research illustrated MediaPipe’s advantage over OpenPose in offering lower deviation in keypoints detection, especially in feet and wrists, along with faster runtime ([Latyshev et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B42)). On the other hand, another study emphasizes OpenPose’s superiority over MediaPipe BlazePose in accurately detecting clinically relevant keypoints closer to anatomical joint centers ([Mroz et al., 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B53)). In conclusion, while both models show promise, further improvements are necessary, and future studies will increasingly rely on AI-based markerless PE tools.

These methods provide a cost-effective and practical solution for studies focusing on movements confined to a single plane. They are particularly beneficial for assessing clinical, physical, and kinematic or biomechanical parameters when high precision across multiple planes is not required ([Stenum et al., 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B72)). Moreover, AI-based 2D-to-3D PE techniques are a fast-developing method to reduce these limitations, further expanding the potential applications of 2D systems ([Fortini et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12378739#B22)). We suggest that future studies aim to evaluate protocols and integrate vision sensors with PE framework software to bridge the gap in the development and validation of the 2D-to-3D PE device in real-world sports, thereby accessing biomedical data such as joint angles and providing real-time feedback.

This is a mini review article published in Frontiers in Physiology (2025) by Edriss, Romagnoli, et al., examining commercial vision sensors and AI-based pose estimation (PE) frameworks for markerless motion analysis in sports and exercise.

**Hardware (Vision Sensors) Covered:**
- **Microsoft Kinect (K1 2010, K2 2014):** Uses IR emitter, IR camera, and RGB camera for depth sensing. K2 offers better joint estimation accuracy and occlusion handling. Validated for gait analysis in the sagittal plane. Limited in measuring internal/external angular rotations. Error range: ~10°–20°.
- **StereoLabs ZED Camera (ZED 2015, ZED2 2019, ZED2i 2021):** Dual high-resolution lenses for depth information. Higher performance at distances >3m. Integrates with Nuitrack and MediaPipe. Error range: ~5°–15°.
- **Intel RealSense (D400, L515, T265):** Combines RGB imaging with depth perception. Outperforms infrared-based systems like Kinect in varied lighting. Valid for close-range tracking (<3m). Error range: ~10°–20°.

**Software (Pose Estimation Models) Covered:**
- **OpenPose (CMU):** 2D PE, detects 25 keypoints. Used for running, baseball, tennis, taekwondo, basketball analysis. Accuracy depends on video quality, lighting, environment. Good multi-person support. Error: ~5°–15°.
- **MediaPipe (Google):** Includes BlazePose detecting 33 keypoints. Fastest runtime, low memory, suitable for mobile apps. Lower error than AlphaPose in some studies. Limited multi-person recognition. Error: <10°.
- **AlphaPose (CUHK):** Detects 25 keypoints. Used for gait and badminton analysis. Higher RMSE and variability compared to MediaPipe. Error: ~15°–25°.
- **DensePose (Facebook AI):** Maps pixels to 3D body surface using mesh. Ideal for multi-person, AR/VR applications. Requires significant GPU resources. Error: ~10°–20°.

**Key Conclusions:**
- 2D systems offer affordable, easy-to-use solutions but struggle with out-of-plane movements and environmental factors.
- Combining vision sensors with AI-based PE frameworks (e.g., Kinect + OpenPose, ZED + MediaPipe) offers a promising path for 3D analysis.
- Selection depends on application: MediaPipe for speed and mobile use, OpenPose for multi-person and anatomical accuracy, DensePose for VR/AR.
- Future studies should focus on integrating vision sensors with PE software for 2D-to-3D pose estimation in real-world sports settings.

Nov 24, 2024

Feb 2, 2026

**Written by:** Maryam Rajaei

**Reviewed by:** Boshra Rajaei, PhD

Athletic performance optimization traditionally relies on subjective visual assessments by coaches. Manual biomechanical analysis requires expensive laboratory equipment and specialized expertise, making comprehensive movement analysis inaccessible to most athletes.

Traditional coaching methods struggle to capture subtle biomechanical deficiencies that impact performance, while quantitative data remains confined to elite training facilities with motion capture systems. This gap between elite and amateur training resources constrains performance improvement across all competitive levels.

Pose estimation wih AI changed this landscape by providing accurate digital representations of athletes in action, mapping key body joints to create virtual skeletons that reveal biomechanical dynamics from standard video footage.

This article goes through how pose estimation technology works, the core algorithms enabling sports analysis, and applications across athletic disciplines.

Finding human faces in images regardless of their different shapes, orientations, sizes, colors and occlusion.

![Pose](https://cdn3.saiwa.ai/Events/pose_estimation_cta_featured_image_86e7885e_721b_4089_ac00_6735fe230731_b8c1633413.jpg)](https://saiwa.ai/app/detection/pose-estimation-1/)

## What is Human Pose Estimation?

[Pose estimation](https://saiwa.ai/app/detection/pose-estimation-1/) is a computer vision technique that identifies critical body points such as elbows, knees, wrists, and ankles to create detailed skeletal representations of human movement. The technology analyzes images or video to locate these key joints, connecting them to form a biomechanical model that reflects posture and motion dynamics accurately.

This digital skeleton enables quantitative analysis of movement patterns, turning subjective coaching observations into measurable data. The versatility of pose estimation spans multiple sports, capturing everything from golf swing mechanics to swimming stroke efficiency.

Read Also: [Skeleton detection online](https://saiwa.ai/landing/skeleton-detection-online/)

## How Pose Estimation Works in Sports

Pose estimation in sports combines advanced AI and computer vision to convert ordinary video footage into precise biomechanical data. Here’s how the process works:  
Joint Detection and Skeleton Mapping:

AI algorithms identify key body landmarks such as elbows, knees, hips, and ankles straight from video frames. These points are connected to form a digital skeleton that mirrors the athlete’s actual movement in real time.

![pose-estimation-in-sports.1.webp](https://cdn3.saiwa.ai/pose_estimation_in_sports_1_8a2369f0d9.webp)

Source: [Freepik](https://www.freepik.com/premium-photo/young-female-athlete-exercising-with-barbell-gym_128189352.htm)

### Spatiotemporal Analysis:

Deep learning models like Spatiotemporal Transformers analyze both spatial (body position) and temporal (movement over time) data simultaneously. This enables accurate tracking of dynamic athletic actions such as swings, kicks, or jumps.

### Sequential Motion Tracking:

[Temporal Convolutional Networks](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/temporal-convolutional-network) (TCNs) process frame sequences to capture how each joint moves across time, revealing subtle technique variations often missed by manual observation.

### Skeletal Relationship Modeling:

[Using Graph Convolutional Networks](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/deep-learning/graph-convolutional-networks-gcns-architectural-insights-and-applications/) (GCNs), the body is represented as a graph where joints are nodes and bones are edges. This structure helps the system understand complex joint interactions, even when some body parts are hidden or occluded.

### 3D Pose Reconstruction:

Multiple camera views or deep neural estimation enable 3D reconstruction of the athlete’s motion, translating 2D images into fully dimensional biomechanical models for precise angle and posture analysis.

## Top Use Cases of Pose Estimation in Sports

Pose estimation transforms multiple aspects of sports performance and athlete development:

* **Technique Refinement and Analysis:** Coaches gain detailed insights into movement mechanics across sports, identifying subtle flaws impacting performance.
* **Biomechanical Risk Assessment:** Analyzing joint and limb movement detects patterns that may cause injuries, such as gait analysis in running that identifies knee injury risk factors. Early identification enables corrective interventions before injuries occur, protecting athlete health and career longevity.
* **Rehabilitation Monitoring:** Post-injury recovery tracking ensures athletes regain proper movement patterns before returning to competition. Pose estimation documents recovery progress objectively, preventing premature returns that risk re-injury while confirming readiness for full activity resumption.

## Sports Using Pose Estimation Technology

3D pose estimation is redefining how coaches and athletes refine their movement mechanics.

* **Golf**: In golf, it helps analyze swings to detect inefficiencies in rotation and posture, leading to smoother, more powerful strokes.
* **Swimming**: In swimming, it monitors body alignment and stroke rhythm to minimize drag, improve efficiency, and boost overall speed. By tracking every angle and joint in real time, the technology provides objective insights that were once possible only with complex motion labs.
* **Football**: When it comes to performance, footballers and coaches constantly seek ways to master precision and power in their kicks. 3D pose estimation technology helps analyze and refine every aspect of a player’s movement and balance them .
* **Baseball and Basketball**:  Basketball shooting analysis provides feedback on mechanics to improve accuracy and consistency. Baseball pitching analysis examines arm angles and release points.

## Advantages and Limitations

Every performance analysis system presents distinct strengths and challenges that organizations must evaluate when integrating technology into athletic training and competition environments.

### Technical Limitations

Implementation challenges exist despite pose estimation's transformative potential:

* **Occlusion and Visibility Issues:** When body parts are hidden behind other objects, limbs, or athletes, detection accuracy decreases significantly. Sports with close contact or equipment obscuring joints present particular challenges for reliable tracking.
* **Computational Resource Requirements**: Real-time processing demands significant computing power, potentially limiting deployment on standard equipment without GPU acceleration or cloud processing infrastructure supporting the analysis pipeline.
* **Movement Complexity Challenges:** Highly dynamic, rapid movements common in many sports can blur imagery or create tracking difficulties, reducing accuracy during the most critical performance moments requiring precise analysis.
* **Training Data Limitations:** Algorithms trained predominantly on certain body types, sports, or movement patterns may perform inconsistently across diverse populations or less-represented athletic disciplines, requiring domain-specific model refinement.

### Primary Advantages

AI-powered pose estimation provides substantial benefits for athletic development:

* **Accessibility and Affordability**: Standard video footage replaces expensive laboratory equipment, democratizing biomechanical analysis for athletes at all competitive levels without requiring specialized facilities or expertise.
* **Comprehensive Movement Capture**: Technology tracks full-body kinematics simultaneously, providing holistic biomechanical understanding rather than focusing on isolated body segments, revealing compensatory patterns across kinetic chains.
* **Scalable Analysis Capacity**: Automated processing handles multiple athletes or extended training sessions efficiently, supporting team-wide performance monitoring and longitudinal studies tracking development over seasons.
* **Immediate Feedback Generation:** Real-time analysis capabilities enable instant technique corrections during training, accelerating skill acquisition and reinforcing proper movement patterns before errors become habitual.

## Transform Your Movement, Unlock Peak Performance With Frame

Fraime’s Pose Estimation service brings advanced biomechanical analysis directly to athletes, coaches, and performance specialists without the need for motion-capture labs or specialized hardware. By combining OpenPose, MediaPipe, and our recent [ViTPose](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/vitpose) transformer-based models, Fraime delivers highly accurate multi-person keypoint detection from any standard video streams.

Users gain access to real-time kinematic tracking, automatic joint-angle measurement, movement-pattern comparison, and customizable analytics dashboards (upon request) tailored to their sport. Whether you aim to refine technique, prevent injury, or quantify performance progress, Fraime transforms raw footage into actionable insights, making elite-level biomechanics accessible to everyone.

## Conclusion

Pose estimation technology fundamentally transforms athletic performance analysis by converting subjective visual assessments into objective, quantifiable data. Applications are technique refinement, injury prevention, personalized training development, and remote From a technical standpoint, what sets modern pose estimation apart is not only its precision and accuracy but its scalability across real-world sports environments.

With transformer-based models like ViTPose capturing global context and bottom-up systems like [OpenPose](https://saiwa.ai/blog/openpose-pose-estimation/) excelling in multi-athlete scenes, we can now analyze movement in situations that were previously too dynamic, crowded, or unpredictable for traditional motion-capture methods.

In my experience, the true breakthrough lies in unifying these algorithms within platforms like Fraime—where raw joint detections are converted into meaningful metrics, comparative reports, and corrective feedback loops. This convergence of AI and sports science is redefining how athletes understand their bodies, enabling a level of technical refinement that was once possible only in elite biomechanics laboratories.

## Abstract

The current investigation delineates the efficacy of AI-facilitated detection of athletic postures within the realm of sports training. Employing a synthesis of literature review and empirical methodologies, data were amassed and scrutinized, affirming the study’s validity. The salient outcomes are manifold: (1) The frame difference algorithm efficaciously discerns inter-frame variances, evidencing pronounced adaptability and robustness, thereby enabling the recognition of weightlifting postures. (2) Confronting the challenge of negligible inter-frame disparities inherent in the frame difference algorithm, the research introduces a novel detection technique predicated on the cumulative inter-frame differences, which precisely pinpoints regions of posture alteration in weightlifting athletes. (3) Leveraging the dynamic space model of optical flow, the study ascertains the directional channel predicated on optical flow trajectory analyses, facilitating the identification of three distinct weightlifting postures: squatting, descending, and standing. (4) In alignment with the distinctive postural attributes of weightlifting athletes, a human posture paradigm was formulated, and a BP neural network classifier was deployed for both training and evaluative purposes, culminating in the successful differentiation of athlete from non-athlete entities within the training milieu. (5) The application of AI in posture recognition was extended to the scrutiny of pivotal postures and motions in weightlifting athletes, with experimental findings revealing a 98.21% accuracy rate in the recognition of force-exertion postures via the inter-frame difference method, and a flawless 100% accuracy in the identification of the apex and squatting postures. The enumeration of detected postures—encompassing knee extension, knee flexion, force application, squatting, and standing—through the poselet keyframe extraction approach, corresponded with the video count. Prospectively, AI’s role in athletic posture detection promises to augment coaches’ and athletes’ comprehension of their proficiencies and deficiencies, thereby steering training refinement and bolstering both the efficacy of training and the athletes’ caliber.

**Keywords**: Sports Training; Athletic Postures; AI-Based Detection

## 1. Introduction

In the vanguard of intelligent sports, the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the analysis of athletic postures heralds a paradigm shift from conventional training methodologies, offering a potent instrument for the precise delineation of athletes’ stances. Particularly, under the ambit of China’s aspirations to excel in both sports and AI, the fusion of sports training with AI-centric detection technologies has tightened. This convergence has garnered scholarly interest, prompting extensive and intensive investigations that furnish theoretical underpinnings for the pragmatic deployment of AI in discerning athletic postures by coaches, thereby refining training regimens and amplifying training efficacy. In practical applications, AI’s ubiquity spans military fitness, educational sports programs, and professional athletic training, notably spotlighted in the Olympics via 3D tracking technologies that unveil nuances beyond human perception and facilitating intelligent adjudication through computer vision, effectively serving as a digital coach. Theoretically, the formulation of an embedded AI detection and recognition system, coupled with the utilization of BP neural network classifiers, sets the stage for posture detection. This inquiry augments the theoretical corpus and proffers robust academic support. Practically, the integration of AI in identifying weightlifting postures during training aligns with diverse training contexts, enabling coaches to rectify incorrect techniques through AI-assisted video analytics. This research also acts as a beacon for other sports mentors, advocating the adaptable application of AI in posture detection tailored to specific sporting disciplines and training objectives, thus ensuring training potency and contributing to the burgeoning prowess of China’s sports domain.

The scholarly landscape of posture detection, both domestically and internationally, has been marked by significant advancements. Ren Wenqiang (2016) posited in his master’s thesis that polyhedral robots are congruent with the exploratory demands of contemporary times, with robotic technology and a universal kinematic model for polyhedral robots facilitating posture detection in intricate environments [1]. Zhang Shijie (2017) elucidated in his master’s thesis that the application of the deepskeleton network to extract skeletal data from weightlifters’ videos is instrumental in pinpointing key postures, thereby aiding coaches in the training process [2]. Li Xiuzhi and Li Jiahao et al. (2020) discerned that deploying deep learning for interactive human-computer posture detection predominantly involves a dual-network architecture for service robots, which is pivotal in detecting the quintessential grasping posture, effectuating precise calculations, and pinpointing the optimal grasping locus, culminating in the consummation of posture grasping [3]. Hou Baichuan and Zhou Li (2021) demonstrated that the YOLOv4 network structure’s utilization for individual posture detection in educational settings entails a sequence of image data procurement, dataset compilation, training, pre-trained model development, and framing operations, thereby ensuring an accurate comprehension of classroom postures [4]. Han Meilin (2019) discovered that the requisites for athletes’ efficient training necessitate enhanced BP neural network algorithms, which are adept at accurately identifying human postures, thus contributing to the augmentation of sports skills [5].

Internationally, scholars have embarked on multidimensional human posture detection research predicated on various scenarios, initially employing deep learning to dissect issues related to human posture detection. Toshev (2014) expounded that the DeepPose model is proficient in predicting joint coordinates [6]. Tompson (2014) revealed that the optimization of human posture joint points is achieved through the utilization of stacked two-dimensional Gaussian functions, engendering heatmaps, and thereby fulfilling joint point regression tasks [7]. Pfister (2015) ascertained that the enhancement of heatmaps necessitates video image predictions of contiguous frames, which are facilitated by optical flow data, buttressed by the Flow Convent model [8]. Newell (2016) highlighted that the amalgamation of network structures and the employment of convolutional residual networks to procure spatial features, in conjunction with the integration of multi-scale feature channels, significantly bolsters target detection efficiency [9]. With the advent of motion posture detection in the sports domain, research endeavors have progressively shifted towards AI-based posture detection in sports.

Pertaining to AI-based Posture Detection Research: Gu Mengmeng (2017) deduced in her master’s thesis that the KNN algorithm’s application to treadmill monitoring videos, encompassing object tracking and image processing, facilitates the recognition of human postures, rectifies running postures, and enhances the impact of running on physiological functions [10]. Ke Yu (2021) indicated that the procurement of images of athletic postures via embedded devices proffers informational support for AI-driven athletic posture detection, which, in turn, provides feedback to athletes, enabling them to adjust their movements in accordance with AI posture detection outcomes, thereby achieving efficacious and qualitative exercise [11]. Post-2020, scholars such as Ma Zhongyu have concentrated on 3D human posture estimation and action recognition predicated on deep learning [12-14]. International scholars have pioneered AI posture detection research, establishing a comprehensive theoretical framework and yielding reliable research findings. Some American researchers have delved into AI-accelerated computing platforms, proffering novel insights for the evolution and application of AI-specific training apparatuses. Concurrently, others have investigated AI-based posture detection models, utilizing model data analytics to steer correct postural alignments.

Within the scholarly domain, domestic research on posture detection and its AI-enhanced counterpart commenced belatedly, characterized by a nascent theoretical framework and a paucity of depth and specificity in model architecture and algorithmic support. Conversely, international research on AI in sports posture detection has not adequately accounted for cross-regional and cross-cultural considerations. This investigation, cognizant of national imperatives, harnesses AI to discern athletic postures in sports training, building on antecedent studies to elucidate the theoretical underpinnings and delineate precise methodologies for integrating AI posture detection within sports training paradigms. The objective is to meticulously detect athletic postures via AI within the training context, rectify postures based on analytical outcomes, and thereby enhance training efficacy. Methodologically, the study amalgamates literature review and experimental techniques. The exposition is structured into four segments: an introduction, an exposition of the research methodology, a presentation of results and discussion, and a concluding synthesis. The research’s impact is manifold, bolstering the empirical exploration of AI in athletic posture detection for sports training, establishing a bedrock for future inquiries; methodically pinpointing and rectifying movement inaccuracies through AI detection, steering the enactment of precise movements, and amplifying training productivity; and enriching the integration of sports training with AI posture detection, fostering intelligent training modalities, and propelling athletes’ performance enhancement.

## 2. Research Methods

### **2.1 Frame Difference Method**

In addressing the computational exigencies local to AI-enhanced athletic posture detection for sports training, a system capable of offline detection and recognition has been instituted. This system is tailored to satisfy the environmental perception and interactive requisites of weightlifting training [12]. The integration of microprocessor technology within portable smart devices has been executed to curtail the expenses associated with AI detection, thereby catering to the demand for cost-effective, high-performance AI detection and the precise discernment of weightlifting athletes’ maneuvers. Consequently, the establishment of an embedded AI detection and recognition system platform has been realized. The constructed architecture, delineated in [Figure 1](#img-1), encompasses three principal components: the procurement of imagery, the processing thereof, and the subsequent output of processed images.

|  |
| --- |
| [Draft Wang 260601743-image1.png](/public/File:Draft_Wang_260601743-image1.png) |

The architecture depicted in the [Figure 1](#img-1) demonstrates the process of capturing video footage of weightlifting athletes during training sessions using a camera. The video images are then subject to initial frame processing, where the frame difference algorithm is employed. As the weightlifting athletes perform different movements in the video, changes occur in the grayscale values of adjacent frames. These changes are calculated by determining the absolute values of the differences. Following this, a threshold analysis is conducted to identify the movements and postures of the athletes, thereby achieving AI-powered athletic posture detection [13]. The application of the frame difference algorithm allows for the convenient acquisition of inter-frame differences. It is highly adaptable to the weightlifting training environment and, due to its robustness, can effectively recognize the postures of weightlifting movements.

### 2.2 Frame difference accumulation method

In the milieu of weightlifting training, the backdrop remains static, allowing for the athletes’ maneuvers to transpire within a predefined vicinity. This staticity ensures that AI-driven posture detection is sharply attuned to the athletes’ foreground activities [14]. Subsequent experimental inquiries proceed as delineated: Commencing with data sampling within the detection zone, followed by the implementation of optical flow tracking. Subsequently, the tracking outcomes inform the segmentation of channels and the execution of pertinent computations. Culminating in the discernment of pivotal posture frames within weightlifting sequences, these frames demarcate the training regimen into distinct stages. The methodology underpinning the detection and analysis of athletic postures throughout the experimental phase is encapsulated in [Figure 2](#img-2).
