The sliding window method is used to divide the continuous time series signal into fixed length samples for model input. The window length is set to 100 frames (corresponding to 2.0 s at 50 Hz sampling rate), and the step size between successive windows is 50 frames (corresponding to 1.0 s), which results in 50% overlap between adjacent windows. This configuration can achieve a good balance between capturing enough action discrimination timing information and generating sufficient training samples. It must be noted that exactly the same sliding window parameters are consistently applied in all experiments, including cross validation with one subject and cross device generalization test, so as to ensure the fairness and reproducibility of the evaluation.

### Dynamic graph structure construction

To model the spatial connections between limb segments during human movement, the eight wearable sensor nodes \(\:\text{V}{={}{\text{v}}\_{{1}}{,}{\text{v}}\_{\text{2}}{,{\cdots},}{{v}}\_{\text{8}}}\) are mapped to the vertex set of graph \(\:\text{G}\text{=(}\text{V}\text{,E,}\text{A}\text{)}\), corresponding to the following anatomical locations: head, thorax, waist, left upper arm, right upper arm, left forearm, right forearm, and left thigh. Initial connectivity relationships are defined based on the human skeletal topology prior, and a basic adjacency matrix \(\:{\text{A}}^{\text{(0)}}{\in}{{0,1}{{}}}^{\text{N}\times\text{N}}\) is constructed. If a node \(\:{\text{v}}\_{\text{i}}\) is anatomically connected to \(\:{\text{v}}\_{\text{j}}\), then \(\:{\text{A}}\_{\text{ij}}^{\text{(0)}}\text{=1}\) is assigned, and otherwise 0. In order to overcome the sensitivity of the fixed graph structure to the differences in individual sensor layouts, a learnable edge weight matrix \(\:\text{W}\in{\text{R}}^{\text{N}\times\text{N}}\) is introduced, where the element \(\:{\text{W}}\_{\text{ij}}\) represents the potential connection strength from node \(\:{\text{v}}\_{\text{i}}\) to \(\:{\text{v}}\_{\text{j}}\)[24](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR24 "Tan, X. et al. Improving graph convolutional network with learnable edge weights and edge-Node Co-Embedding for graph anomaly Detection[J]. Sensors 24 (8), 2591 (2024).")[25](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR25 "Afsar, M. M. et al. Body-worn sensors for recognizing physical sports activities in exergaming via deep learning model[J]. Ieee Access. 11, 12460–12473 (2023)."). The learnable adjacency matrix is defined as:

$$\:\begin{array}{c}{A}\_{\text{learnable}}={A}^{\left(0\right)}+W\end{array}$$

(5)

In formula ([5](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#Equ5)), \(\:\text{W}\) is used as a trainable parameter to participate in back-propagation optimization, achieving data-driven adaptation of the topological structure. The learnable weight matrix \(\:\text{W}\) is not constrained to be symmetric, allowing the model full flexibility in learning. This formula ensures the physical rationality of the initial skeletal structure, laying the foundation for subsequent data-driven refinement. To prevent over-connection and overfitting, a sparse regularization strategy is implemented for \(\:{A}\_{\text{learnable}}\). A Top-K selection mechanism is used to retain only the K non-diagonal elements with the largest absolute values in \(\:\text{|}{A}\_{\text{learnable}}\text{|}\), and the rest are set to zero[26](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR26 "Huang, W. et al. The convolutional neural networks training with channel-selectivity for human activity recognition based on sensors[J]. IEEE J. Biomedical Health Inf. 25 (10), 3834–3843 (2021)."),[27](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR27 "Navakauskas, D. & Dumpis, M. $$\:\begin{array}{c}{A}\_{sparse}\text{=}{\text{S}}\_{\text{K}}\text{(}{A}\_{\text{learnable}}\text{)}\text{=}{A}\_{\text{learnable}}{\odot}\text{I}\text{(}{\mid}{A}\_{\text{learnable}}{\mid}\in{\text{Top}}\_{\text{K}}\text{(}{\mid}{{A}\_{\text{learnable}}}\_{\text{i}{\neq}\text{j}}{\mid}\text{)}\text{)}\end{array}$$

(6)

In formula ([6](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#Equ6)), \(\:{\odot}\) is the Hadamard product, \(\:\text{I}\)(⋅) is the indicator function, and Ktop is set to 2 N to maintain sparse connection density. \(\:{A}\_{\text{learnable}}\:\)ensure that both initial prior knowledge and learned data-driven adjustments contribute to the final topology. To ensure compatibility with the subsequent Chebyshev spectral graph convolution, we explicitly enforce symmetry on the learned topology. After Top-K sparsification, we explicitly symmetrize \(\:{A}\_{\text{s}\text{p}\text{a}\text{r}\text{s}\text{e}}\):

$$\:\begin{array}{c}{A}\_{\text{s}\text{y}\text{m}}=\frac{1}{2}({A}\_{\text{s}\text{p}\text{a}\text{r}\text{s}\text{e}}+{A}\_{\text{s}\text{p}\text{a}\text{r}\text{s}\text{e}}^{{\top\:}})\end{array}$$

(7)

This operation guarantees that \(\:{A}\_{\text{s}\text{y}\text{m}}\) is symmetric, forming an undirected graph. Next, a self-loop is added to ensure the propagation of node self-information, forming the augmented matrix \(\\hat :{A}\), as defined in Eq. ([8](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#Equ8)). $$\hat A = {A\_{{\text{sym}}}} + {I\_N}$$

(8)

In formula ([8](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#Equ8)), \(\:{I}\_{N}\) is the identity matrix of size N×N. The final normalized adjacency matrix is:

$${{\tilde A = }}{{{\tilde D}}^{{\text{ - 1/2}}}}\hat A{{{\tilde D}}^{{\text{ - 1/2}}}}$$

(9)

This dynamic graph construction mechanism enables the model to automatically optimize inter-node connectivity during training, adapting to individual sensor deployment deviations and providing adaptive topological support for subsequent spatiotemporal feature extraction.

### Adaptive Spatiotemporal feature extraction network

To effectively model the complex spatiotemporal dependencies in wearable sensor data, a deep, stacked adaptive spatiotemporal graph convolutional network backbone is constructed. This backbone consists of four cascaded ST-GCN layers, each containing a spatial graph convolution module and a temporal convolution module. This allows for hierarchical abstraction of inter-Sensor node coordinated motion patterns and the temporal dynamics of motion sequences[28](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR28 "Huang, Z. et al. Motion-driven Spatial and Temporal adaptive high-resolution graph convolutional networks for skeleton-based action recognition[J]. IEEE Trans. Circuits Syst. Video Technol. 33 (4), 1868–1883 (2022)."),[29](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR29 "Sun, B. et al. Adaptive Spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks for motor imagery classification[J]. IEEE. Signal. Process. Lett. 28, 219–223 (2021)."). Spatial graph convolution uses Chebyshev polynomials to approximate graph convolution to efficiently capture local structural information between nodes in the spectral domain. Compared with other graph neural network methods, this choice has significant advantages: high computational efficiency: Chebyshev approximation converts the complex spectral domain filtering into recursive operations within the k-order local neighborhood on the graph, and its computational complexity is linearly related to the number of edges of the graph, avoiding the expensive matrix factorization required for direct graph Fourier transform. A clear local receptive field: The K-order Chebyshev polynomial corresponds to the information of aggregated K-hop neighbors, which makes the receptive field of the model clear and controllable, and is very suitable for graphs like the human skeleton with a clear hierarchical structure, enabling precise capture of the cooperative relationship from direct connections to second-order neighbors. Strong flexibility: It does not rely on a predefined normalized Laplacian matrix and can naturally be combined with the learnable adjacency matrix proposed in this paper to Sensor node optimize the topological structure of the graph and the filter parameters. Let the input feature of the \(\:\text{l}\) layer be \(\:{\text{H}}^{\text{(}\text{l}\text{)}}\in{\text{R}}^{\text{N}\times{\text{C}}\_{\text{in}}\times{T}}\), N be the number of nodes, \(\:{\text{C}}\_{\text{in}}\) be the number of input channels, and \(\:\text{T}\) be the time step. The symmetric normalized form of the normalized Laplacian matrix \(\:\stackrel{\text{~}}{\text{A}}\) is:

$$\:\begin{array}{c}\stackrel{\text{~}}{\text{L}}\text{=}{\text{I}}\_{\text{N}}\text{-}\stackrel{\text{~}}{\text{A}}\end{array}$$

(10)

This maps the spectrum of \(\:\stackrel{\text{~}}{\text{L}}\) to the interval [0,2]. For numerical stability in the Chebyshev approximation, this spectrum is scaled to [− 1,1] via:

$${{\hat L = }}\frac{{{2}}}{{{{{\lambda }}\_{{{max}}}}}}{{\tilde L - }}{{\text{I}}\_{{N}}}$$

(11)

In formula ([11](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#Equ11)), \(\:{\lambda}\_{\text{max}}\) is the maximum eigenvalue of \(\:\stackrel{\text{~}}{\text{L}}\). To ensure the stability of the Chebyshev spectral convolution, before model training begins, a one-time \(\:{\lambda}\_{\text{max}}\) estimate is performed on the corresponding normalized Laplacian matrix using the power iteration method based on the initial adjacency matrix constructed using the skeleton prior. This estimate serves as the initial value. During the dynamic training phase, a strategy combining periodic updates and exponential sliding averages is employed to track the evolution of the graph topology: \(\:{\lambda}\_{\text{max}}\) is re-estimated every 10 training epochs using the power iteration method on the current normalized Laplacian matrix. This result is then updated with the historical values using an exponential sliding average (EMA) to obtain the smoothed global \(\:{\lambda}\_{\text{max}}\). While this periodic estimation introduces a small computational overhead, it is significantly cheaper than performing a full eigendecomposition at every step, making the approach feasible for end-to-end training. To further analyze the cost-benefit trade-off of this dynamic estimation strategy, we consider an alternative approximation proposed by ChebNet, this method fixes the upper bound of the spectrum to \(\:{\lambda}\_{\text{max}}\) ≈2, which simplifies the computation and eliminates the need for any eigenvalue estimation during training[30](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR30 "Defferrard, M., Bresson, X. & Vandergheynst, P. Convolutional neural networks on graphs with fast localized spectral filtering[J]. Adv. Neural. Inf. Process. Syst., 29 (2016)."). This adjacency matrix is constructed by adding an initial skeleton prior to a learnable weight matrix, maintaining sparsity through Top-K sparsification. Subsequently, self-loops are added and symmetric normalization is performed to prepare the graph for stable convolution operations. Temporal convolution is then used to capture the temporal dynamics of the action, and batch normalization and ReLU activation are combined to output high-level features. During backpropagation, the loss gradient simultaneously updates the network weights and adjacency matrix parameters, achieving end-to-end Sensor node optimization of topology and feature extraction. This allows the model to adapt to individual differences during training and gradually focus on the coordinated motion paths between key Sensor node.

### Topology-feature sensor node optimization mechanism

To achieve the coordinated adaptation of graph structure and feature representation, this paper constructs a topology-feature Sensor node optimization framework that incorporates the learnable adjacency matrix parameters \(\:{W}\epsilon{\text{R}}^{{N}\times\text{N}}\) and the ST-GCN backbone network weights \(\theta\) into a unified end-to-end optimization objective. Assume that the model input is the mth sample \(\:{\text{X}}^{\text{(}\text{m}\text{)}}\in{\text{R}}^{\text{N}\times\text{C}\times\text{T}}\), corresponding to the real action category label \(\:{\text{y}}^{{(}\text{m}\text{)}}{\epsilon{0,1}{\text{}}}^{\text{K}}\), the forward propagation output is the predicted probability distribution \(\:\hat {{\text{y}}}^{\text{(}\text{m}\text{)}}\text{=}\text{f}\text{(}{\text{X}}^{\text{(}\text{m}\text{)}}{;{\theta},W){\in}[0,1}{\text{]}}^{\text{K}}\), and \(\:\text{f}\)(⋅) is the overall network mapping function. The optimization objective is the regularized multi-class cross entropy loss function:

$$\:\begin{array}{c}{\text{L}}\_{\text{total}}\text{=}\frac{\text{1}}{\text{M}}\sum\:\_{\text{m}\text{=1}}^{\text{M}}{\text{L}}\_{\text{ce}}^{\text{(}\text{m}\text{)}}\text{+}\lambda{\parallel}W{{\parallel}}\_{\text{F}}^{\text{2}}\end{array}$$

(15)

In formula ([15](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#Equ15)), \(\:\text{M}\) is the batch size, \(\:{{\parallel}W}{{\parallel}}\_{\text{F}}^{\text{2}}\) is the Frobenius norm of the adjacency weight matrix, which is used to constrain the amplitude of \(\:\text{W}\) to prevent the topological parameters from diverging, and λ is the regularization coefficient. The classification loss term is:

$$\:\begin{array}{c}{\text{L}}\_{\text{ce}}^{\text{(}\text{m}\text{)}}\text{=}\text{-}\sum\:\_{\text{k}\text{=1}}^{\text{K}}{\text{y}}\_{\text{k}}^{\text{(}\text{m}\text{)}}\text{log}\hat {{\text{y}}}\_{\text{k}}^{\text{(}\text{m}\text{)}}\end{array}$$

(16)

During the backpropagation process, the gradient is simultaneously propagated back to \(\:\text{W}\) and \(\theta\) through the automatic differentiation system. Let the gradient of the loss function with respect to the learnable adjacency matrix be:

$$\:\begin{array}{\*{20}{c}}{\nabla {\rm{WLtotal}} = \frac{{\partial {{\rm{L}}\_{{\rm{ce}}}}}}{{\partial {\rm{A}}}}{\rm{\cdot}}\frac{{\partial {\rm{A}}}}{{\partial {\rm{W}}}} + {\rm{2}}\lambda {\rm{W}}}\end{array}$$

(17)

To maintain topological sparsity and enhance interpretability, a periodic structural sparsification strategy is introduced. The paper defines the effective connection set \(\:{{\text{E}}\_{eff}} = (i,j)\parallel {W\_{ij}}\mid> {t\_K}\), and \(\:{\tau}\_{\text{K}}\) as the top-K threshold. This operation is performed between gradient updates without interrupting the backpropagation path, ensuring that topological evolution focuses on the most discriminative cross-node dynamic coupling relationships. Through this Sensor node optimization mechanism, the model achieves data-driven topology self-correction during training: the initial prior-based skeleton graph is gradually optimized into a dynamic connection structure that adapts to individual sensor layouts and action semantics, improving robustness and generalization to cross-user posture variations.

### Classification head design and model training

Assume that the high-level spatiotemporal feature tensor output by the fourth-layer ST-GCN is \(\:\text{F}\in{\text{R}}^{\text{N}\times{\text{C}}^{{\prime\:}}\times{\text{T}}^{{\prime\:}}}\), N is the number of nodes, \(\:{\text{C}}^{{\prime\:}}\) is the channel dimension, and \(\:{\text{T}}^{{\prime\:}}\) is the time step after temporal convolution compression. To fuse the global spatiotemporal context information and generate a fixed-dimensional classification representation, a two-axis global average pooling (GAP) operation is used[33](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR33 "Li, J. et al. Multi-scale residual network model combined with global average pooling for action recognition[J]. Multimedia Tools Appl. 81 (1), 1375–1393 (2022)."),[34](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR34 "Tong, L. et al. A novel deep learning Bi-GRU-I model for real-time human activity recognition using inertial sensors[J]. IEEE Sens. J. 22 (6), 6164–6174 (2022)."):

$$\:\begin{array}{c}{\text{f}}\_{\text{gap}}{=}\frac{\text{1}}{\text{N}{\cdot}{\text{T}}^{{\prime\:}}}\sum\:\_{\text{i}\text{=1}}^{\text{N}}\sum\:\_{\text{t}\text{=1}}^{{\text{T}}^{{\prime\:}}}{\text{F}}\_{\text{i}t{,:,}\text{t}}\in{\text{R}}^{{\text{C}}^{{\prime\:}}}\end{array}$$

(18)

This operation reduces the dimensionality of the three-dimensional feature map to a single vector, effectively retaining the most discriminative cross-node and cross-time statistical features, while eliminating the dependence on the input time series length and enhancing the robustness of the model. A fully connected classification layer is connected for category mapping[35](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR35 "Kiran, S. et al. Multi-layered deep learning features fusion for human action recognition[J]. Comput. Mater. Contin. 69 (3), 4061–4075 (2021)."),[36](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR36 "Morshed, M. G. et al. Let the weight matrix \(\:{\text{W}}\_{\text{c}}\in{\text{R}}^{\text{K}\times{\text{C}}^{{\prime\:}}}\), the bias vector \(\:{\text{b}}\_{\text{c}}\in{\text{R}}^{\text{K}}\), and K be the number of sports action categories, then the logits output is:

$$\:\begin{array}{c}\text{z}\text{=}{\text{W}}\_{\text{c}}{\text{f}}\_{\text{gap}}\text{+}{\text{b}}\_{\text{c}}\in{\text{R}}^{\text{K}}\end{array}$$

(19)

The final category probability distribution is normalized by the Softmax function:

$$\:\begin{array}{c}\hat {{\text{y}}}\_{\text{k}}\text{=}\frac{\text{exp}\text{(}{\text{z}}\_{\text{k}}\text{)}}{\sum\:\_{\text{j}\text{=1}}^{\text{K}}\text{exp}\text{(}{\text{z}}\_{\text{j}}\text{)}}\text{,}\text{k}\text{=}\text{1,2}\text{,}\ldots\text{,}\text{K}\end{array}$$

One-Dimensional deep residual network with aggregated transformations for internet of things (IoT)-Enabled human activity recognition in an uncontrolled Environment[J]. Technologies 12 (12), p242 (2024)."),[38](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#ref-CR38 "Jiang, A., Ye, J. & SelfVis Self-supervised learning for human activity recognition based on area charts[J]. IEEE Trans. Emerg. Top. Comput. 13 (1), 196–206 (2024)."). The optimizer uses the adaptive moment estimator (Adam), and its parameter update mechanism is as follows: let the gradient of the t-th iteration be \(\:{\text{g}}\_{\text{t}}\text{=}{{\triangledown}}\_{\theta}{\text{L}}\_{\text{total}}\text{(}{\theta}\_{\text{t}\text{-1}}\text{)}\), and the first-order and second-order momentum be estimated as:

$$\:\begin{array}{c}{\text{m}}\_{\text{t}}{=}{\beta}\_{\text{1}}{\text{m}}\_{\text{t}\text{-1}}\text{+}\left(\text{1-}{\beta}\_{\text{1}}\right){\text{g}}\_{\text{t}}\end{array}$$

(21)

$$\:\begin{array}{c}{\text{v}}\_{\text{t}}\text{=}{\beta}\_{\text{2}}{\text{v}}\_{\text{t}\text{-1}}\text{+}\text{(}\text{1}\text{-}{\beta}\_{\text{2}}\text{)}{\text{g}}\_{\text{t}}^{\text{2}}\end{array}$$

(22)

After bias correction, the parameter update is:

$$\:\begin{array}{c}{\theta}\_{\text{t}}{=}{\theta}\_{\text{t}\text{-1}}{-}\eta\frac{\hat {{\text{m}}}\_{{t}}}{\sqrt{\hat {{\text{v}}}\_{\text{t}}}\text{+}{\epsilon}}\end{array}$$

(23)

η is the learning rate, β1 and β2 are momentum coefficients, and \(\epsilon\) is a numerical stabilization term. Gradients are independently calculated and parameters updated for each batch of samples. An early stopping mechanism is implemented during training to prevent overfitting: the classification accuracy of the validation set is monitored. If it does not improve for 15 consecutive epochs, training is terminated and the model parameters are rolled back to the optimal state. The model parameter settings are shown in Table [2](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#Tab2). All calculations are performed on the NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) based on the PyTorch deep learning framework. Graph convolution operations are implemented through custom modules in collaboration with PyTorch Geometric to ensure the differentiability of the dynamic adjacency matrix and efficient backpropagation. Figure [3](/articles/s41598-025-34288-6#Fig3) illustrates the overall process of the dynamic topology-adaptive ST-GCN proposed in this paper: The system takes raw motion data collected by eight wearable IMU sensors as input. After filtering, normalization, and sliding window segmentation, it constructs a dynamic human body graph. A learnable adjacency matrix is introduced to automatically optimize the connection weights between nodes. This matrix is Sensor node trained with the ST-GCN backbone network to achieve data-driven topology adaptation. The backbone network consists of four stacked layers of spatiotemporal convolutional modules. Each layer integrates spatial graph convolution to capture Sensor node coordination and temporal convolution to model the temporal evolution of movements. Finally, high-level features are compressed into fixed-dimensional vectors using biaxial global average pooling. Then, a fully connected layer and softmax are used to output the recognition probability of the sports movement. This forms an end-to-end recognition framework from raw sensor signals to movement categories, fully embodying the core concept of “data-driven and structure-adaptive.”

This scientific article, published in Scientific Reports (Volume 16, Article 4160, 2026), presents a novel approach to sports posture recognition using wearable sensor data. The authors propose a dynamic topology-adaptive Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (ST-GCN) framework for recognizing sports postures from eight IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) sensors.

**Key Problem:** Existing deep learning models for action recognition rely on fixed, predefined human skeletal topologies and struggle to adapt to individual differences in sensor placement, limiting their generalization across users and devices.

**Core Innovation:** The framework strategically initializes a learnable adjacency matrix with a human skeleton prior (ensuring biomechanically plausible connections) and then refines it through end-to-end training. It incorporates L2 regularization and periodic Top-K sparsification to prevent overfitting and maintain a sparse, interpretable structure. This allows the model to dynamically correct for structural deviations caused by variations in sensor positioning without deviating from realistic body kinematics.

**Methodology:**
- Uses eight IMU sensors collecting 6-axis inertial data (3-axis acceleration + 3-axis angular velocity) at 50 Hz from key body parts (head, thorax, waist, left/right upper arms, left/right forearms, left thigh).
- Data preprocessing includes low-pass Butterworth filtering, global normalization, and sliding window segmentation (100-frame windows, 50-frame step, 50% overlap).
- A dynamic graph construction module combines a fixed skeleton prior with a learnable weight matrix, applying Top-K sparsification and symmetric normalization.
- The backbone consists of four stacked ST-GCN layers using Chebyshev graph convolution for spatial modeling and causal dilated convolution for temporal modeling.
- Classification uses two-axis global average pooling followed by a fully connected layer with Softmax.
- Optimized using Adam with early stopping.

**Results:**
- Achieves 94.1% ± 0.6% average recognition accuracy in cross-user scenarios.
- Achieves 91.5% ± 0.5% in cross-device tests.
- Demonstrates superior robustness for sports posture recognition under non-standardized deployment conditions.
- The paper also includes systematic robustness evaluation through cross-device zero-shot generalization tests and sensor anomaly simulation experiments.

**Ethical Approval:** The study was approved by Yili Normal University (Ethics Approval Number: EA-YN-CPEH00159).

args.summary:
This is a video transcript explaining the ST-GCN (Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks) paper for skeleton-based action recognition, published on 20 Oct 2023. ST-GCN is the first graph convolutional network (GCN)-based method for skeleton-based action recognition.

**Key concepts explained:**
- Skeleton sequences are represented as graphs where human body joints are nodes and bones are edges, based on human topology.
- Each joint is initially a 2D (XY) or 3D (XYZ) vector, which gets mapped to higher dimensions (64→128→256) through the network.
- The network uses GCN blocks for spatial modeling (passing information between connected joints within a frame) combined with TCN (Temporal Convolutional Networks) blocks to model temporal relationships across frames using 1D convolutional kernels.
- Global average pooling is applied to reduce dimensionality before action classification.

**Performance results:**
- On NTU RGB+D dataset (60 actions): Cross-subject accuracy = 81.5%, Cross-view accuracy = 88.0%. After 5 years, improved to ~93% and ~97% respectively.
- On Kinetics dataset (400 actions from YouTube): Top-1 accuracy = 30%. After 5 years, improved to ~40%.

The video concludes by noting that newer methods have since improved upon these results, and hints at discussing HGCN from ICCV 2023 in a future video.

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network for Skeleton-based Action Recognition Rui Hang and MinXian Li(�) Nanjing University of Science and Technology, China {hangrui,minxianli}@njust.edu.cn Abstract. Skeleton-based action recognition approaches usually con-struct the skeleton sequence as spatial-temporal graphs and perform graph convolution on these graphs to extract discriminative features.
However, due to the fixed topology shared among different poses and the lack of direct long-range temporal dependencies, it is not trivial to learn the robust spatial-temporal feature. Therefore, we present a spatial-temporal adaptive graph convolutional network (STA-GCN) to learn adaptive spatial and temporal topologies and effectively aggregate features for skeleton-based action recognition. The proposed network is composed of spatial adaptive graph convolution (SA-GC) and tempo-ral adaptive graph convolution (TA-GC) with an adaptive topology en-coder. The SA-GC can extract the spatial feature for each pose with the spatial adaptive topology, while the TA-GC can learn the temporal feature by modeling the direct long-range temporal dependencies adap-tively. On three large-scale skeleton action recognition datasets: NTU RGB+D 60, NTU RGB+D 120, and Kinetics Skeleton, the STA-GCN outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/hang-rui/STA-GCN Keywords: Action recognition · Adaptive topology · Graph convolu-tion.
1 Introduction Action recognition is an essential task in human-centered computing and com-puter vision, which plays an increasingly crucial role in video surveillance, human-computer interaction, video analysis, and other applications [26, 1, 38]. In recent years, skeleton-based human action recognition has attracted much attention due to the development of depth sensors [46] and pose estimation algorithms [2, 33]. Conventional deep learning methods adopt re-current neural networks (RNN) [8, 20, 43] and convolutional neural networks (CNN) [14–16] to analyze the skeleton sequence by representing it as vector sequence or pseudo-image.
However, the skeleton sequence is naturally structured as a spatial-temporal graph. For this reason, Yan et al. [40] firstly proposed the spatial-temporal graph convolutional network (ST-GCN) to model the motion patterns of action on a 1265 2 R. Hang and M. Li (a) fixed topology (b) adaptive topology Time fixed spatial topology fixed temporal topology adaptive spatial topology adaptive temporal topology Time Time Time Fig. 1. Illustration of (a) the fixed spatial and temporal topology and (b) the adap-tive spatial and temporal topology. Different color points indicate the different human joints, and the lines correspond to the spatial and temporal direct correlation between joints. Best viewed in color.
skeleton spatial-temporal graph. After that, a series of graph convolutional net-works (GCN) methods based on spatial-temporal graphs have been proposed for skeleton-based action recognition [29, 7, 22].
However, there are still two disadvantages to the feature extraction operations on the spatial-temporal graph: (1) In the stage of learning spatial features, the fixed spatial topology is shared among all poses, which may not be optimal for the action with large changes in pose. For action such as “throw”, before and after the throw, the human pose presents two forms of backward-leaning and forward-leaning, which represents different semantics. Using the fixed spatial topology may mistakenly enhance irrelevant connections or weaken critical ones, failing to accurately represent the spatial dependencies. This fact suggests that the spatial topology should be adaptive to each pose in the skeleton sequence.
(2) In the stage of learning temporal features, existing methods apply temporal convolution with a fixed small kernel to extract the short-range temporal feature.
It leads to the weak capacity to model temporal long-range joint dependencies vital for action recognition.
To learn the robust feature representation in the spatial and temporal di-mensions, we propose a spatial-temporal Adaptive Graph Convolutional Net-work (STA-GCN) in this work. The proposed network is composed of two key modules: Spatial Adaptive Graph Convolution (SA-GC) and Temporal Adaptive Graph Convolution (TA-GC). Both SA-GC and TA-GC have a critical embedded component: Topology Adaptive Encoder (TAE). The SA-GC module is designed to extract spatial features by modeling the spatial adaptive joint dependencies.
The TA-GC module is designed to learn temporal features by capturing the di-rect long-range joint dependencies in the temporal dimension. Combined with SA-GC and TA-GC modules, the proposed model can learn the discriminative features both in the spatial and temporal dimensions.
1266 STA-GCN: Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network 3 The TAE component is proposed to learn spatial adaptive topology and temporal adaptive topology. The existing GCN methods use fixed spatial and temporal topology (Figure 1(a)). This fixed spatial topology forces each skele-ton frame to adopt the same spatial topology, while the fixed temporal topology forces all trajectories to use the same temporal topology. We argue that this fixed topology is insufficient to represent the joint dependencies per pose or per trajectory. Therefore, we propose the TAE to solve this problem by learning the spatial adaptive topology and the temporal adaptive topology (Figure 1(b)). The spatial adaptive topology can generate the pose-specific dependencies for each frame in the skeleton sequence to learn discriminative spatial features. The tem-poral adaptive topology can model the direct long-range dependencies between any two joints in the trajectory graph to extract robust temporal features.
The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: – A spatial adaptive graph convolution (SA-GC) module is proposed to extract the spatial feature for each pose with the spatial adaptive topology.
– A temporal adaptive graph convolution (TA-GC) module is proposed to learn the temporal feature by modeling the direct long-range temporal de-pendencies.
– A topology adaptive encoder (TAE) embedded into graph convolution is pro-posed to generate the adaptive spatial topology and the adaptive temporal topology.
– We propose a Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (STA-GCN) composed of SA-GC and TA-GC, which outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on three large-scale skeleton action recognition datasets: NTU RGB+D [27], NTU RGB+D 120 [19], and Kinetics-skeleton [13].
2 Related Work 2.1 Skeleton-Based Action Recognition With the development of deep learning based video understanding technology, a series of video-based methods were proposed for action recognition. Specifically, 2D CNNs [36, 18] efficiently recognize actions by modeling the relationships in the temporal dimension, while 3D CNNs [34, 3] capture motion information in a uni-fied network through a simple extension from the spatial domain to the spatial-temporal domain. Recently skeleton-based methods [8, 20, 43, 14–16, 40, 29, 7, 22, 39, 42, 24] have been developed extensively since skeleton data are more computa-tionally efficient and exhibit stronger robustness. Skeleton data can eliminate the influences of variations of illumination, camera viewpoints, background changes, and clothing variance in real-world videos [35, 21, 37]. Therefore, we adopt the skeleton-based action recognition approach in this paper.
2.2 Graph Convolution Networks in Action Recognition The type of skeleton-based action recognition approaches is divided into three categories: RNN-based, CNN-based, and GCN-based. RNN represents the skele-1267 4 R. Hang and M. Li ton sequence as a vector sequence [8, 20, 43], while CNN represents it as a pseudo-image [14–16]. However, both RNN and CNN methods ignore the information of skeleton topology among joints. GCN-based methods represent the skeleton sequence as a spatial-temporal graph and extract features in spatial and tem-poral dimensions by graph convolution and temporal convolution respectively.
Yan [40] et al. firstly introduce graph convolution and temporal convolution into the skeleton-based action recognition to model the spatial configurations and temporal dynamics simultaneously. The following works improved the model by performing multi-hop methods to extract multi-scale features [17, 12], applying additional mechanisms to adaptively capture the relations between distant joints [17, 44, 41], and adding additional edges between adjacent frames to extract fea-tures based on the extended graph [9, 22, 23]. However, all these methods only apply Graph Convolution Network (GCN) in the spatial dimension. In the tem-poral dimension, Temporal Convolution Network (TCN) is used to learn the temporal feature. It is not powerful due to the use of a fixed small temporal convolution kernel. In this work, we apply graph convolution both in spatial and temporal dimensions. Temporal graph convolution can effectively learn the temporal feature by modeling the direct long-range temporal dependencies.
2.3 Topology Adaptive-Based Methods The topology-based adaptive methods [29, 17, 41, 45] aim to generate the appro-priate spatial topology based on the input data. This spatial topology indicates whether and how important a connection exists between any two joints in the graph. Existing methods focus only on the spatial dimension, and they mainly use parametric adjacency matrices to learn a spatial topology optimized for all data [29] or generate a specific spatial topology for each action sample based on the input data [17, 41, 45]. These methods alleviate the limitation caused by the fixed pre-defined spatial topology of GCN methods. However, existing meth-ods force all frames to share the same spatial topology, which is unreasonable because each pose represents a different semantic and cannot use the same spa-tial topology to extract features. Moreover, these approaches do not consider topology in the temporal dimension, which hinders the long-range dependencies modeling in the temporal dimension. To address these problems, we propose the Topology Adaptive Encoder (TAE) to learn spatial adaptive topology for each frame in the spatial graph and temporal adaptive topology for each trajectory in the temporal graph. The spatial adaptive topology can efficiently help spatial graph convolution extract the features of different poses in action. On the other hand, the temporal adaptive topology is used in temporal graph convolution to extract long-range dependencies.
3 Methodology 3.1 Preliminaries Notations. A human skeleton with N joints is presented as an undirected spatial graph G = (V, E), where V = {vi|i = 1, . . . , N} is the set of N vertices 1268 STA-GCN: Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network 5 (c) TAE S-GC (a) SA-GC (c) TAE T-GC (b) TA-GC T-CN S-GC STA-GC block Spatial Adaptive Topology Temporal Adaptive Topology Pre-defined Spatial Topology Input Action Classifier Result Fig. 2. The overview of the proposed Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (STA-GCN). (a) The spatial adaptive graph convolution (SA-GC) module is adopted to learn the spatial feature for each pose with the spatial adaptive topology. (b) The temporal adaptive graph convolution (TA-GC) module is subsequently adopted to learn the temporal feature for each trajectory with the temporal adaptive topology. (c) The Topology Adaptive Encoder (TAE) is used both in SA-GC and TA-GC modules to learn the spatial adaptive topology and the temporal adaptive topology.
representing joints and E is the edges set representing bones. The topology of G is formulated as an adjacency matrix A ∈RN×N and its element aij ∈(0, 1) denoting weather an edge exists between vertex vi and vj.
Graph Convolution. According to Yan et al.[40], the spatial dependencies of the joints in each frame can be conveniently encoded with Graph Convolution.
The operation of Graph Convolution is formulated as: X(l+1) = σ K X k=0 e A(k)X(l)W(l) (k) !
(1) where X is the feature of each layer, σ(·)is an activation function. K denotes the pre-defined maximum graphic distance. e A(k) = Λ −1 2 (k) (A(k) + I(k))Λ −1 2 (k) is the k-th order normalized adjacency matrix, where A + I is the skeleton graph with added self-loops to keep identity features, Λ is the diagonal degree matrix of (A + I). W(k) is learnable parameters to implement the convolution operation.
3.2 Overview To learn discriminative features on the spatial and temporal graph, we propose a Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (STA-GCN). An overview of our proposed method is illustrated in Figure 2. After extracting lo-cal skeleton features using a pre-defined spatial topology (i.e. human skeleton structure), we adopt Spatial Adaptive Graph Convolution (SA-GC) and Tem-poral Adaptive Graph Convolution (TA-GC) to learn discriminative features.
The SA-GC is proposed to extract the spatial feature for each pose with the spatial adaptive topology. The TA-GC is proposed to learn the temporal feature 1269 6 R. Hang and M. Li by modeling the direct long-range temporal dependencies. Both SA-GC and TA-GC have an embedded Topology Adaptive Encoder (TAE), which generates a unique and appropriate topology for each pose and each trajectory. On the top of SA-GC and TA-GC, we apply a temporal convolutional convolution to aggregate the features in the temporal dimension. Based on the discriminative features ex-tracted by several STA-GC blocks, we use a fully connected layer with softmax activation function to obtain the final class. The method will be discussed in detail in subsequent sections.
3.3 Spatial and Temporal Graph Convolution Most existing works treat the human skeleton sequence as a spatial-temporal graph where features are extracted through spatial graph convolution and tem-poral convolution. However, the temporal convolution is not powerful to learn the temporal feature due to the use of a fixed small temporal convolution kernel.
Therefore, in this section, we introduce a more robust feature extraction opera-tor on the spatial and temporal graph. Let us first consider a graph convolution in spatial-temporal graph Gst = (Vst, Est) where Vst = {vnt|n = 1, . . . , N, t = 1, . . . , T, } is the set of all nodes across T frames in the skeleton sequence and Est is the spatial-temporal edge set.
We further deconstruct a spatial-temporal graph into T spatial graphs across time and N temporal graphs across joints. The spatial graphs are represented as Gs = (Vst, Es) where Es is the spatial edge set and is formulated as a spatial adjacency matrix As ∈RT ×N×N. Note that the spatial adjacency matrix is de-graded to vanilla form A ∈RN×N when all spatial graphs have the same spatial correlations. Similarly, the temporal graphs are represented as Gt = (Vst, Et) and the temporal adjacency matrix At ∈RN×T ×T can be formulated. After the graph decomposition, we develop two graph convolutions: spatial graph convo-lution (S-GC) and temporal graph convolution (T-GC). However, different poses represent different semantics, and using the same topology will incorrectly extract spatial features for different poses, which leads to weak performance in recognizing action with large changes in pose.
Moreover, existing methods do not apply graph convolution in the temporal dimension. If graph convolution is to be performed in the temporal dimension, a suitable temporal topology is needed to represent the relationships between joints in the temporal graph.
To generate a more detailed topology, we propose a unified topology gener-ation module, Topology Adaptive Encoder (TAE), which applies an unshared topology generation strategy. Specifically, the TAE module generates the spatial topology for each pose in spatial graph convolution and the temporal topology for each trajectory in temporal graph convolution. Technically, the TAE applies self-attention operations to extract correlations between joints in the embedding space. The function is formulated as: A = ℓ2_norm(XWϕWT ψXT ) (5) where X is the input feature, we first utilize two linear transformation functions ϕ and ψ to embed input feature into the embedding space, Wϕ and Wψ are the parameters of the embedding functions ϕ and ψ, respectively. Then, the two embedded feature matrices are multiplied to obtain a topology matrix A. Finally, the ℓ2 normalization is applied to each row of the adjacency matrix, which eases the optimization and with the help of ℓ2 normalization, the normalization of node degree is unnecessary.

1272 STA-GCN: Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network 9 3.6 Model Details.
The entire network consists of five STA-GC blocks, and the number of output channels of five blocks are 64-64-64-128-256. We apply a data BatchNorm layer at the start to normalize the input data. The temporal dimension is halved at the 4-th and 5-th blocks by strided temporal convolution. The temporal convolutional network used (TCN) in the STA-GC block is designed as multi-scale temporal convolutions following [22]. The main difference is that we reduce the number of channels and fuse six branches with a point-wise convolution. We also add extra residual connections to facilitate training. Due to the operations in SA-GC and TA-GC are equivalent, we only introduce a detailed implementation of SA-GC.
We first utilize two linear transformation functions to transform input features into two neatly compact representations. Then, the two embedded features are multiplied to obtain spatial adaptive topology. We further apply ℓ2 normalization to normalize the adjacency matrix, and the resulting adjacency matrix is used to apply the graph convolution.
4 Experiments 4.1 Datasets NTU RGB+D 60 [27] is currently the most widely used indoor skeleton-based action recognition dataset, which contains 56, 880 skeleton action sequences with 60 action classes performed by 40 volunteers and captured by three Microsoft Kinect v2 cameras from different views concurrently. Each sample contains one action with two subjects at most, and each skeleton is composed of 25 joints.
The dataset is separated into two benchmarks: (1) Cross-subject (X-Sub): 40, 320 samples performed by 20 subjects are separated into the training set, and the other 16, 560 samples performed by different 20 subjects belong to the test set.
(2) Cross-view (X-View): the training set contains 37, 920 samples from camera views 2 and 3, and the test set contains 18, 960 samples from camera view 1.
NTU RGB+D 120 [19] is the largest indoor skeleton-based action recogni-tion dataset, which extends NTU RGB+D 60 with additional 57,367 skeleton sequences over 60 extra action classes, totalling contains 114, 480 skeleton action sequences in 120 action classes performed by 106 volunteers, and has 32 different camera setups, each setup representing a specific location and background. Sim-ilarly, the dataset is separated into two benchmarks: (1) Cross-subject (X-Sub): 63, 026 samples performed by 53 subjects are separated into the training set, and the other 50, 922 samples performed by different 53 subjects belong to the test set. (2) Cross-setup (X-Set): the training set contains 54, 471 samples with even setup IDs, and the test set contains 59, 477 samples with odd setup IDs.
Kinetics Skeleton. Kinetics 400 [13] is a large-scale human action dataset that contains 300, 000 video clips of 400 classes collected from the Internet. After ap-plying Openpose [2] pose-estimation algorithm on Kinetics 400, the Kinetics 1273 10 R. Hang and M. Li Skeleton dataset obtain 240, 436 training and 19, 796 evaluation skeleton clips, where each skeleton graph contains 18 body joints, along with their 2D coordi-nates and confidence score.
4.2 Implementation Details All experiments are implemented on two RTX 3090 GPUs with the PyTorch deep learning framework. The stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with the momentum of 0.9 and the weight decay of 0.0001 is used for optimization. The model is trained for 70 epochs in total. The initial learning rate is set to 0.1 and decays with a cosine schedule after the 10-th epoch. Moreover, a warm-up strategy [10] was applied over the first 10 epochs, gradually increasing the learning rate from 0 to the initial value in order to make the training procedure more stable. The batch size is set to 32. Input data are preprocessed following [32], and cross-entropy loss is employed.

The STA-GCN is composed of spatial adaptive graph convolution (SA-GC) and temporal adaptive graph convolution (TA-GC). The SA-GC module is designed to extract spatial features by modeling the spatial adaptive joint de-pendencies. The TA-GC module is designed to learn temporal features by cap-turing the direct long-range joint dependencies in the temporal dimension. Both SA-GC and TA-GC have a critical embedded component: Topology Adaptive Encoder (TAE). The TAE is adopted to generate spatial adaptive topology and temporal adaptive topology for learning the discriminative features. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed modules. On three large-scale skeleton action recognition datasets, the proposed STA-GCN achieves the state-of-the-art performance.

args.summary:
This paper presents a Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (STA-GCN) for skeleton-based action recognition, developed by Rui Hang and MinXian Li at Nanjing University of Science and Technology. The key innovation addresses two limitations of existing methods: (1) fixed spatial topology shared across all poses, which fails to capture pose-specific semantics, and (2) lack of direct long-range temporal dependencies due to fixed small temporal convolution kernels.

The STA-GCN consists of two main modules: Spatial Adaptive Graph Convolution (SA-GC) and Temporal Adaptive Graph Convolution (TA-GC), both incorporating a Topology Adaptive Encoder (TAE). SA-GC extracts spatial features for each pose using adaptive spatial topology, while TA-GC models direct long-range temporal dependencies adaptively. The TAE generates unique, appropriate topologies for each pose and each trajectory using self-attention operations.

The network architecture comprises five STA-GC blocks with output channels of 64-64-64-128-256. Experiments were conducted on three large-scale datasets: NTU RGB+D 60, NTU RGB+D 120, and Kinetics Skeleton.

Key results:
- 4s-STA-GCN achieves 92.8% and 97.0% on NTU RGB+D 60 (X-Sub and X-View), 89.4% and 90.8% on NTU RGB+D 120 (X-Sub and X-Set).
- On Kinetics Skeleton, 4s-STA-GCN achieves 40.2% Top-1 and 63.5% Top-5 accuracy, outperforming prior state-of-the-art MST-GCN by 2.1% and 2.7%.
- Ablation studies show SA-GC improves baseline by 1.4%, TA-GC by 0.4%, and their combination achieves 89.5% Top-1 accuracy on NTU 60 X-Sub.
- The adaptive topology approach outperforms both fixed topology and other adaptive methods (2s-AGCN, Dynamic-GCN).
- The unshared topology generation strategy (generating specific topology for each frame/trajectory) surpasses shared topology approaches.

The model uses three/four modality streams: joint (J), bone (B), joint motion (JM), and bone motion (BM). Code is available at https://github.com/hang-rui/STA-GCN.

## TRAN Ngoc Thach

# Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (ST-GCN) — Explained

![TRAN Ngoc Thach](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/2*KB2ILfxSj7nMIcx0JHH5QQ.jpeg)

--

Listen

Share

Explaination for the paper “*Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks for Skeleton-Based Action Recognition*” [1] (aka. ST-GCN) as well as key findings in its source code [2].

## Introduction

Graph Neural Network and Knowledge Graph have been my research interest. During Literature Review, there were some noteable papers that opened up new directions or enabled new techniques. Among those is the paper “*Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks for Skeleton-Based Action Recognition*” [1]. Its source code is also publicly available [2], which is beneficial as [reproducibility](https://www.kdnuggets.com/2023/06/importance-reproducibility-machine-learning.html) is highly appreciated. I have spent some time on this paper, and hope that my short article can get like-minded people to comprehend the paper quicker. Time is our precious asset. 😀

## Paper Summary

### Inspiration

The paper itself is an extension of another paper: “*Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks*” [3], which defined the formula for convolving nodes within a graph to create Node Embeddings:

![]()

It looks scary at first, but thanks to [4], interpreting this formula can be untangled step-by-step. Its main idea is, given a specific node, to aggregate features from its neighbor nodes with its own’s, then embed the aggregated features into another latent space. The new features becomes *that node*’s features. Due to matrix multiplication, all the nodes’ features get updated at once . This is *one way* how convolution is carried out in graph. Notice that the above neighbors are direct ones; what if we are also interested in convolving neighbors at a further distance? In this case, the same process is repeated. Every repetition allows to convolve the neighbor nodes at an one-step further distance. The *deeper* representation a node ends up with through the convolution, the more representative it can be: it is not only aware of itself, but also the surrounding nodes near it. Typical tasks can be: 1). Node classfication, 2). Graph classfication. For 1), the node features are put through a Fully Connected layer with appropriate outputs, e.g. Softmax for multiclass classification. For 2), all the nodes’ features can be concatenated into one Tensor, and we apply the same processing.

### ST-GCN

The above described convolution is *spatial*. When adding another dimension to the nodes, such as *time*, it is motivating to convolve in *both spatial and temporal dimensions*. That is the idea behind the paper ST-GCN [1]. The task to be solved is *Human Action Recognition*, using skeleton sequence, denoted with body joints, each of which is a triplet of (Coordinate-X/Coordinate-Y/Confidence-Level):

![]()

ST-GCN’s archiecture:

![]()

### Code Explanation

First and foremost, where is the formula in Figure 1 applied? Here is it:

![]()

Matrices multiplication is not *commutative*, but surely *associative*. Originally, it was thought that one would first aggregate the features between the current nodes and its neighbors, then proceed to embedding the result to another latent space. But the code was implemented in a way that the embedding takes place first, then the aggregation.

After convolving Node spatially, it moved to convolving temporally *for each node separately*. We notice here the tuple `kernel=(temporal_ker, 1)`, where `temporal_ker` was hardcoded with `9` (9 time steps).

`kernel=(temporal_ker, 1)`
`temporal_ker`
`9`
![]()

The main training loop is defined in file “recognition.py” [5], the content of which is typical. *Although not discussed in the paper*, the implementation made use of Residual Connection (aka. Skip Connection) *in each ST-GCN Block* to deal with Gradient Degradation. Because of different input-output channels, the Connection is indeed a mini-Neural Network (instead of Identity connection):

![]()

Within ST-GCN block, to prevent Gradient explosion and achieve a more stable convergence, BatchNorm is used before and after non-linear layers, as often advised [6]. The DropOut layer also helps in reducing overfitting [8]. But the code uses default setting for Dropout (meaning: probability of `0.5`) while recommended value for Convolution layer is `0.1` or `0.2` [9].

`0.5`
`0.1`
`0.2`

Similarly to Convolution Layers for images, *10* ST-GCN Blocks are chained to hopefully generate high-level feature maps on skeleton sequences.

Another worthy point to mention is the Adjacency Matrix, constructed as a Tuple `(spatial_ker, V, V)`. The neighbors of a specific node can be grouped into subsets. The easiest way is to just treat all of them equally (“Uni-labeling” as per paper), or the node connected to itself has distance 0 while its direct neighbors have distance of 1 (“Distance partitioning”). The number of such subsets is denoted as `spatial_ker`; each subset has its own Adjacency matrix to describe which nodes are considered neighbor, *given a specific node*. Each subset also has its own `(o_channel, T, V)`. Thanks to `einsum()`, those datapoints are afterwards aggregated neatly.

`(spatial_ker, V, V)`
`spatial_ker`
`(o_channel, T, V)`
`einsum()`

## Final Remark

I must admit that when first reading the paper [1], I got a certain perception about its main idea. For example, section “Spatial Temporal Modeling” page 4 [1], the authors extended the spatial modeling in temporal dimension by tweaking the Neighboring Function B(vₜᵢ) to include temporal neighbors (of the same node (joint)). I imagined we would have a dedicated function like this, but through the real implementation, it turned out to be just matrices multiplication. This once again reinforces my preference in focusing on papers that have code available. Otherwise, one would take the paper with a grain of salt. 😕

Hopefully, my effort in summarizing ST-GCN could help other people understand it quicker and more reliably. 💪 The spatial temporal convolution in this paper can be framed as generic multi-dimensional convolution with one dimension denoting nodes within a graph, from where the Graph Convolution formula (Figure 1) is applicable.

## References

[1] Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks for Skeleton-Based Action Recognition, Yan et al., 2018 (<https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.07455>)

[2] st-gcn (<https://github.com/yysijie/st-gcn>)

[3] Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks, Kipf et al., 2017, (<https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907>)

[4] Graph convolutional neural networks (<https://mbernste.github.io/posts/gcn/>)

[5] ST-GCN training loop (<https://github.com/yysijie/st-gcn/blob/master/processor/recognition.py#L78>)

[6] Where do I call the BatchNormalization function in Keras? (<https://stackoverflow.com/questions/34716454/where-do-i-call-the-batchnormalization-function-in-keras>)

[7] st\_gcn.py (<https://github.com/yysijie/st-gcn/blob/master/net/st_gcn.py>)

[8] Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting, Srivastava et al., 2014 (<https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/srivastava14a.html>)

[9] Where should I place dropout layers in a neural network? (<https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/240305/where-should-i-place-dropout-layers-in-a-neural-network>)

args.summary:
This Medium article by TRAN Ngoc Thach explains the Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (ST-GCN) paper by Yan et al. (2018) for skeleton-based human action recognition, along with key findings from its source code.

The article begins by introducing Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) based on Kipf et al. (2017), which aggregate features from neighbor nodes to create node embeddings. ST-GCN extends this concept by adding a temporal dimension, enabling convolution across both spatial (joint connections) and temporal (time steps) dimensions for action recognition using skeleton sequences of body joints (Coordinate-X, Coordinate-Y, Confidence-Level).

Key implementation details from the code include: (1) The graph convolution formula performs embedding first, then aggregation (contrary to initial intuition). (2) Temporal convolution uses a kernel size of 9 time steps, applied per node separately. (3) Each ST-GCN block uses residual (skip) connections with a mini-Neural Network instead of identity connections to handle gradient degradation. (4) BatchNorm is used before and after non-linear layers for stable convergence. (5) Dropout is used (default 0.5 probability, though 0.1-0.2 is recommended for convolutions). (6) 10 ST-GCN blocks are chained together. (7) The adjacency matrix uses spatial partitioning (e.g., 'Uni-labeling' or 'Distance partitioning'), with each subset having its own adjacency matrix.

The author emphasizes the importance of papers with available code for reliable understanding, noting that the temporal extension was implemented simply as matrix multiplication rather than a complex neighborhood function as described in the paper. References include the original ST-GCN paper, source code repository, and related works.

## Abstract

Existing training decision support systems mostly rely on preset rules or frameworks based on prior knowledge. When faced with significant individual differences or rapid changes in the environment, it is difficult for the system to dynamically adapt to the physiological conditions, skill levels, and training progress of different athletes. To achieve efficient and personalized training support for athletes, this article constructs a new training decision support system that combines DRL (Deep Reinforcement Learning) technology. Through multi-sensor fusion technology, the system comprehensively collects athletes’ physiological and external environmental data. The data is preprocessed by a sliding window average filter algorithm to eliminate noise and outliers. The system adopts the DQN (Deep Q-Network) architecture and applies dual DQN technology to improve model stability. The priority experience replay strategy is used to accelerate model convergence and improve training efficiency. The system combines real-time strategy adjustment and optimization modules to dynamically adjust training strategies according to athlete performance to meet individual needs. The system feedback mechanism continuously optimizes the training plan according to athlete performance to ensure long-term effectiveness and personalized services. The research results show that the average response time of the DRL-based system in the initialization and data loading test scenarios is 13.21 ms, and the average accuracy, consistency, and failure rate of the system are 96.31%, 95.0%, and 2.37%, respectively. This shows that the system response time period and long-term operation stability are better, and it can provide personalized suggestions, thereby significantly improving training efficiency and providing scientific support for athletes.

In modern competitive sports, training systems are very important for improving athletes’ training effects and competition results [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-025-00473-9#ref-CR1 "Yang J, Lv Wu. Optimization of sports training systems based on wireless sensor networks algorithms. IEEE Sens J. 2020;21(22):25075–82. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/JSEN.2020.3046290
                  
                .")]. In the past, coaches mainly relied on personal experience to develop training plans, but this method has limitations. It often ignores individual differences and makes it difficult to achieve truly personalized training. Meanwhile, changes in the training environment and the athletes' condition also require more flexible training strategies. The existing methods (such as association rules, Kinect system) rely on preset rules or specific environmental hardware, and are difficult to dynamically adapt to individual differences and environmental changes. With the advancement of AI (Artificial Intelligence) technology, especially the development of deep learning and reinforcement learning, new ideas and technical support have been provided to solve the above problems [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-025-00473-9#ref-CR2 "Yan F, Peng Q. ### 2.1 Data collection and preprocessing
