* [Conclusion](#viewer-m5t2i805)

## **What Motion Capture for Sports Actually Measures**

**Motion Capture for Sports** converts human movement into trackable positional data across time. In practical terms, that means joint trajectories, segment rotation, stride timing, ground contact sequencing, limb symmetry, trunk alignment, and movement variability can all be studied with far more precision than standard replay footage allows.

For sports biomechanics, the purpose is not simply to visualize motion. It is to understand cause and effect inside an athlete’s movement pattern. A coach may see that a sprinter is losing efficiency in late acceleration. A capture pipeline can reveal whether the issue comes from pelvic control, foot strike timing, excessive vertical displacement, or asymmetry between left and right leg extension. That level of specificity is where **motion capture sports** becomes genuinely valuable.

**The same principle applies across disciplines:**

* In football, teams can study cutting mechanics, tackle preparation posture, and return to play movement quality.
* In baseball, staff can inspect rotational sequencing from pelvis to thorax to throwing arm.
* In tennis, analysts can look at serve loading, shoulder rotation, and recovery timing.
* In basketball, they can examine deceleration, landing posture, and repeated jump mechanics.
* In golf, they can measure swing sequencing with far tighter temporal accuracy than visual review alone.

For organizations working across athlete performance and digital representation, this connects naturally with Mimic’s [sports and fitness solutions](https://www.mimicproductions.com/3d-sports-fitness), where human movement data can support both analysis and high quality visual output.

## **Why Biomechanics Teams Use Capture Instead of Video Alone**

Video remains essential. It is fast, familiar, and useful for broad technique review. But it is still an image based record, which means depth, joint rotation, occlusion, and timing precision can be limited unless the setup is extremely controlled.

**Motion Capture for Sports** adds measurable structure. Instead of debating what the eye thinks it sees, staff can work with trackable kinematics. That matters when the margin between efficient and inefficient movement may be only a few degrees of rotation or a few milliseconds of phase timing.

A high quality capture session helps answer questions such as:

* Is the athlete producing the same mechanics under fatigue
* Does a return to play athlete show compensatory loading on one side
* Is a technical adjustment improving force transfer or only changing appearance
* Are repeated training interventions creating stable movement adaptation over time

This is where **motion capture sports** becomes more than technology. It becomes a decision support system for coaching, rehabilitation, and long term athlete development.

## **Core Technologies Behind motion capture sports**

Not every capture system is built for the same purpose. In practice, sports labs and performance environments typically draw from three broad categories.

### **Marker based optical capture**

This is often the highest precision approach in controlled studio or laboratory conditions. Reflective markers are placed on anatomical landmarks, multiple calibrated cameras track their motion, and the recorded data is solved into a digital skeleton.

Advantages include strong spatial accuracy and deep biomechanical analysis potential. The tradeoff is setup complexity, greater sensitivity to occlusion, and the need for disciplined calibration and processing.

### **Inertial capture**

Inertial systems use wearable sensors to estimate body segment motion through gyroscopes, accelerometers, and magnetometers. These systems are portable and useful outside a traditional stage, especially in field environments where optical volume control is difficult.

Their strength is flexibility. Their limitation is that long session drift, magnetic interference, and model assumptions can affect output quality.

### **Computer vision and video AI tracking**

This category uses one or more cameras and machine learning models to estimate pose without markers or suits. It has become more accessible and often works well for broad movement screening, quick feedback, or lower friction setups.

Its appeal is obvious, but for high stakes biomechanics, especially where rotational fidelity and joint level interpretation matter, it still requires careful validation.

In many advanced pipelines, teams combine methods. Optical systems may be used for benchmark studies. Inertial systems may capture on field training. Video based pose estimation may support daily review or remote analysis. Choosing the right approach depends on the performance question, the environment, and the required accuracy.

Teams comparing movement data pipelines often benefit from understanding how capture differs from broader actor or character workflows. Mimic’s article on [motion capture versus performance capture](https://www.mimicproductions.com/post/motion-capture-vs-performance-capture) helps frame that distinction clearly in a way that is also useful for sports related planning.

## **The Production Pipeline Behind Athlete Movement Analysis**

Sports science often talks about data collection, but the most reliable outcomes come from thinking in terms of pipeline design. That mindset is common in film grade character production and equally important here.

A robust **Motion Capture for Sports** workflow usually follows this sequence:

### **1. Objective definition**

The capture team defines what needs to be measured. Sprint efficiency, landing asymmetry, serve sequencing, rotational power transfer, gait recovery, and fatigue related compensation all demand different setups.

### **2. System selection**

The team chooses optical, inertial, computer vision, or a hybrid configuration based on movement type, venue, and resolution requirements.

### **3. Calibration and body setup**

This stage is often underestimated. Poor calibration undermines everything downstream. Marker placement, sensor alignment, body model configuration, and coordinate consistency all shape the integrity of the final data.

### **4. Capture session**

Athletes perform controlled tests, sport specific drills, or full movement sequences. Good operators capture enough context to interpret the movement correctly rather than recording disconnected fragments.

### **5. Data cleaning and solving**

Here, gaps are filled, noise is reduced, trajectories are reviewed, and the skeletal solve is checked against real movement behavior. In sports contexts, this is where technical credibility is won or lost.

### **6. Interpretation**

Biomechanists and coaches examine timing, symmetry, joint behavior, segment coordination, and movement consistency. The goal is not abstract data accumulation. The goal is intervention.

### **7. Visualization and communication**

This is where many performance teams now want more than charts. They want intuitive 3D playback, side by side comparisons, and real time review environments that athletes can understand instantly. Mimic’s [realtime integration](https://www.mimicproductions.com/realtime-integration) capabilities are especially relevant here because clear visualization often determines whether analysis becomes actionable.

### **8. Iteration**

The athlete returns, movement is captured again, and the system tracks whether changes are durable or only temporary.

## **Marker based systems versus inertial systems versus video AI**

Choosing the wrong method can create false confidence. A system should be selected according to the question being asked, not according to trend or convenience.

Marker based capture is usually best when the environment can be tightly controlled and when fine joint level analysis matters. Inertial capture is useful when portability and practical deployment matter more than lab grade volume control. Video AI can be extremely useful for scalable observation, but it should not automatically be treated as equivalent to a rigorously calibrated biomechanics setup.

The strongest teams understand this as a spectrum of use, not a winner takes all debate. In many modern setups, **motion capture sports** is most effective when different systems serve different layers of the performance workflow.

## **Where capture data becomes useful in coaching**

The value of **Motion Capture for Sports** appears when movement data changes coaching behavior.

A sprint coach might use it to identify excessive backside mechanics and limited front side projection. A strength and conditioning coach may use it to examine landing stiffness or trunk control under fatigue. A rehabilitation specialist may use it to verify whether a recovering athlete still protects one side during change of direction. A technical coach may use it to compare pre intervention and post intervention movement signatures with much greater confidence.

This is also where digital character experience becomes unexpectedly relevant. Teams that can build accurate skeletal structures, preserve joint behavior, and present movement clearly often communicate performance insights more effectively. Mimic’s [body and facial rigging](https://www.mimicproductions.com/body-and-facial-rigging) work reflects the same discipline that high quality movement interpretation requires, even when the end use is not entertainment.

| **Approach** | **Primary strength** | **Primary limitation** | **Best retail use** |
| **Traditional search and filters** | Fast access to known items | Weak guidance for uncertain customers | Direct product lookup |
| **Rule based chatbot** | Controlled answers for simple flows | Limited nuance, low emotional presence | Basic support and FAQs |
| **Text only generative assistant** | Flexible language interaction | Lacks embodied trust and visual identity | Complex question handling |
| **Digital human with AI retail intelligence** | Guided conversation, presence, brand expression | Requires stronger production and integration discipline | Personalised selling, education, premium service |

## **Applications**

**motion capture sports** supports far more than elite lab research. Its usefulness expands wherever movement quality matters and where performance teams are willing to act on evidence.

### **Performance optimization**

Athletes and coaches can identify inefficiencies in acceleration, deceleration, rotation, jumping, and directional transition. Small technical changes become measurable rather than impressionistic.

### **Injury risk monitoring**

No capture system predicts injury with certainty, but it can reveal movement patterns linked to elevated loading, poor symmetry, unstable landing behavior, or persistent compensation.

### **Return to play assessment**

This is one of the most practical uses of **Motion Capture for Sports**. Rather than relying only on general strength benchmarks or visual confidence, teams can compare movement quality against baseline or expected norms.

### **Technique refinement**

Throwing, serving, striking, sprinting, and skating all depend on sequencing. Capture makes sequencing visible in a way athletes can study and repeat.

### **Athlete education**

When a player can see their movement in a clear 3D form, coaching language often becomes easier to absorb. The athlete stops guessing what “stay stacked” or “control your trunk” is supposed to feel like.

### **Digital visualization and simulation**

Captured athletic data can support training tools, replay systems, XR experiences, and performance driven animation. Teams interested in how movement extends into downstream visualization can explore Mimic’s [3D animation workflows](https://www.mimicproductions.com/3d-animation), where clean motion data becomes a readable visual asset rather than a technical abstraction.

## **Benefits**

The main benefits of **motion capture sports** are not theoretical. They are operational.

* Greater measurement precision than observational coaching alone
* Better visibility into timing, sequencing, and asymmetry
* More confidence when tracking change across training cycles
* Stronger communication between coaches, therapists, analysts, and athletes
* More credible return to play evaluation
* Clearer integration between biomechanics, visualization, and digital production
* A more durable record of athletic movement for benchmarking and longitudinal review

One overlooked advantage is consistency. Human observation varies across staff, fatigue, angle, and context. Capture data, when collected well, creates a more stable reference point. It does not replace experienced coaching judgment, but it sharpens it.

## **Future Outlook**

The future of **Motion Capture for Sports** will likely be defined by convergence rather than replacement.

Optical systems will continue to matter where precision is critical. Wearable sensing will remain important for applied field use. Video AI will become more capable and more common. Real time visualization will improve, and movement data will increasingly feed into simulation, digital twins, XR coaching environments, and athlete specific virtual representations.

What will separate useful systems from noisy ones is not novelty. It will be validation, calibration discipline, and the ability to translate capture into meaningful coaching decisions.

This is why the future of **motion capture sports** looks increasingly similar to mature digital human production pipelines. Accurate capture alone is not enough. Teams also need clean solving, intelligible rig behavior, efficient playback, and presentation formats that support fast interpretation. The organizations that understand this full chain will get more value from every recorded session.

## **FAQs**

**What is Motion Capture for Sports used for?**

It is used to measure and analyze athletic movement with more precision than standard observation alone. Common use cases include performance optimization, movement screening, return to play review, and technical skill refinement.

**Is motion capture sports only for elite athletes?**

No. Elite environments often lead adoption because they have the resources and performance pressure to justify it, but the same methods can support youth development, rehabilitation, university sport, and applied coaching environments.

**Which is better for sports biomechanics, optical or inertial capture?**

Neither is universally better. Optical systems are often stronger for controlled, high precision analysis. Inertial systems are often better when portability and real world deployment matter. The right choice depends on the question, the venue, and the required level of detail.

**Can video based pose estimation replace traditional capture systems?**

For some use cases, it can support screening and practical feedback. For high confidence biomechanics, especially when joint level interpretation matters, it should be validated carefully and not assumed to match a calibrated capture stage.

**How often should athletes be captured?**

That depends on the program objective. Some teams use capture at key checkpoints, such as pre season, post intervention, and return to play. Others use it more regularly to monitor technical adaptation across a season.

**Why does rigging matter in a sports capture workflow?**

Because movement data still needs to be solved onto a body model that behaves coherently. Poor rig structure can distort interpretation, especially when the output is visualized in 3D or used downstream in simulation, replay, or animation.

## **Conclusion**

The real strength of **Motion Capture for Sports** lies in its ability to turn movement into something measurable, reviewable, and coachable without flattening the complexity of human performance. When it is handled with technical discipline, it helps performance teams move beyond surface level observation and toward precise intervention.

For sports biomechanics and athlete training, that means better questions, better evidence, and better decisions. It means seeing not just what an athlete did, but how they did it, why it happened, and whether it can be improved. In a field where marginal gains matter and where return to play choices can carry serious consequences, that level of clarity is no longer optional. It is becoming part of the modern performance standard.

This article from Mimic Productions (published April 10, 2026) explains how Motion Capture for Sports is used in sports biomechanics and athlete training. It converts human movement into trackable positional data, enabling coaches and analysts to measure timing, posture, symmetry, coordination, and joint motion with far greater precision than video alone.

**Key Technologies Covered:**
- **Marker-based optical capture** – Highest precision, but requires controlled lab conditions and complex setup.
- **Inertial capture** – Wearable sensors; portable for field use but prone to drift and magnetic interference.
- **Computer vision/video AI** – Markerless pose estimation; accessible but requires careful validation for high-stakes biomechanics.

**Production Pipeline (8 steps):** Objective definition → System selection → Calibration & body setup → Capture session → Data cleaning & solving → Interpretation → Visualization & communication → Iteration.

**Applications:** Performance optimization, injury risk monitoring, return-to-play assessment, technique refinement, athlete education, and digital visualization/simulation.

**Benefits:** Greater measurement precision, visibility into timing/sequencing/asymmetry, tracking change across training cycles, stronger communication between coaches/therapists/analysts, credible return-to-play evaluation, and a durable record for benchmarking.

**Future Outlook:** Convergence of optical, inertial, and AI systems; real-time visualization; digital twins and XR coaching environments. Success depends on validation, calibration discipline, and translating capture into coaching decisions.

**FAQs address:** Uses (performance optimization, injury screening, return-to-play), applicability beyond elite athletes, optical vs. inertial choice (depends on context), limitations of video AI, capture frequency, and importance of rigging for accurate 3D visualization.

<summary>
This is a Technology and Code article published in Frontiers in Computer Science (February 25, 2026) by Chao Deng and Bo Yuan from Guangdong University of Science and Technology, China. The paper presents a framework for an Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS) based on automatic construction of multimodal knowledge graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

**Key Contributions:**
1. A cross-modal knowledge fusion pipeline that aligns and merges entities from video transcripts (via FFmpeg/Whisper ASR) and textbook PDFs (via OCR and layout analysis)
2. A hybrid retrieval-augmented paradigm combining graph database queries (Neo4j) with vector similarity matching (HNSW index) to drive LLM-based Q&A
3. Direct processing of unstructured course videos as the application source

**System Architecture:**
- Knowledge Construction Layer: Processes multimodal inputs (video audio, textbook PDFs) through automatic speech recognition (Whisper), OCR (PaddleOCR), BERT-based entity recognition, relation extraction, entity disambiguation/fusion, and instructional context enrichment
- Dual Storage: Structured triples stored in Neo4j graph database; text chunks embedded as vectors in a vector database using HNSW indexing
- Q&A Layer: Hybrid retrieval (graph + vector) feeds into a RAG engine with streaming output via SSE

**Evaluation:**
- Case study used three videos (~45 min total) from a "Data Structures and Algorithms" course on "Stacks and Queues" plus corresponding textbook PDF
- Instructor review confirmed >90% of core syllabus concepts and prerequisite links were correctly identified
- Evaluation metrics included knowledge graph quality (Precision, Recall, F1), Q&A accuracy/relevance, and user satisfaction
- 50-question test set with blind evaluation by domain experts

**Key Innovations:**
- Cross-modal fusion mechanism integrating auditory knowledge (video explanations) with visual-textual knowledge (textbook content)
- Hybrid retrieval strategy balancing logical grounding (graph) and semantic flexibility (vectors)
- Human-in-the-loop maintenance via Knowledge Graph Review Interface and continuous feedback loop

This open-access study (published in *Applied Sciences*, Vol. 15, Issue 3, February 2025) presents an AI-based sports broadcasting system capable of real-time game analysis and automated commentary for basketball games. The system was developed by researchers Sunghoon Jung, Hanmoe Kim, Hyunseo Park, and Ahyoung Choi from the Department of AI and Software, Gachon University, Republic of Korea.

**Methodology:**
- The system first acquires background knowledge (court layout, game rules, team/player info).
- YOLO model-based segmentation is applied for local camera view court recognition.
- Player actions and ball tracking are performed via YOLO algorithms; a proposed tracking algorithm computes IoU from previous frames to link bounding boxes and track player movement paths.
- Player behavior is detected using the R(2+1)D action recognition model (actions: running, dribbling, shooting, blocking).

- Action recognition: SpaceJam dataset (49,901 augmented data points)

**System Architecture:**
- Uses AWS S3 for video storage, Lambda triggers for model execution, GPU endpoints (FastAPI) for model inference.
- Processes a 20-second video in approximately 1 minute; requires minimum 16 fps for commentary generation.

2. Incorporates domain-specific basketball knowledge to distinguish teams, players, referees, and in-bounds/out-of-bounds events.

**Key Models Discussed:**
- **OpenPose** (2017, Carnegie Mellon): 135 landmarks, 2D, multi-person detection. Widely used but computationally expensive.

1. **Posture Analysis**: ML PEMs automate anatomical landmark detection for objective posture assessment. A study on 200 healthy adults found significant sex differences in shoulder and hip adduction angles (ICC up to 0.95).

3. **Sports Motion Analysis**: Enables in-field and post-match analysis. OpenPose showed high validity for squat assessment (ICC 0.92-0.96). Challenges remain with accuracy under varying conditions (camera angles, lighting).

5. **Remote Physical Activity Tracking**: Applications like PoseBuddy and ExerCam use ML PEMs for telerehabilitation, exercise correction, and real-time feedback.

**Key Problem:** Existing deep learning models for action recognition rely on fixed, predefined human skeletal topologies and struggle to adapt to individual differences in sensor placement, limiting their generalization across users and devices.

**Core Innovation:** The framework strategically initializes a learnable adjacency matrix with a human skeleton prior (ensuring biomechanically plausible connections) and then refines it through end-to-end training. --- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | Multimodal human action recognition and personalized sports health promotion: a deep learning framework integrating wearable sensor fusion ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurorobotics/articles/10.3389/fnbot.2026.1785114/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Neurorobotics on April 10, 2026 (Volume 20), authored by Ying Xi, Taibin Huang, and Zhiyu Yang from the School of Physical, Xinyu University, Jiangxi, China. The study proposes a multimodal human action recognition (HAR) framework for personalized sports health promotion, integrating wearable sensor fusion with deep learning.

**Background:** Traditional HAR methods rely on camera-based visual recognition, which suffers from lighting, occlusion, and privacy issues. Wearable sensor-based approaches offer more discreet, continuous monitoring, but a gap remains between accurate activity recognition and personalized, real-time interventions.

**Methods:** The system uses a layered architecture:
- **Sensing layer:** Wearable sensor array capturing 12-dimensional multimodal data (3-axis acceleration, heart rate variability, galvanic skin response, environmental parameters) at 50–200 Hz dynamic frequency modulation via BLE 5.2.
- **Preprocessing layer:** Adaptive pipeline with wavelet threshold denoising (Daubechies9), LSTM-based imputation for missing data, Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) for alignment, and sliding window segmentation (2-s windows, 50% overlap).
- **Core analysis layer:** Transformer-GCN hybrid model (8-head self-attention, 512-dim hidden layer, GCN with skeleton topology adjacency matrix) for spatiotemporal feature extraction, with Federated Learning (FedAvg) for privacy preservation.
- **Real-time intervention module:** Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement learning dynamically generates personalized exercise prescriptions (type, duration, intensity) based on user health goals, real-time physiological indicators, and fatigue states.

**Key Results:**
- **Action recognition accuracy:** Transformer-GCN achieved an average accuracy of 95.16% across five activity types (Running 98.2%, Jumping 95.6%, Squat 94.8%, Stretching 96.9%, Bending 90.3%), outperforming LSTM and CNN baselines.
- **12-week Randomized Controlled Trial (40 participants):** The intervention group (n=20) showed a 20.1% increase in VO2max (from 41.295 to 49.615 mL/kg/min, p<0.001) and a 99.3% improvement in muscular endurance (push-ups from 22.95 to 45.75), compared to 3.9% and 35.5% in the control group (n=20). Cohen's d values of 1.51 and 1.48 indicated substantial practical significance.
- **Safety:** Sports injury rate was maintained below 15% in the intervention group versus 45% in the control group (p<0.05).
- **System robustness:** After preprocessing, SNR improved across all sensors (e.g., accelerometer from 15.2 to 28.7 dB), feature retention >96%, alignment error <12 ms. Edge inference latency on smartphones with TensorRT was 8.7 ms, well under the 30 ms physiological response threshold.
- **PPO algorithm performance:** Converged in ~80 episodes with average reward 94.8, adaptability score of 9/10, significantly outperforming rule-based strategies.

**Conclusion:** The proposed multimodal fusion architecture effectively bridges the gap between action recognition and personalized sports health intervention, providing a practical solution for AI-driven motion analysis and adaptive health promotion in land sports scenarios.
</summary>

URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2501.03103v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents MVP (Multimodal for Video and Physio), a novel transformer-based architecture for emotion recognition that fuses facial video data with physiological signals (ECG/PPG and EDA). The key innovation is enabling the use of long input sequences (1-2 minutes) through attention mechanisms, addressing limitations of prior approaches that use short 10-second segments or traditional machine learning pipelines.

The authors systematically study video backbones (comparing VideoMAE deep learning features vs. Action Units extracted via OpenFace) and physiological backbones (1D-CNN + MLP for full-length sequences). They find that Action Units outperform VideoMAE features for video, and their full-sequence physiological backbone outperforms the state-of-the-art 10-second segment approach by ~3 percentage points.

The MVP architecture uses mid-fusion cross-attention, where physiological data serves as queries and video data as keys/values. Experiments on AMIGOS and DEAP datasets show MVP achieves state-of-the-art results: on AMIGOS, MVP achieves 58±6 F1 for arousal and 66±4 F1 for valence (multimodal), outperforming classical ML approaches (SVM, MLP) and adapted transformer baselines. On DEAP, MVP achieves 55±5 F1 for arousal and 61±4 F1 for valence.

Key contributions: (1) comprehensive study of video and physiological backbones for long sequences, (2) MVP architecture for fusing video and physiological signals, (3) state-of-the-art results demonstrating that combining behavioral and physiological components outperforms each modality individually. Code is available on GitHub.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS blog post (published Feb 2021) describes a multimodal deep learning approach for sports event detection developed by the Amazon ML Solutions Lab using Amazon SageMaker. The solution combines video (RGB frames), optical flow, and audio data to improve event detection performance while minimizing the impact of low-quality data.

**Dataset:** The Sports-1 Million dataset was used, containing 400 classes of sports video clips. The authors selected 89 frequently occurring sports and consolidated them into 25 classes: americanfootball, athletics, badminton, baseball, basketball, bowling, boxing, cricket, cycling, fieldhockey, football, formula1, golf, gymnastics, handball, icehockey, lacrosse, rugby, skiing, soccer, swimming, tabletennis, tennis, volleyball, wrestling.

**Data Processing:** Videos were cut into 1-second intervals (~190,000 clips), from which approximately 3.8 million frames were extracted. Multi-processing on a SageMaker notebook (ml.c5.large instance with 64 cores) was used to parallelize the clip extraction. Data was split 80/10/10 for training/validation/test sets using stratified sampling.

**Three Modalities:**
1. **Computer Vision (RGB):** Fine-tuned ResNet50 architecture on extracted frames using a two-step approach (10 epochs with last layer unfrozen, then 30 epochs with all layers unfrozen). Training used TensorFlow with Horovod on AWS Deep Learning AMI instances.
2. **Optical Flow:** ResNet50 architecture trained on dense optical flow features (using OpenCV's Farnebäck algorithm) to capture motion between consecutive frames.
3. **Audio:** MobileNetV2 architecture trained on Mel Spectrogram and MFCC features extracted from audio samples in M4A format.

**Postprocessing:** A boosting algorithm using majority voting combined predictions from all three modalities at the 1-second level, then converted to video-level predictions. The RGB model performed best for most classes, while the audio model performed best for badminton.

**Results:** The multimodal approach improved performance by 5.10% over single RGB model, 55.68% over optical flow alone, and 34.2% over audio alone for the 25-class classification task. The postprocessing module allows updates after new training to enhance model performance.
</summary>

Authors include Mustafa Hikmet Bilgehan Uçar, Serdar Solak, Ali Olow Jimale, Hakan Ünal, and Süleyman Eken.

**Key Content:**
- **Scope:** Comprehensive survey of pose estimation and tracking technologies applied to sports, covering traditional approaches (geometric/statistical models) and the transformative impact of deep learning (CNNs, transformers, hybrid architectures).

- **Challenges Identified:** Occlusions (body parts obstructed), variable lighting conditions, rapid/unpredictable motion, dynamic backgrounds, and computational efficiency.
- **Technologies Covered:** CNNs, transformers, RNNs, multi-modal data fusion (depth maps, wearable sensors, multi-camera systems), and hybrid architectures.
- **Datasets & Ground-Truthing:** Discusses creation of sports-specific datasets emphasizing multimodal data, scalability, and representativeness.
- **Future Directions:** Integration of multimodal data, edge computing, ethical considerations, and improving accuracy, interpretability, and generalizability.
- **Metrics:** The article has 7883 Accesses, 4 Citations, and 1 Altmetric score as of publication.

The study addresses challenges in human pose estimation for sports training within IoT environments, particularly real-time processing and accuracy during high-speed movements. The authors propose a novel dual-channel architecture combining a Spatiotemporal Transformer and a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), integrated into an IoT system. The model collects real-time motion data through IoT devices (videos, depth information, and sensor data), combining global spatiotemporal features with local temporal dependencies.

The Spatiotemporal Transformer uses multi-head self-attention to process global features, while the TCN captures local temporal dependencies across frames. A residual fusion mechanism integrates these features for comprehensive pose estimation.

Extensive experiments on Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP datasets demonstrate significant outperformance over existing methods, achieving Mean Per Joint Position Error (MPJPE) scores of 42.2 mm and 29.1 mm on Human3.6M. --- SOURCE 5: Deep learning-based human body pose estimation in providing feedback for physical movement: A review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11401083

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Heliyon (2024) by Tharatipyakul, Srikaewsiew, and Pongnumkul, examining deep learning-based human body pose estimation for providing feedback on physical movement. The authors systematically reviewed 45 articles from Scopus and Web of Science across four domains: exercise (26 articles), sports (8 articles), performing arts (4 articles), and healthcare (7 articles).

The paper analyzes three key modules in physical movement feedback systems:
1. **Pose Estimation**: Primarily uses CNNs, with popular libraries including OpenPose, MediaPipe, PoseNet/MoveNet, and custom CNN architectures. Most systems use a single general camera/video input, though mobile cameras, binocular/multiple cameras, and depth-sensing cameras (Kinect, RealSense) are also used.
2. **Movement Assessment**: Methods vary from mathematical formulas/models, rule-based approaches, to machine learning. Pre-processing is commonly applied to keypoints before assessment.
3. **Augmented Feedback Presentation**: Feedback is primarily presented visually in verbal forms (text, scores) and nonverbal forms (visual overlays, color changes, graphical representations). Feedback types include knowledge of results (KR) and knowledge of performance (KP), delivered either concurrently or terminally.

Key findings include:
- Pose estimation libraries (OpenPose, MediaPipe) play a crucial role in advancing this field
- The effectiveness and factors for choosing movement assessment methods for new contexts remain unclear
- More studies are needed on feedback prioritization and handling erroneous feedback
- The gap in existing literature is that prior reviews had not examined how applications assess movement and provide feedback to users

The methodology followed PRISMA guidelines, with searches conducted in July 2022 and March 2024. The authors focused on methods rather than experimental results, reporting how experiments were conducted rather than assessing risk of bias.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 11: Sports training in virtual reality with a focus on visual perception: a systematic review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11966202

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review published in *Frontiers in Sports and Active Living* (2025) by Witte, Bürger, and Pastel, examining virtual reality (VR) sports training with a focus on visual perception. The review analyzed 58 articles (12 reviews, 46 research articles) from PsychInfo, Pubmed, Scopus, SportDiscus, and IEEE Explore, published between January 2015 and March 2024.

**Objectives:**
1. Identify sports domains and disciplines where VR has been used with visual components.
2. Identify requirements for visualizing the user's body and other players in VR.
3. Determine which visualization options enable successful transfer of VR training effects to real-world (RE) athletic performance.

**Key Findings:**
- Early VR applications focused on endurance sports (cycling, running, rowing), but within the last 5 years, VR has expanded to almost all sports including team sports, martial arts, and individual sports.
- Common VR applications include motor learning, visual perception training, decision-making, anticipation skills, and sport-specific training.
- VR offers visualization options such as: different viewing perspectives, variation of movement speed, virtual mirrors, body part visualization, visual manipulation for identifying important stimuli, movement trajectory displays, and graphic aids.
- Limitations of current HMDs include restricted field of view (e.g., HTC Vive Pro: 94° horizontal vs. human ~200°), lower resolution, and the vergence-accommodation conflict affecting depth perception.
- For body visualization, a complete virtual body representation (exact equivalent of the user's real body using high-precision 3D scans and markerless tracking) is recommended to improve immersion and distance estimation.
- Evidence on transfer from VR to RE remains mixed: 10 of 12 VR intervention studies found positive transfer effects in target sports and bat/racquet sports, but one study found VR-trained groups performed significantly worse in dart-throwing accuracy than real-world-trained groups.
- The review recommends future studies compare VR training with real conditions, investigate transfer effects, use eye-tracking to compare visual perception in VR vs. reality, and examine optimal frequency, duration, and intensity of VR training.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: An Architecture for Intelligent Tutoring in Virtual Reality: Integrating LLMs and Multimodal Interaction for Immersive Learning ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/16/7/556

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents an open-access academic article titled "An Architecture for Intelligent Tutoring in Virtual Reality: Integrating LLMs and Multimodal Interaction for Immersive Learning," published in the journal *Information* (Volume 16, Issue 7, 556) on June 29, 2025. The authors are Mohamed El Hajji, Tarek Ait Baha, Anas Berka, Hassan Ait Nacer, Houssam El Aouifi, and Youssef Es-Saady, affiliated with Ibnou Zohr University in Morocco.

The paper proposes an architecture for intelligent tutoring in immersive VR environments that uses LLM-based non-playable characters (NPCs). Key capabilities include natural language understanding, real-time adaptive dialogue, and multimodal interaction through hand tracking, gaze detection, and haptic feedback. The system synchronizes speech output with NPC animations to enhance interactional realism and cognitive immersion.

**Methodology and Architecture:** The system uses a pipeline where user speech is captured via microphone, transcribed using OpenAI's Whisper (STT), processed by a locally deployed LLM (either llama3.2:3b or Deepseek-r1:14b depending on hardware), and converted back to speech via the Kokoro TTS model. Lip movements are synchronized using Oculus Lipsync with visemes. The system employs a structured, role-based prompt design with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, enabling the NPC tutor to adapt explanations based on user expertise level (e.g., beginner vs. advanced). The virtual environment is built in Unity using the Universal Render Pipeline (URP), with avatars generated via ReadyPlayerMe. NPC interaction uses raycasting mechanics.

**Comparison with Existing Systems:** The proposed framework is compared against LearningVerseVR, VREd, and a VR NPC-based tutoring system, showing advantages in real-time adaptivity, locally deployed LLM, real-time lip synchronization, multimodal input (speech, gaze, gesture), pedagogical flexibility via role-based behavior and CoT prompting, and broad platform compatibility.

**Results:** System performance was generally stable, though minor latency was observed during speech processing. The research highlights the potential of AI-driven VR interactions to improve learner engagement and emphasizes the need for ongoing optimization in immersive learning contexts.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Frontiers | Research on an intelligent tutoring system based on automatic construction of multimodal knowledge graphs and retrieval-augmented generation ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/computer-science/articles/10.3389/fcomp.2026.1777749/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Frontiers in Computer Science research article (published February 25, 2026) proposing an Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS) based on the automatic construction of multimodal knowledge graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The system addresses key challenges in ITS development: the costly manual knowledge base construction, difficulty handling unstructured teaching resources, and issues with large language models such as factual inaccuracies (hallucination) and insufficient reasoning.

**Key Contributions:**
1. A cross-modal knowledge fusion pipeline that aligns and merges entities from video transcripts (via FFmpeg + Whisper ASR) and textbook PDFs (via OCR, layout analysis, and BERT-based extraction) into a unified multimodal knowledge graph.
2. A hybrid retrieval-augmented paradigm combining precise relational queries from a Neo4j graph database with semantic similarity matching from a vector database (HNSW indexing), driving a RAG engine for accurate, explainable answers.
3. Direct processing of unstructured course videos as the primary knowledge source, broadening ITS applicability in online education.

**System Architecture:**
- **Knowledge Construction Layer:** Processes multimodal inputs (video audio → Whisper transcription; PDFs → OCR/layout analysis → semantic chunking). Extracts entities and relationships using BERT-based models, performs entity disambiguation/fusion, and enriches with instructional context (core concepts, prerequisite relations). Stores in Neo4j (graph triples) and vector database (embeddings).
- **Q&A Interaction Layer:** Hybrid retrieval combines graph queries (Cypher) and vector similarity search, weighted by a composite scoring function. The LLM generates answers grounded in retrieved context, with streaming output via SSE.

**Evaluation:**
A case study on a "Data Structures and Algorithms" course (45 min of video + textbook PDF on "Stacks and Queues") was conducted. Evaluation covered: (1) Knowledge graph quality (precision, recall, F1-score on 300 sampled sentences with expert annotation); (2) pedagogical logic consistency (instructor confirmed >90% of core syllabus concepts correctly identified); (3) Q&A performance (50-question test set across definition, characteristics, comparison, and application types, blind-evaluated by domain experts on accuracy and relevance).

The system's modular, domain-agnostic design supports cross-disciplinary scalability, and a "human-in-the-loop" maintenance mechanism allows instructors to review and correct extracted knowledge via a dedicated interface, with user feedback driving continuous improvement.
</summary>

The article systematically reviews Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) for psychomotor skills—skills requiring physical movement, coordination, and mental processing. The authors note that while ITS have been successful in cognitive domains, research progress in psychomotor skills seems stagnating, partly due to developing ITS for very specific skills.

**Methods:** The authors conducted a systematic literature review using Harrow's taxonomy (to classify skill proficiency), a skill continua framework (to classify skill types), and dimensions of psychomotor skill learning.

**Key Findings:**
- ITS for psychomotor skills predominantly target fine, closed, internally paced, discrete, individual, and simple skills.
- ITS focus mainly on technical/coordination aspects of motor abilities.
- Feedback and repetition are the primary methods used to promote psychomotor skill learning.
- There is a lack of consideration for offering different tasks to promote skill proficiency.
- The cognitive domain is often implicitly present in ITS, but the affective domain is neglected.

**Research Questions Addressed:**
1. RQ1: What is the general state-of-the-art of ITS for psychomotor skills?
2. RQ2: To what extent does the state-of-the-art ITS provide a holistic solution for developing psychomotor skills?

**Theoretical Background:** The paper discusses five psychomotor taxonomies (Dave, Simpson, Harrow, Thomas, and Ferris & Aziz), with Harrow's taxonomy selected as most suitable because it includes physical abilities (strength, flexibility) and non-discursive communication. The skill continua framework covers six dimensions: granularity (fine-gross), environment (open-close), pace (internally-externally paced), continuity (discrete-serial-continuous), interactivity (individual-coactive-interactive), and complexity (simple-complex). The dimensions of psychomotor skill learning examined include strength, flexibility, coordination, speed, team, and mental training.

**Conclusions:** The authors identify potential for exploring ITS for gross and open skills, integrating tasks targeting motor abilities like strength or flexibility, and incorporating theories from related fields such as training periodization. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908)Abstract

Current trends in sports monitoring are characterized by the massive collection of tech-based biomechanical, physiological and performance data, integrated through mathematical algorithms. However, the application of algorithms, predicated on mechanistic assumptions of how athletes operate, cannot capture, assess and adequately promote athletes’ health and performance. The objective of this paper is to reorient the current integrative proposals of sports monitoring by re-conceptualizing athletes as complex adaptive systems (CAS). CAS contain higher-order perceptual units that provide continuous and multilevel integrated information about performer–environment interactions. Such integrative properties offer exceptional possibilities of subjective monitoring for outperforming any objective monitoring system. Future research should investigate how to enhance this human potential to contribute further to athletes’ health and performance. This line of argument is not intended to advocate for the elimination of objective assessments, but to highlight the integrative possibilities of subjective monitoring.

**Keywords:**Complex adaptive systems, Self-regulation, Technology, Awareness, Health, Performance

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908)Key Points

There is a disconnect between the complexity underpinning human health and performance and the deterministic models through which athletic monitoring and assessment are conceptualized.While focusing on collecting and processing large amounts of data, analysts, scientists and coaches may forget the outstanding potential of the human neurobiological system to dynamically, and rapidly, integrate massive amounts of personal and environmental information.Understanding and valuing subjective-based monitoring are crucial to enhance athletes’ awareness and promote their self-consciousness, autonomy and self-regulation of health and performance.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908)Introduction

In sporting contexts, the use of monitoring tools and physical activity trackers providing training and general health data has recently expanded dramatically. In 1954, hand-timing regular training runs was considered unusual [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR1)]. However, as technology, beginning in the early 1980s, began to rapidly evolve, new possibilities to assess internal and external training loads during training and competition became available [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR1)]. Today, new wireless technologies are expanding to provide simultaneous data related to biomechanical, physiological and performance variables [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR2)–[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR5)].

Compiling and integrating multiple internal and external variables through a variety of mathematical algorithms (e.g., ACWR) [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR6)–[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR8)] and making predictions on the basis of artificial intelligence software [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR9), [10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR10)] seem to be leading current, and future, steps in sports monitoring. In effect, there appears to be a tacit assumption that the collection of objective ‘big data’ is the key to provide more pertinent and relevant information to promote athletes’ health and improve athletic performance [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR11)]. Further, moves towards cyborgization—the integration of measurement and computational technologies into human bodies [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR12), [13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR13)]—suggest that current trends of sports monitoring are continuing to evolve towards the tracking of ever-increasing streams of objective data.

Accordingly, coaches and sports scientists are motivated to collect a growing diversity of data, using an array of commercially available assessment technologies [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR14)]. Professional sport organizations are also investing heavily (in terms of time, money and specialized human resources) in new technologies. Providing previously unavailable metrics (e.g., acceleration) without any clear vision of how the new information will be interpreted and actioned appears to be the rule [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR14)]. This approach, however, is not well aligned to the scientific ideal of developing models and hypotheses and then testing deductively. Instead, there is a commercial drive to develop new technologies in advance of hypotheses, to market these technologies based on non-existent or insufficient evidence and to encourage practitioners to embark on little more than 'fishing expeditions' to see what new technologies may offer [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR15)].

The expansive range of emerging technologies may leave analysts and sports science practitioners struggling to deal with collecting, processing and interpreting large quantities of objective data, as occurs, for example, in elite soccer contexts [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR16), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR17)]. This, potentially excessive, focuses on objective data may serve to distract practitioners from the outstanding potential of humans to innately integrate and process multiple streams of highly sophisticated information at high speed [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR18)]. Although objective data may be helpful in some contexts (e.g., position data of teams, athletes’ physiological response) [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR19), [20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR20)], it may not inevitably lead to greater insight and better understanding of health and performance [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR21)]. Importantly, there is a clear and problematic disconnect between the neurobiological complexity underpinning human performance and the mechanistic, deterministic, albeit complicated and intricate, biomedical model through which we conventionally conceptualize both athletic training paradigms and athletic assessment protocols [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR22)–[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR24)].

This apparent disconnect highlights an evident need to evaluate the advantages and costs of technology-enabled objective information against those of athlete-generated subjective information for continuously integrating multilevel, multisource and multimodal information. Accordingly, the objective of this paper is to reorient the current integrative proposals of sports monitoring by re-conceptualizing athletes as CAS.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908)Monitoring Complex Adaptive Systems

Contemporary athletic monitoring philosophies perpetuate a mechanistic and reductionist philosophical stance in sports training that envisions athletes and teams as linear, deterministic systems composed by multiple components. This view, founded in an historically pervasive, but scientifically inaccurate conception, guides coach decision-making processes in relation to athletes’ health prevention and performance [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR7), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR25)].

Neurobiological systems are seen as dominated by components that establish inherently linear, deterministic cause-and-effect relationships among them. Such deterministic systems, when perturbed, respond to imposed stimuli with proportional and predictable adaptive responses as an externally predesigned product of their component behaviours. Yet, across the biological and neurological sciences, this conventional biomedical interpretation has been overthrown by the overwhelming evidence illustrating that human neurobiology is more appropriately conceptualized as a CAS: a nonlinear and dynamic system comprised of multiple embedded complex sub-systems which collaboratively and collectively share co-modulating information both vertically (e.g., genes, cells, tissues, organs, etc.) and horizontally (e.g., among molecules, cells, organs, etc.) to support the continued survival of the unified whole [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR22), [26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR26)].

Sport behaviours, accordingly, are guided and constrained by an embedded and embodied, experience-dependent and goal-directed performer–environment interactions. Hence, athletes’ self-monitoring and self-regulation are important competencies of biological intelligence to perform in cooperative–competitive environments [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR27)].

The failings of applying traditional linear logic to complex sport phenomena have been previously reported, such as in the case of sport injuries [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR14), [28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR28)–[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR31)]. For example, the critical tensile forces that produce muscle rupture in vitro cannot be directly transferred to the complex muscle contraction in vivo [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR23), [32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR32)]. Over the past two decades, the science of complex systems, and particularly the nonlinear dynamic systems theory, has begun to percolate into various branches of sports science [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR22), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR23), [33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR33)–[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR35)]. Recently, the network physiology of exercise—a framework studying the nested dynamics of vertical and horizontal physiological network interactions to understand how physiological states and functions emerge—has been introduced to exercise [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR22), [26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR26)]. This complex system-based approach appears more capable of eloquently capturing the theoretically and methodologically sport-related phenomena such as injuries [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR29), [30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR30)], fatigue [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR36), [37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR37)] or motor control and learning [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR38)–[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR40)].

In contrast to complicated machines, CAS’ behaviours cannot be accurately predicted from a particular variable or set of variables. While machine behaviours emerge as a product of their individual component behaviours, in CAS, characterized by an interaction-dominant dynamics, behaviour emerges as a product of the nonlinear integration of personal and environmental influences acting across multiple levels and timescales [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR45), [46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR46)]. A fundamental implication of this inherent and undeniable complexity is that, in the context of complex biological and/or medical contexts, fragmented metrics or even the aggregation of multiple metrics, do not appear to provide meaningful predictive validity [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR47), [48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR48)].

Therefore, some authors have questioned the logic underpinning contemporary trends in sports monitoring [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR21)]. They point out that the empirical assessment of surrogate measures of activity intensity, or isolated measures of physical function, even when blended using integrative algorithms or machine learning techniques, does not provide sufficiently reflective snapshots of current health status and/or performance potential. The prevailing fallacy of completing the puzzle through large quantities of multidimensional (e.g., biomechanical, behavioural, morphological, etc.) athlete-centred objective information lacks theoretical support in uncertain and complex scenarios [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR49), [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR50)]. Collecting isolated snapshots of a limited number of quantifiable measures, in the absence of a clearly defined and appropriately weighted relational hierarchy of performance priorities, promotes a distorted reality [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR51), [52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR52)]. Importantly, these misleading distortions serve to inappropriately prioritize readily accessible, while neglecting seemingly inaccessible, information [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR6), [7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR7), [53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR53)–[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR55)]. A famous quote says ‘not everything that counts can be counted, and not everything that can be counted counts’ [[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR56)].

The perpetuation of protocols and procedures developed under the influence of this conventional biomedical depiction of the brain _as a (predominantly) passive, stimulus-driven organ that_ waits to receive sensory feedback before processing data and generating responses [[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR57)] continues to shape coaches–athlete interactions. The conception of athletes’ as mere executors of coaching instructions does not promote athletes’ awareness, such as quality of attention, depth of understanding and the athletes’ perception of the utility and value of subjective monitoring processes [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR23)]. In addition, this perception dramatically oversimplifies the nature, relevance and influence of interpersonal interactions between coaches, athletes and teams [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR22), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR23)]. Through this conceptual lens, the properties which enable CAS to spontaneously, dynamically and adaptively customize behavioural responses to continuously changing context-specific demands are typically either ignored or despised.

As shown in Table [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#Tab1), acknowledging athletes as CAS drives a reframing of the training process: an appreciation of the mutually entwined integration between biopsychosocial influences, training workloads and training outcomes, while also highlighting existing limitations of conventional athletic monitoring.

In Table [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#Tab2), the traditional role of coaches is re-envisioned. Instead of fixing objectives and task outcomes, and controlling workloads based on personal opinion blended with monitoring information, through the lens of a CAS-informed philosophy the coach is better perceived as a co-learner, a co-designer and a co-adapter of the training process [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR23)]. A mentor, over time, facilitates the athletes’ journey from dependency to autonomy. Athletes in turn, instead of being mere executers of the coaches’ directives, participate actively in the process, cooperating with the coach in the design and adaptation of training workloads. Although conventional monitoring tools can complement co-designed training processes, the key sources of information come from the athletes’ subjective perceptions.

CAS’ approaches have promoted subjective monitoring [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR22), [29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR29), [58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR58)] but also objective monitoring connected to new methods of analysis or old methods applied to new phenomena [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR22), [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR59)]. Based on coordination dynamics properties, such methods aim to gain new insights into the changing relationships between groups of variables. Uncontrolled manifold method to capture interpersonal synergies in sport [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR60)], squared coherence to capture cardiorespiratory coupling on acute hypoxia [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR61)], network analysis to capture multilevel organs’ interactions [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR26), [62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR62)] or fractal analysis to capture physiological or kinematic variability of athletes in exhausting exercises [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR36), [37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR37)] may stand as examples. The applicability of this approach, together with the development of adequate technology, should enable in the future a more effective, integrative and realistic encapsulation of CAS’ behaviours. For example, cardiorespiratory coordination variables, extracted by a principal component analysis approach, seem to be more sensitive than common measures (e.g., VO 2max or ventilatory thresholds) to reveal specific training adaptations [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR63), [64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR64)], testing manipulations [[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR65)], workload accumulation [[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR66)] and nutritional interventions [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR67)].

However, at this moment the capacity to quantify, process and instantaneously integrate, interpret and deliver multilevel and multidimensional information may not work if attempted. In contrast, subjective monitoring may provide a practical, efficient and effective means of acquiring continuous high-level actionable information [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR22), [29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR29), [58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR58)].

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908)Subjective and Objective Sports Monitoring: Advantages and Limitations

Subjective and objective sports monitoring are distinct in acquiring information and their interpretations do not always agree [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR18), [68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR68)–[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR72)]. As illustrated in Fig.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#Fig1), objective monitoring commonly fragments the scale of observations to permit the quantitative precision of isolated metrics. Instead of fragmenting, subjective monitoring enables re-composition, integration and dimensional reduction, e.g., compression of psychological, biomechanical and physiological information. Thereby, the generation of subjective perceptions reflects the blended inputs of multiple channels of information, including the organism–environment interaction, highly relevant for health/performance regulation [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR24), [73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR73)]. General health, well-being, recovery, happiness, readiness to train, stress and mood, all stand as examples [[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR74)]. Subjective monitoring may also integrate multiple dimensions of awareness, such as proprioceptive [[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR75)], kinaesthetic [[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR76)], body [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR77)–[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR79)], somatic [[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR80)], interoceptive [[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR81)–[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR84)], environmental [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR85)]. Some authors have defined the in situ interactions of these various flavours of awareness, as prospective situational awareness, conceptualizing it under the term of informed awareness [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR85)–[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR87)]. In that regard, in comparison with conventional objective monitoring, subjective data collection provides opportunities to capture and integrate online multiple streams of relevant and actionable sensory and perceptual information. The potential of such multidimensional subjective information, dwelling at different timescales [[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR88), [89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8964908#CR89)], relates to the sensitivity for capturing the relevant changes of the organism–environment interaction.Fig. 1Integrative proposals of objective and subjective monitoring. Objective monitoring:"integration achieved by algorithmic treatment of a collection of independent variables". Subjective monitoring: "integration achieved by experiential dimensional reduction (i.e.,information compression) of multilevel organism–environment interactions acting at multiple timescales".
