## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155)Abstract

With the increasing need for precision and personalization in athletic training, artificial intelligence (AI) offers powerful tools for monitoring, evaluating, and optimizing athlete performance. This study presents a Generalized Adaptive Backpropagation (GABP) neural network that combines Genetic Algorithms (GA) with Backpropagation (BP) to model physiological adaptation and guide data-driven training decisions. The proposed system is designed specifically for sports training contexts, emphasizing real-time feedback and individualized load management based on multivariate physiological inputs. The GABP model extends traditional backpropagation networks by incorporating genetic algorithms, which accelerate convergence, reduce the risk of local minima, and enhance predictive accuracy. By integrating diverse input modalities–such as physical performance indicators, training schedules, and biometric data from wearables, video analysis, and electromyography (EMG)–the system achieves high-precision evaluation of training effectiveness. In addition to detecting fatigue and performance plateaus, the model provides interpretable insights to refine training strategies at both individual and programmatic levels. Experimental validation on physiological datasets demonstrates measurable improvements in prediction accuracy and convergence efficiency. This work contributes a domain-specific, interpretable, and adaptive modeling framework for modern sports science, supporting personalized coaching and intelligent performance monitoring.

**Keywords:**Artificial Intelligence, Sports Training, GABP Neural Network, Genetic Algorithm, Athletic Performance Optimization

**Subject terms:**Engineering, Mathematics and computing

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155)Introduction

In recent years, the demand for scientific, personalized, and efficient sports training programs has significantly increased, driven by growing health awareness and the development of competitive sports[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR1). Traditional training methods, though partially effective, often depend on subjective assessments from coaches and lack the capacity to systematically model and quantify physiological responses and performance-related metrics[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR2). The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into sports training not only enhances the objectivity and precision of performance assessment but also enables real-time feedback and adaptive training strategies[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR3). Neural networks have demonstrated strong capabilities in modeling high-dimensional and nonlinear data common in sports science, particularly for predicting and optimizing training outcomes. Among these, the Generalized Adaptive Backpropagation (GABP) network is a notable variant that enhances weight update mechanisms and accelerates convergence, enabling more precise modeling of complex physiological and biomechanical responses[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR4). Therefore, research on sports training effects based on GABP neural networks and AI is not only timely but also essential for revolutionizing training paradigms and achieving individualized sports coaching systems[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR5).

Early attempts to support sports training relied on symbolic AI and knowledge representation[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR6), where rule-based systems and domain-specific ontologies were employed to model training strategies and athlete profiles[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR7). Expert systems encoded coaching heuristics into logical rules, while knowledge graphs mapped relationships between training stimuli and performance outcomes[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR8). Although these symbolic approaches provided structure and transparency, they were limited in adaptability and heavily reliant on the completeness of predefined rules[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR9). More critically, they could not learn from data, rendering them ineffective in modeling the nonlinear, dynamic patterns seen in physiological signals and biomechanical behavior. As a result, research shifted toward data-driven models capable of learning directly from empirical observations[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR10).

To overcome the rigidity of symbolic systems, supervised machine learning (ML) techniques were introduced to analyze large datasets from athletes, including motion capture, heart rate, and biometric signals[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR11). Algorithms such as decision trees, support vector machines (SVM), and k-nearest neighbors (KNN) were used to detect training effectiveness, classify movement patterns, and flag performance anomalies[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR12). These models improved adaptability and required fewer handcrafted rules, but they still relied on manual feature engineering and struggled with temporal dependencies[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR13). Moreover, their performance was sensitive to data quality, which is a challenge in sports settings where signals are often noisy, sparse, or irregularly sampled[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR14). These constraints limited their effectiveness for continuous performance monitoring.

Deep learning methods emerged to address these limitations by enabling automatic feature extraction and end-to-end modeling of sequential data[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR15). Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architectures were applied to video[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR16), biomechanical sequences, and physiological time series[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR17). These models captured both spatial and temporal dependencies critical for performance interpretation. More recently, adaptive variants such as GABP neural networks have been explored to improve training efficiency and personalization[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR18). By introducing adaptive learning rates and dynamic feedback mechanisms, GABP networks optimize the backpropagation process and reduce overfitting, making them particularly effective in personalized sports training scenarios[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR19). While deep learning has improved modeling fidelity, it remains constrained by high data and computational demands[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR20).

Building on this progression, this study proposes a novel training analysis framework based on the Generalized Adaptive Backpropagation (GABP) neural network. Designed specifically for athlete modeling, the proposed system integrates adaptive weight adjustment and real-time feedback mechanisms to address nonlinearity and inter-individual variability in physiological responses. Integrating this with real-time feedback systems enhances the model’s applicability in diverse training scenarios. This approach improves the prediction of training outcomes and enables continuous optimization, fostering intelligent decision-making in sports coaching and athlete development. By focusing on interpretable modeling and personalized evaluation, our method contributes to the development of a responsive, evidence-driven sports training system that advances beyond the limitations of symbolic, conventional ML, and standard deep learning approaches.The proposed framework introduces a novel GABP-based training evaluation model, enhancing learning precision and stability through adaptive weight adjustments.It features high generalizability across different sports scenarios, with efficient real-time feedback integration for personalized training adaptation.Experimental results achieve a 15% improvement in prediction accuracy–supporting more precise identification of fatigue trends–and a 30% reduction in convergence time, enabling faster model updates in real-time training environments.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155)Related work

### GABP neural networks in sports training

The integration of Genetic Algorithm–Back Propagation (GABP) neural networks into sports training evaluation has received considerable attention in recent years. GABP networks combine the global optimization capability of genetic algorithms with the local search proficiency of backpropagation neural networks, resulting in a robust model for solving complex, nonlinear problems[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR21). In the domain of sports training, these networks have been used to develop predictive models that assess and enhance athletic performance. A notable application of GABP neural networks is the construction of models that evaluate the effects of training[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR22). By applying artificial intelligence principles, researchers have developed systems that vectorize sample matrices to enhance code conciseness and computational efficiency. These models demonstrate excellent performance in terms of training sample fitting accuracy and generalization, all while maintaining low memory consumption and reduced training time[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR23). GABP neural networks have been employed to predict sports performance by analyzing the relationships between quality training indicators and specific athletic outcomes[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR24). This approach provides a more intuitive representation of the benefits of various training methods, thereby informing the development of targeted training plans. The integration of genetic algorithms further improves neural network parameter optimization, enhancing training efficiency and reducing computational burden[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR25).

### AI-driven performance analysis tools

The advent of artificial intelligence has revolutionized performance analysis in sports by providing coaches and athletes with sophisticated tools to monitor and improve training outcomes[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR26). These AI-enabled systems allow for precise tracking of physical performance, biomechanics, and in-game behaviors, helping identify performance gaps that might otherwise go unnoticed. AI-driven evaluation tools support sports managers in making informed decisions about team composition and strategy by offering predictive analytics and real-time assessments. By utilizing data analytics and artificial neural networks, these tools enhance sports performance, management, and decision-making processes[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR27), providing insights and levels of accuracy that surpass traditional analytical approaches. A notable example involves the use of deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) to process unstructured image inputs and extract latent features from large datasets[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR28). These networks are particularly effective at identifying complex visual patterns-such as athlete posture, movement dynamics, or ball trajectories-which are critical for tailoring training programs and refining competitive strategies.

### AI in personalized training programs

Traditional training often follows a one-size-fits-all approach, which may neglect individual differences in fitness levels, biomechanics, and recovery capacity. In contrast, AI leverages data from wearable devices, fitness trackers, and comprehensive physiological assessments to customize training protocols tailored to each athlete’s unique profile[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR29). AI-powered systems can analyze large volumes of performance and health-related data to detect patterns, trends, and correlations that are not easily discernible through conventional methods. These insights enable the design of training programs that are not only personalized but also adaptive, taking into account an athlete’s strengths, weaknesses, injury history, and performance goals[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR30). For example, AI can continuously monitor metrics such as workload, heart rate variability, and sleep quality to assess recovery status and physical readiness. Based on this data, it can provide intelligent recommendations to adjust training intensity, duration, and frequency, thereby minimizing overtraining risk and promoting sustainable athletic development[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR31). The incorporation of AI into personalized training programs also plays a vital role in injury prevention. By identifying subtle abnormalities in movement or tracking physiological indicators-such as muscle fatigue or asymmetrical motion-AI can detect early warning signs of potential injury. This proactive capability allows for timely interventions, such as adjusting training loads or adding corrective exercises, to mitigate injury risks and support long-term athlete health[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR32).

Recent studies in sports science have demonstrated the importance of accurately modeling the relationship between training load and athlete-specific physiological responses. Padulo et al.[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR33) reported that variations in training intensity significantly influence running gait variability, indicating that subtle biomechanical responses can be used as feedback for optimizing workload. Similarly, Kale et al.[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR34) explored how different jump pre-conditioning routines result in measurable post-activity performance differences, highlighting the need for adaptive intervention strategies. These findings support the rationale for employing data-driven latent modeling–such as the GABP framework proposed in this study–to track individual training responses and fatigue progression over time. In parallel, advancements in sensor technologies have enabled the real-time collection of multidimensional performance data, which can be integrated into AI systems for decision-making. Gadea-Uribarri et al.[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR35) validated the use of inertial measurement units (IMUs) in live indoor sports scenarios, confirming their suitability for continuous athlete monitoring in game-like conditions. At a broader level, a systematic review by Pietraszewski et al.[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR36) synthesized trends in AI deployment across sports analytics, emphasizing its role in performance forecasting, injury risk assessment, and adaptive load planning. Together, these studies provide both empirical and theoretical support for the use of personalized, AI-driven modeling frameworks in modern training environments.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155)Experimental setup

### Dataset

TSSB Competition Dataset[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR37) is a widely recognized benchmark in the field of time series segmentation and behavior prediction. It contains a variety of multivariate time series instances captured from different dynamic systems. Each series is annotated with change points that reflect structural or behavioral transitions, making the dataset suitable for training and evaluating algorithms that aim to detect temporal shifts. The dataset includes both synthetic and real-world signals to facilitate generalized learning. The synthetic portion offers controlled complexity to examine model robustness under known variations. The real-world signals, collected from actual system logs and sensor arrays, exhibit natural noise, drift, and non-linearities. The series length varies, requiring models to handle irregular durations. It is used in annual competitions, setting a standard for performance comparison. Each instance is labeled with categorical identifiers, enabling supervised learning. Researchers utilize this dataset for benchmarking purposes in tasks involving unsupervised segmentation, anomaly detection, and multale temporal pattern discovery. UTSD Dataset[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR38) is designed for traffic scene understanding and urban trajectory analysis. It provides sequential GPS traces and visual context for vehicular and pedestrian dynamics in metropolitan areas. Collected via dashboard-mounted sensors and urban surveillance, it offers multimodal information including location, time, speed, heading, and traffic density. The data is temporally ordered and annotated with event-level transitions such as lane changes, turns, and stops. Each sequence captures real-world behaviors under diverse conditions like lighting variations and weather changes. The dataset supports research on spatiotemporal modeling, path prediction, and behavior classification. It includes manually validated labels to ensure semantic consistency across frames. The diversity in motion patterns and environmental noise enables robust learning in complex urban scenarios. With varying sequence lengths and overlapping motion types, it challenges conventional time series models to generalize across heterogeneities in urban contexts. TimeHetNet Dataset[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR39) is curated for heterogeneous temporal graph modeling tasks. It represents complex relationships between entities over time, combining sequential features with graph connectivity. Nodes represent temporal instances of various types such as users, items, and events, while edges encode their dynamic interactions. Each node is timestamped, and interactions evolve across time steps, forming a dynamic heterogeneous graph. It includes structural meta-paths and event-based sequences to capture both topological and temporal dependencies. The dataset supports tasks such as temporal node classification, event forecasting, and relation reasoning. Label imbalance and high-order dependencies are inherent characteristics, providing a realistic evaluation ground. Node attributes are multimodal, including categorical, numerical, and textual embeddings. Temporal resolution varies across entity types, introducing asynchronous evolution patterns. The dataset is widely used in research on temporal knowledge graphs, graph neural networks, and sequence-aware recommender systems. Amazon Sports Dataset[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR40) is derived from user behavior logs and product metadata on the Amazon platform, focusing on the sports category. It contains timestamped user-item interaction sequences with auxiliary features such as ratings, reviews, and product descriptions. Each sequence captures the evolution of user preferences over time. The dataset also includes static user demographics and dynamic browsing histories, enabling hybrid modeling. Product relations such as also bought, also viewed, and similar to are embedded as temporal edges, creating an interaction graph. It supports research in sequential recommendation, temporal attention mechanisms, and personalized ranking. Cold-start and sparsity are intrinsic properties, reflecting real-world e-commerce dynamics. Reviews provide rich textual context for item representation. The data is structured into sessions, and user behavior patterns exhibit seasonal and event-driven trends. Variability in interaction density across users provides a challenging benchmark for time-aware recommendation systems.

The selection of TSSB, UTSD, TimeHetNet, and Amazon Sports datasets was initially motivated by the need to validate the generalizability and sequence modeling capability of the proposed GABP framework across heterogeneous time-series environments. Although these datasets are not collected from direct sports training scenarios, each of them encapsulates key structural and temporal characteristics that are also inherent in athlete performance modeling tasks. The TSSB dataset provides structured segmentation and regime-shift patterns in multivariate signals, which reflect the kind of performance state transitions observed during different phases of training or recovery. The UTSD dataset captures human mobility and context-aware temporal shifts under real-world conditions such as lighting and environmental changes. This aligns with training monitoring tasks where athlete movements vary with context, such as weather, surface type, or session goals. TimeHetNet, with its temporal graph structure, offers a foundation for modeling complex relational dynamics over time, similar to how different physiological systems (like cardiovascular, muscular, nervous) interact during training adaptation. The Amazon Sports dataset includes user-item interaction histories that evolve temporally, resembling longitudinal training histories of athletes, where performance is influenced by prior sessions, fatigue accumulation, and recovery intervals. These datasets serve as proxy environments to assess the model’s ability to handle nonstationary, high-dimensional, and temporally dependent input sequences under varied noise and context conditions. While they are not direct representations of sports training records, their structural diversity enables rigorous stress-testing of the model’s adaptive learning capabilities. Moreover, the model architecture is designed to be domain-agnostic in structure but domain-specializable in application. This justifies using these datasets as part of the pre-deployment evaluation stage. To bridge the domain gap, additional experiments on SPHERE and WESAD datasets with real physiological data were conducted, ensuring the model is also validated in genuine sports-like conditions.

### Experimental details

All experiments were conducted using PyTorch 1.13 on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with 80GB memory. The model parameters were optimized using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 1e-4. A cosine annealing learning rate scheduler was adopted to gradually decrease the learning rate over the training epochs. For all datasets, the batch size was fixed to 64. The training process was run for 200 epochs with early stopping based on validation loss, using a patience threshold of 15 epochs. The hidden size of temporal encoders was set to 128. For graph-based modules in TimeHetNet and Amazon Sports, we used a two-layer Graph Attention Network (GAT) with 4 attention heads. The dropout rate was set to 0.3 for both attention and feedforward layers to mitigate overfitting. The input sequence lengths were determined based on the dataset characteristics. For short-span sequences such as in UTSD, we used a sliding window of 20 time steps with a stride of 5. For longer and irregular series in TSSB and Amazon Sports, the sequence length was capped at 100, and padding was applied for shorter series. Positional encodings were included to maintain temporal order. For TimeHetNet, temporal edge encodings were integrated via a relational attention mechanism, aligning with heterogeneous node types. Each dataset was split into 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% test sets. For evaluation metrics, we used F1-score, Precision, Recall, AUC, and for sequence tasks, the Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG@10) and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR@10) where appropriate. Change point detection tasks in TSSB were evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and F1-score over predicted segment boundaries. For Amazon Sports, sequential recommendation performance was measured using Hit Rate and NDCG at multiple cutoff points (5, 10, 20). We also implemented all baseline methods using their official repositories or re-implemented them following the settings described in the original papers to ensure fair comparison. Each experiment was repeated five times with different random seeds, and we report the average result with standard deviation. Hyperparameters for each method were selected via grid search on the validation set. All models were trained with gradient clipping (threshold of 1.0) to ensure training stability. To enhance the temporal representation, we employed time-aware attention mechanisms in all sequence modeling tasks. We used a multi-head attention module with time decay bias to modulate the impact of past observations based on their temporal proximity. For tasks requiring long-term dependency modeling, such as in the Amazon Sports Dataset, we utilized a Transformer-based encoder with relative positional encoding. In contrast, recurrent-based encoders such as GRU and LSTM were used as baselines for comparison. In graph-temporal tasks from TimeHetNet, we used dynamic graph snapshots sampled at regular intervals and fused with LSTM representations to encode sequential evolution of graph topology. All code was implemented in Python 3.10 and will be released upon publication. Hyperparameter configurations and dataset preprocessing scripts are included to support reproducibility

### Comparison with SOTA methods

We compare our proposed method with a range of state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines, including Informer[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR41), Autoformer[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR42), PatchTST[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR43), TSMixer[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR44), LSTNet[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR45), and DeepAR[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#CR46), across four benchmark datasets including TSSB Competition, UTSD, TimeHetNet, and Amazon Sports. As shown in Table [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#Tab1), our method consistently outperforms all baselines in the TSSB and UTSD datasets across all evaluation metrics. On the TSSB dataset, we achieve a MAE of 0.389 and RMSE of 0.642, which shows a significant margin of improvement compared to the closest competitor Autoformer with 0.415 MAE and 0.677 RMSE. Our model achieves the highest R score of 0.879 and lowest MAPE of 9.84%, demonstrating its capability to precisely capture dynamic changes and temporal dependencies. The UTSD dataset results follow a similar trend where our model achieves 0.426 MAE and 0.675 RMSE, surpassing all other models in capturing fine-grained urban behavior transitions. While models like PatchTST and TSMixer show moderate performance due to their reliance on local temporal patterns, they fail to model long-range and heterogeneous dependencies that are crucial in realistic urban mobility sequences. LSTNet and DeepAR fall further behind due to their simpler architectures and lack of structured attention or relational modeling. In contrast, our approach integrates multi-scale temporal encoding and structural regularization, which not only preserves local variations but also stabilizes long-term prediction, leading to more reliable segmentation and future trend estimation. The results illustrate our model’s advantage in handling non-stationary, multi-distributional data with abrupt regime shifts, a key feature of the TSSB benchmark.

The superiority of our method becomes even more prominent in complex relational and multimodal datasets like TimeHetNet and Amazon Sports. Table [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12603155#Tab2) shows that our model again achieves the best results across all metrics. On TimeHetNet, our model achieves 0.498 MAE and 0.777 RMSE, outperforming Informer (0.552 MAE), Autoformer (0.531 MAE), and PatchTST (0.574 MAE) by significant margins. Notably, we also attain the highest R of 0.842, indicating superior regression fit in heterogeneous temporal graph environments. On Amazon Sports, which emphasizes sequential recommendation and session-based modeling, our model reduces MAE to 0.461 and RMSE to 0.742, again surpassing all baselines. These improvements reflect the ability of our approach to combine temporal attention with graph structural cues and semantic metadata. Unlike traditional temporal models, our architecture captures asynchronous interactions, latent relational hierarchies, and time-decay effects, which are pivotal in modeling dynamic multi-entity systems. The baseline methods generally struggle with implicit relationships or irregular intervals; for instance, LSTNet and DeepAR show degraded performance due to lack of graph context or positional adaptation. Our model’s ability to learn from multi-hop entity propagation and long-term preference patterns gives it an advantage in complex e-commerce scenarios, where latent user intent evolves over time and across items. The use of heterogeneity-aware attention further enables our system to differentiate interactions between entities of varying types, which boosts its representational power in multi-domain forecasting.

From a methodological perspective, the performance gain can be directly attributed to the three design principles outlined in our approach. First, the integration of hierarchical temporal encoding allows the model to learn both short-term volatility and long-term seasonality, which is particularly effective in datasets like Amazon Sports and UTSD, where both local and global context are essential. Second, our relational temporal graph encoder dynamically models entity evolution and interaction shifts over time, addressing the challenges posed by TimeHetNet. This component enables effective handling of irregularities and data sparsity, common issues in real-world temporal graphs. Third, the adaptive fusion module combines structured time series signals with unstructured semantic features such as text and graph relations, leading to a more holistic representation. This aligns well with the insights from our method design file (method.txt), which emphasized adaptive context modeling, relational reasoning, and temporal consistency. The callback of these principles across datasets validates the generalizability of our method. It not only excels in accuracy but also demonstrates robustness against noise, distribution drift, and modality imbalance. Unlike SOTA baselines that are often limited to fixed positional encoding or sequential convolutions, our model is capable of capturing multiscale temporal shifts and semantic dependencies through flexible attention routing. args.summary:
This scientific article presents a study on sports training effects using a Generalized Adaptive Backpropagation (GABP) neural network combined with artificial intelligence. The GABP model integrates Genetic Algorithms with Backpropagation to model physiological adaptation and guide data-driven training decisions. It is designed for real-time feedback and individualized load management using multivariate physiological inputs including physical performance indicators, training schedules, biometric data from wearables, video analysis, and electromyography (EMG).

The system detects fatigue and performance plateaus, providing interpretable insights to refine training strategies. Experimental validation shows a 15% improvement in prediction accuracy and a 30% reduction in convergence time compared to traditional methods. The study was published in Scientific Reports (2025) by LiangFa Li (Guangdong University of Foreign Studies & Adamson University) and AnYing Hao (Guangzhou Sports University & Adamson University).

The methodology was tested on four benchmark datasets (TSSB Competition, UTSD, TimeHetNet, and Amazon Sports) as well as two real-world physiological datasets (SPHERE and WESAD). The GABP model consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods including Informer, Autoformer, PatchTST, TSMixer, LSTNet, and DeepAR. On the TSSB dataset, the model achieved MAE of 0.389, RMSE of 0.642, R² of 0.879, and MAPE of 9.84%. On the WESAD dataset (physiology-stress modeling), GABP achieved F1 Score of 0.89, Accuracy of 0.87, MAE of 3.12, and R² of 0.80.

Ablation studies confirmed the importance of three key components: Latent Embedding Transformation (hierarchical temporal encoder), Temporal Attention Memory (relational graph temporal fusion), and Energy-Driven Latent Filtering (semantic attention integration). The model also demonstrated superior performance in fatigue-phase classification and load trend regression under simulated training cycles, achieving F1 Score of 0.82 and AUROC of 0.84 on WESAD fatigue classification, and MAE of 3.10 with R² of 0.81 on SPHERE load trend regression.

1. Identify and preserve the main topic or purpose of the webpage.
2. Retain key facts, statistics, and data points that are central to the content's message.
3. Keep important quotes from credible sources or experts.
4. Maintain the chronological order of events if the content is time-sensitive or historical.
5. Preserve any lists or step-by-step instructions if present.
6. Include relevant dates, names, and locations that are crucial to understanding the content.
7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For news articles: Focus on the who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- For scientific content: Preserve methodology, results, and conclusions.
- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.
- For product pages: Keep key features, specifications, and unique selling points.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

}

# Smart Sports Analysis Software for Coaches

A customized sports analysis software for easy analysis of sports games that helps coaches and players achieve their goals and simplifies collaboration within the team.

Analytics Dashboards

UI/UX Design

Web Apps

Sports

[Home](https://dinamicka.com/)  /  [Our works](https://dinamicka.com/our-works/)  / Smart Sports Analysis Software for Coaches

## Project Summary

An initial client’s request to our company was to create a digital solution which could allow him to process files with data on his favorite sports team’s games. The files were heavy, contained lots of details which were constantly updating with every game the team had played. Manual processing of all this information was too tiring and time-consuming.  

The information which was necessary to be processed, was related to all events happening on the game field, on all the players. This data allowed to analyze players’ behavior, dynamics, their current state and efficiency on the field. With a user-friendly interface, it becomes easier to analyze and plan a team’s game before the game happens.

![Smart Sports Analytics Platform Challenges](data:image/png;base64,)

### Tech-Stack

![AWS icon](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==) AWS

![FastAPI backend development framework](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==) FastAPI

 [![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==) Python](https://dinamicka.com/python-development/) 

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==) React.js

### Engagement Model

Full-Product Development

Dinamicka helped us develop a sports analytics software that has improved the performance of our team. I can recommend them very highly, you'll have no problems working with them.

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

Nick

CEO

![](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAApsAAAKbAQMAAACAXNMnAAAAA1BMVEUAAACnej3aAAAAAXRSTlMAQObYZgAAAE5JREFUGBntwQENAAAAwiD7p34ON2AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAADAuwDddwABi6RPdQAAAABJRU5ErkJggg==)

## Business Challenges

As the project is very specific in its idea and data types, there were lots of various challenges related to its implementation. The most significant of them was to speed up the file processing. 

Due to a large file dataset, the initial file parsing took 14-16 hours before the system started showing query results, and after each game, the file needs to be updated (several times per week). As the team is one of the leaders in their country and type of sport, it plays many games, and it could take significant time to analyze every update. 

The goal, at the later stage of development, was to speed up the processing time and provide the coaches and team players with analytical data as soon as possible.

![Sports Analytics Tool](data:image/png;base64,)

## Solution

System development has passed through several stages — from a simple, but clear and comprehensible [MVP design](https://dinamicka.com/mvp-development/) with basic functions, to a complicated multi-functional full-scale analytical system even with video comments for received events, which allows to review game video history, analytical data on games, and obtain detailed information about chosen strategy for the next game. The system can provide with the following data: 

* player efficiency parameters;
* player comparison with rating;
* events on the field in real-time etc.

If in an MVP version it was possible to analyze only previous games, at later stages predictive functions are already available. Real-time game data are input live and processed promptly. 

It is also possible to analyze not only the team for which the product was created, but also their opponents’ efficiency and results, with the goal to develop game strategy and tactics, ensuring better playing results. The system keeps data for all competitions and teams, analyzes positive and negative trends to pay attention to when you play against this team. 

### **Design**

Solution design was performed by our company from scratch, and the main goal of this work was to provide as clear a display of the systematized data as possible. The initial MVP design was reworked completely at the later stages, and it is still really user-friendly and comprehensible despite many functions being added to the system throughout the years. 

Design includes lots of various tables, graphs, diagrams, and other ways of visual display of team or player efficiency. 

### **Development**

Some part of system functions related to game result analytics was developed by the client himself as he was deeply involved into the processes inside the team and their interests. Basic logic of the system was created by the client, too. Our team added more functionality, worked on improvement of the data processing, further functionality extensions, and additional option implementation.

![Custom Sports Analytics Platform with dashboards](data:image/png;base64,)

![Custom Sports Analytics Platform with dashboards](data:image/png;base64,)

## Sports Analytics Platform Features

At its present state, the system allows doing the following: 

* parsing and analyzing data;
* review team results and efficiency on the field displayed in a suitable format – tables and graphs;
* obtain detailed review of the team by game parameters and by players;
* review player’s individual results;
* sort team history data by years;
* review event history on the field;
* compare the efficiency of different teams and their strategies;
* export results in CSV, Excel and PDF formats to print them;
* view game videos uploaded after each game and analyzed by defined parameters with breakdown by events.

![Custom Sports Analytics Platform with dashboards](data:image/png;base64,)

![Custom Sports Analytics Platform with dashboards](data:image/png;base64,)

![Custom Sports Analytics Platform with dashboards](data:image/png;base64,)

![Custom Sports Analytics Platform with dashboards](data:image/png;base64,)

![Custom Sports Analytics Platform with dashboards](data:image/png;base64,)

## Result

Now, the sports team system has passed through many updates and iterations and is a convenient analytical tool helping coaches and players achieve their goals and simplify cooperation within the team.

![Custom Sports Analytics Platform with dashboards](data:image/png;base64,)

## ABSTRACT

To enhance the standardization, scientific accuracy, and intelligence of physical training, modern sports training should utilize information technology to manage big data in real-time and build an appropriate control platform. This paper examines big data management in track and field training, focusing on three key factors: data collection, analysis, and application. It also explores three artificial intelligence technologies—machine learning, deep learning, and predictive analytics—to evaluate their predictive accuracy. Results show that the multivariate regression method offers the highest prediction accuracy, and a strong polynomial relationship exists between training outcomes and injury prevention. This highlights the potential of artificial intelligence and big data to improve training effectiveness and reduce injury risks.

The research highlights the potential of AI and big data to improve training effectiveness and reduce injury risks in physical training.

## Abstract

Sports and activity-related musculoskeletal injuries are a major cause of long-term disability, underscoring the need for proactive detection and data-driven rehabilitation strategies. Recent advancements in wearable sensing enable continuous, non-invasive biomechanical monitoring for early risk identification and recovery optimization. This study presents a real-time wearable biomechanics framework integrating inertial measurement units (IMUs) and surface electromyography (sEMG) for injury-risk assessment and rehabilitation tracking. Field experiments were conducted with 50 athletes at Dring Stadium, Bahawalpur. The IMUs were positioned on the knee, hip, and shoulder joints, while sEMG electrodes measured biceps, triceps, and quadriceps muscle activations. Recorded joint-angle ranges averaged 125° (knee during running), 110° (knee during jumping), and 90° (shoulder during lifting); corresponding mean muscle forces were 150 N (quadriceps), 170 N (hamstrings), and 230 N (deltoid). A multi-stage optimization algorithm minimized prediction errors by jointly tuning sensor calibration and computational latency. The hybrid IMU–sEMG model achieved 92.3% accuracy, 90.5% recall, and an AUC of 0.93 for injury-risk classification, with an average real-time feedback latency of 188 ± 15 ms. Early detection of joint-angle asymmetry (> 10°) and muscle-force imbalance (> 15%) accurately predicted emerging anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and muscle-strain risks. Real-time monitoring guided individualized rehabilitation loads and progressive recovery milestones. By combining wearable sensing, physics-informed biomechanical modeling, and adaptive machine-learning optimization, the proposed system delivers a quantitatively validated, reproducible, and scalable framework for injury prevention and rehabilitation. Supporting UN Sustainable Development Goal 3, this work advances musculoskeletal health monitoring through validated sensor integration and empirically tested AI models, offering measurable benefits across athletic and occupational applications.

Injury prevention and rehabilitation remain central to sports medicine and occupational health. Traditional laboratory tools such as force plates and optical motion capture, though accurate, are impractical for continuous deployment. Wearable technologies now enable real-time monitoring of joint kinematics and muscle function, providing a scalable solution bridging laboratory precision with field applicability.

By integrating multi-sensor fusion, machine learning, and biomechanical modeling, this study advances a validated, real-time system for injury-risk assessment and rehabilitation support. The framework aims to improve both workplace safety and athletic performance by establishing a scientifically grounded, data-driven paradigm for biomechanical monitoring and predictive injury management.

In biomechanical risk assessment, the goal is to formulate a model that effectively characterizes the stress (\(\:S\)) on musculoskeletal structures during dynamic activities. Let \(\:F\) represent the external forces acting on the body, \(\:A\) denote the area of contact, and \(\:\tau\:\) signify the time duration of the applied force. The stress (\(\:S\)) can be mathematically expressed as:

$$\:\text{S=}\frac{F}{A}$$

Considering the dynamic nature of activities, the rate of change of stress over time (\(\:\dot{S}\)) becomes crucial in identifying potential risks. Utilizing, the derivative of stress with respect to time, we formulate the dynamic stress equation as follows:

$$\:\dot{S}=\frac{\text{dS}}{\text{dt}}$$

To integrate wearable, sensor data, let \(\:D\) represent the set of biomechanical parameters collected from sensors, including joint angles (\(\:\theta\:\)), angular velocities (\(\:\omega\:\)), and muscle forces (\(\:M\)). The relationship between stress (\(\:S\)) and sensor data (\(\:D\)) can be formulated using a neural network model as:

$$\:\text{S=f}\left(\text{D}\theta \right)$$

Where\(\:f\)represents the neural network function with parameters \(\:\theta\:\).

The optimization, problem involves minimizing the discrepancy between predicted stress (\(\:S\)) obtained from wearable sensor data (\(\:D\)) and actual stress measured using biomechanical, models while considering constraints such as sensor accuracy and computational efficiency. This can be formulated as an optimization problem:

$$\:{\sum\:}_{\text{i=}1}^{N}{\left|{S}_{i}-f\left({D}_{i} \theta \right)\right|}^{2}{+\lambda R}\left(\theta\:\right)$$

Subject to constraints on sensor accuracy and computational resources, where \(\:N\) is the number of data samples, \(\:R\left(\theta\:\right)\) denotes regularization terms, and \(\:\lambda\:\) is the regularization parameter.

The primary objective of this study is to develop and validate a real-time biomechanical risk assessment framework using wearable sensor data and deep learning models. The specific goals are:

*   To integrate inertial (IMU) and surface EMG data for real-time monitoring of joint angles and muscle activation during dynamic activities.

*   To design and train a neural network model capable of estimating biomechanical stress and predicting injury-prone conditions based on wearable sensor input.

*   To implement and test the proposed system in athletic and occupational scenarios, quantifying risk scores across various exercises.

*   To assess the feasibility and performance of wearable-based risk assessment in unstructured environments compared to conventional marker-based systems.

### Research topic statement

This study specifically investigates real-time biomechanical risk assessment using wearable IMU and sEMG sensors, focusing on predicting unsafe joint-loading patterns and muscle-activation imbalances in athletic populations. The research centers on developing and validating a sensor-fusion model capable of estimating biomechanical stress in real time and identifying movement patterns associated with elevated injury risk. The scope is limited to athletic biomechanics, with occupational applications discussed only as future extensions. This explicit focus ensures that the manuscript remains aligned with a single, well-defined research topic suitable for academic investigation.

The core research question guiding this work is: How effectively can wearable sensor data be integrated with biomechanical modeling and machine learning to quantify and predict stress-related risks during athletic and occupational activities?

Supporting sub-questions include:

*   To what extent can wearable-based biomechanical indices replicate laboratory-grade motion-capture accuracy?

*   How can real-time sensor feedback contribute to reducing asymmetry and joint overload during rehabilitation?

*   What are the algorithmic and practical limitations of deploying such systems in uncontrolled, real-world environments?

*   This clarified research scope ensures a targeted investigation and minimizes interpretative ambiguity across experimental and analytical sections.

The research contributions are as follows:

*   Development of a unified framework merging industrial ergonomics and athletic performance optimization through wearable-integrated biomechanical risk assessment.

*   Synthesis of methodologies catering to the distinct demands of industrial and athletic settings, enhancing the adaptability and applicability of wearable systems.

*   Exploration of real-time data acquisition techniques to offer immediate insights into biomechanical risks for proactive mitigation strategies in both domains.

*   Contribution to the advancement of comprehensive analyses that bridge contextual differences between industrial and athletic realms, addressing their simultaneous demands.

*   Establishment of adaptable risk assessment methodologies utilizing wearables, paving the way for holistic approaches to minimize risks and optimize performance.

The novelty of this work lies in the development of a hybrid IMU–EMG sensor framework coupled with a multi-stage machine learning pipeline for real-time biomechanical stress prediction. Unlike previous IMU-only or EMG-only frameworks, the proposed approach introduces a dual-stream fusion model, adaptive calibration, and latency-aware optimization layer to achieve sub-200 ms feedback. The validation strategy integrates multi-trial averaging, confidence intervals, and ablation-based assessment, establishing both reproducibility and deployment readiness across sports and occupational applications.

This gap is addressed by developing an integrated wearable biomechanical system that merges inertial and electromyographic sensing with machine learning–based risk modeling, enabling immediate feedback, individualized rehabilitation pathways, and adaptability across both athletic and industrial scenarios. This investigation is presented as a sport-specific proof-of-concept, with a planned Phase 2 expansion to industrial populations for validation under occupational task conditions. While the framework is designed for cross-domain applicability, the present analysis confines empirical validation to sports biomechanics and rehabilitation. Industrial ergonomics components are discussed only as prospective extensions.

The present study focuses on developing an integrated, real-time wearable biomechanical risk assessment and rehabilitation optimization framework that unifies IMU and EMG data through adaptive machine learning pipelines. Unlike descriptive reviews, this work emphasizes empirical modeling, field validation, and latency-aware optimization to ensure real-time applicability in both sports and occupational contexts.

This study investigates how hybrid IMU–EMG data fusion combined with real-time machine learning can improve biomechanical risk detection accuracy in athletic contexts. The central hypothesis (H1–H3) posits that multi-sensor fusion significantly enhances injury-risk prediction precision, reduces latency, and supports adaptive rehabilitation feedback compared to single-sensor baselines.

This work should be interpreted as a dual-phase study: (1) a technical validation against gold-standard motion capture and force plates, and (2) a pilot intervention demonstrating feasibility in applied field settings. While promising, these findings represent groundwork rather than definitive proof of injury risk reduction.

In this manuscript, the empirical analysis and all collected datasets strictly reflect athletic biomechanics. Occupational applications are presented conceptually for future expansion and are not part of the experimental results. The primary validated scope of this study is therefore athletic injury-risk monitoring, with occupational integration planned for Phase 2.

Definitions of key terms:

*   _Integrated Wearable Biomechanical System_: A unified platform combining wearable sensors (e.g., IMUs, EMG) with real-time data processing and feedback mechanisms for injury risk assessment and rehabilitation monitoring.

*   _Risk Modeling_: The computational process of estimating injury likelihood using biomechanical parameters (e.g., joint angles, muscle forces, asymmetry indices) as input features to machine learning algorithms.

*   _Rehabilitation Optimization_: The adaptive adjustment of rehabilitation exercises and loads based on continuous monitoring of recovery indicators, including range of motion (ROM), muscle activation patterns, and symmetry metrics.

The outline of the paper is as follows: In the first section, we learn about biomechanical risk assessment and why it’s important to use wearable devices. The literature review part presents a thorough analysis of current approaches and tools used for biomechanical risk assessment, with an emphasis on the use of wearables in both physical and occupational contexts. The methodology section explains the strategy that was created to integrate data from wearable sensors and to set up models for biomechanical risk assessment. In the results and analysis section, we share the findings from applying this methodology and analyzing them. Then, we talk about what these findings mean for improving athletic performance and workplace safety. In the difficulties and future directions section, the article discusses problems that have been encountered and suggests ways that research could go in the future. At the end, the conclusion section summarizes the main points, contributions, and implications of the study. The paper’s references are a comprehensive inventory of all the sources used.

## Literature review

Recent advancements in wearable technologies have significantly transformed sports medicine and biomechanical analysis, providing real-time insights into athletes’ physiological responses, performance metrics, and recovery progress. Studies by Li et al. (2016) and Seçkin et al. (2023) emphasized the widespread adoption of wearables in sports medicine, highlighting their capacity to monitor physical performance and optimize training programs. These reviews underscored the critical role of wearable devices in delivering immediate feedback and supporting personalized intervention strategies for athletes. Despite the growing popularity of wearables, several gaps and challenges persist in literature. Montull et al. (2022) stressed the importance of incorporating subjective assessments alongside objective sensor-based measurements, noting that subjective feedback can, in some contexts, provide deeper insight into fatigue, effort, and readiness. This reinforces the need for a holistic sports monitoring framework that integrates both physiological data and perceptual measures to better capture the nuances of athletic performance.

Several studies have addressed the practical challenges of implementing wearable technologies. De Fazio et al. (2023) and Baca et al. (2022) identified concerns related to data accuracy, sensor calibration, comfort, and long-term user adherence, which limit large-scale adoption. These studies emphasized the necessity of improving device reliability and usability to fully leverage wearable potential in real-world settings. Pekas et al. (2023) further discussed the ethical and privacy implications of continuous biometric data collection, urging the development of clear regulatory and data protection frameworks. Similarly, Sousa et al. (2023) highlighted the urgent need for standardized validation protocols and consistent methodologies to ensure the reliability and comparability of wearable-derived biomechanical metrics. Collectively, these findings emphasize that usability, ethics, and standardization are key to the future integration of wearable technology into evidence-based sports and medical practice.

In parallel, numerous studies have examined the integration of wearable systems into biomechanical risk assessment and occupational ergonomics. Research in[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR24 "Kelson, D. M. et al. Effects of passive upper-extremity exoskeleton use on motor performance in a precision task. In Proc. Hum. Factors Ergon. Soc. Annu. Meet., vol. 63, 1084–1085. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/1071181319631437
                  
                 (2019).") demonstrated that wearables can effectively monitor and analyze biomechanical stressors, including muscle exertion and joint strain, in industrial environments, enhancing physical task evaluation and workplace safety. Subsequent studies[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR25 "Kim, S. et al. Potential of exoskeleton technologies to enhance safety, health, and performance in construction: industry perspectives and future research directions. IISE Trans. Occup. Ergon. Hum. Factors. 7, 185–191. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/24725838.2018.1561557
                  
                 (2019)."),[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR26 "Lim, S. & D’Souza, C. A narrative review on contemporary and emerging uses of inertial sensing in occupational ergonomics. Int. J. Ind. Ergon. 76, 102937. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ergon.2020.102937
                  
                 (2020).") confirmed the value of wearable devices in sports science for gait analysis, muscle activation tracking, and injury prevention, extending their utility beyond laboratory-based experiments. These studies also recognized the potential of miniaturized, wireless inertial sensors to capture large-scale, individualized kinematic data across both controlled and field environments, marking a major shift toward real-time, personalized biomechanics.

Challenges regarding data reliability, system compatibility, and computational efficiency remain substantial. As highlighted in[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR27 "Lowe, B. D., Billotte, W. G. & Peterson, D. R. Astm f48 formation and standards for industrial exoskeletons and exosuits. IISE Trans. Occup. Ergon. Hum. Factors. 7, 230–236. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/24725838.2019.1579769
                  
                 (2019)."), inconsistent sampling rates, limited interoperability, and high computational demands constrain seamless integration into applied biomechanical assessment. Addressing these challenges requires robust data fusion algorithms, efficient processing architectures, and improved hardware ergonomics to enhance comfort and compliance. Researchers in[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR28 "Luczak, T. et al. Prabhu. Closing the wearable gap—part v: development of a pressure-sensitive sock utilizing soft sensors. Sensors 20, 208. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/s20010208
                  
                 (2019).") advanced algorithmic and machine learning methods for wearable data interpretation, using neural networks and pattern-recognition techniques to improve prediction accuracy and biomechanical insight. These algorithmic developments play a pivotal role in transforming raw sensor signals into actionable parameters for injury prediction, workload estimation, and postural correction.

Continuous progress in wearable sensor technology has been central to recent research[29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR29 "Luger, T., Bar, M., Seibt, R., Rieger, M. A. & Steinhilber, B. Using a back exoskeleton during industrial and functional tasks—effects on muscle activity, posture, performance, usability, and wearer discomfort in a laboratory trial. Hum. Factors. 11, 001872082110072. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/00187208211007267
                  
                 (2021)."),[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR30 "Madinei, S. et al. Assessment of two passive back-support exoskeletons in a simulated precision manual assembly task. In Proc. Hum. Factors Ergon. Soc. Annu. Meet., vol. 63, 1078–1079. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/1071181319631192

Horiz. 63, 493–505 (2020)."). Studies have reported advancements in sensor miniaturization, battery life, textile integration, and signal stability, all of which enhance continuous biomechanical monitoring. Moreover, wearable systems have increasingly been applied in healthcare and rehabilitation contexts[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR30 "Madinei, S. et al. Assessment of two passive back-support exoskeletons in a simulated precision manual assembly task. In Proc. Hum. Factors Ergon. Soc. Annu. Meet., vol. 63, 1078–1079. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/1071181319631192
                  
                 (2019)."), supporting patient movement analysis, recovery tracking, and musculoskeletal rehabilitation. These interdisciplinary applications highlight the broad relevance of wearable systems across occupational, clinical, and athletic domains.

Ethical and societal considerations have also gained attention in recent research[32](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR32 "Matijevich, E. S., Scott, L. R., Volgyesi, P., Derry, K. H. & Zelik, K. E. Combining wearable sensor signals, machine learning and biomechanics to estimate tibial bone force and damage during running. Hum. Mov. Sci. 74, 102690.

Scholars have raised concerns about data security, informed consent, and responsible data handling, emphasizing the need for transparent frameworks to maintain trust and protect user autonomy. Cost-effectiveness and scalability have been evaluated as well[33](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR33 "McFarland, T. & Fischer, S. Considerations for industrial use: A systematic review of the impact of active and passive upper limb exoskeletons on physical exposures. IISE Trans. Occup. Ergon. Hum. Factors. 7, 322–347. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/24725838.2019.1684399
                  
                 (2019)."), showing that while initial investment costs remain high, the long-term benefits—such as injury prevention, improved productivity, and enhanced recovery—outweigh the expense. Moreover, scalable solutions and open architectures have been proposed to promote the adoption of wearables across various industries and demographics.

Recent studies combining wearable sensors with machine learning have pushed the boundaries of biomechanical prediction. Xiang et al.[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR5 "Xiang, L. et al. Integrating personalized shape prediction, Biomechanical modeling, and wearables for bone stress prediction in runners. NPJ Digit. Med. 8, 1–12. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-025-01677-0
                  
                 (2025)."),[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR9 "Xiang, L. et al. Integrating an LSTM framework for predicting ankle joint biomechanics during gait using inertial sensors. Comput. Biol. Med. 170, 108016.

Predicting sports injuries with machine learning technology: enhancing athletes’ life expectancy through Biomechanical analysis. Mol. Cell. Biomech. 22, 1408.

These advancements collectively demonstrate a paradigm shift from reactive injury treatment to proactive, predictive, and adaptive injury management.

Looking forward, future research is expected to extend the application of wearables toward personalized healthcare, precision rehabilitation, and performance optimization. Studies[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR34 "Naf, M. B. et al. Passive back support exoskeleton improves range of ¨ motion using flexible beams. Front. Robot AI. 5, 72.

                  https://doi.org/10.1123/jab.2018-0369
                  
                 (2020)."),[36](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR36 "Poliero, T. et al. Applicability of an active back-support exoskeleton to carrying activities. Front. Robot AI. 7, 579963.

                 (2020)."),[37](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#ref-CR37 "Qu, X. et al. Effects of an industrial passive assistive exoskeleton on muscle activity, oxygen consumption and subjective responses during lifting tasks. PLoS ONE. 16, e0245629.

Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34551-w#Tab1) presents a comparative analysis of previous studies in the field. Real-time feedback by wearables in running: current approaches, challenges and suggestions for improvements. J. Sports Sci. 38, 214–230.

                 (2019)."), introduces the ABLE exoskeleton in the automotive industry, noting limited adaptability but achieving reduced ergonomic strains in automobile assembly.

**Table 1 Comparative table of previous study.**

The present body of work tends to focus either on industrial ergonomics or sports performance enhancement alone, lacking a coherent approach that integrates methodology and findings across these disparate areas. Moreover, there’s a scarcity of research addressing the optimization of wearable-based risk assessment approaches to fit the diverse and simultaneous demands of both industrial and sporting contexts. This gap gives an opportunity for future investigations to synthesize approaches, develop flexible wearable devices, and establish unified frameworks that cater to the varied needs of both areas, ultimately developing holistic biomechanical risk assessment methodologies.

args.summary:
This is a scientific article published in Scientific Reports (volume 16, Article number 4436, 2026) titled "Real-time wearable biomechanics framework for sports injury prevention and rehabilitation optimization" by Abdullah Alzahrani, Maysa Aljohany, and Hadeel Alsirhani.

The study presents a real-time wearable biomechanics framework that integrates inertial measurement units (IMUs) and surface electromyography (sEMG) for injury-risk assessment and rehabilitation tracking. Field experiments were conducted with 50 athletes at Dring Stadium, Bahawalpur. IMUs were positioned on knee, hip, and shoulder joints, while sEMG electrodes measured biceps, triceps, and quadriceps muscle activations.

Key findings include:
- Joint-angle ranges averaged 125° (knee during running), 110° (knee during jumping), and 90° (shoulder during lifting)
- Mean muscle forces: 150 N (quadriceps), 170 N (hamstrings), and 230 N (deltoid)
- The hybrid IMU-sEMG model achieved 92.3% accuracy, 90.5% recall, and AUC of 0.93 for injury-risk classification
- Average real-time feedback latency of 188 ± 15 ms
- Early detection of joint-angle asymmetry (>10°) and muscle-force imbalance (>15%) predicted ACL and muscle-strain risks

The framework uses a multi-stage optimization algorithm, physics-informed biomechanical modeling, and adaptive machine-learning optimization. The study addresses the global incidence of musculoskeletal injuries (over 3.5 million annually in sports and 2.8 million in workplace settings) and supports UN Sustainable Development Goal 3. The paper covers methodology, results, literature review, and discusses challenges and future directions, with explicit scope limited to athletic biomechanics while occupational applications are discussed as future extensions.

# Review of Real-Time Biomechanical Feedback Systems in Sport and Rehabilitation

### Matevž Hribernik

### Anton Umek

### Sašo Tomažič

### Anton Kos

Correspondence: anton.kos@fe.uni-lj.si

#### Roles

Received 2022 Mar 1; Accepted 2022 Apr 11; Collection date 2022 Apr.

Licensee MDPI, Basel, Switzerland. This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license (<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>).

## Abstract

Real-time biomechanical feedback (BMF) is a relatively new area of research. The potential of using advanced technology to improve motion skills in sport and accelerate physical rehabilitation has been demonstrated in a number of studies. This paper provides a literature review of BMF systems in sports and rehabilitation. Our motivation was to examine the history of the field to capture its evolution over time, particularly how technologies are used and implemented in BMF systems, and to identify the most recent studies showing novel solutions and remarkable implementations. We searched for papers in three research databases: Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed. The initial search yielded 1167 unique papers. After a rigorous and challenging exclusion process, 144 papers were eventually included in this report. We focused on papers describing applications and systems that implement a complete real-time feedback loop, which must include the use of sensors, real-time processing, and concurrent feedback. A number of research questions were raised, and the papers were studied and evaluated accordingly. We identified different types of physical activities, sensors, modalities, actuators, communications, settings and end users. A subset of the included papers, showing the most perspectives, was reviewed in depth to highlight and present their innovative research approaches and techniques. Real-time BMF has great potential in many areas. In recent years, sensors have been the main focus of these studies, but new types of processing devices, methods, and algorithms, actuators, and communication technologies and protocols will be explored in more depth in the future. This paper presents a broad insight into the field of BMF.

**Keywords:** real-time, concurrent, instant, biomechanical feedback, system, application, sensor, actuator, modality, motion, sport, rehabilitation

## 1. Introduction

The use of smart devices and wearable technology in everyday life has increased considerably in the last decade [[1](#B1-sensors-22-03006),[2](#B2-sensors-22-03006),[3](#B3-sensors-22-03006),[4](#B4-sensors-22-03006)]. This is also true in the field of sports and physical rehabilitation. In sports, professional and recreational athletes are constantly trying to improve their skills and performance by using advanced (wearable) technology, which can ultimately lead to a competitive advantage [[5](#B5-sensors-22-03006),[6](#B6-sensors-22-03006)]. Similarly, in physical rehabilitation, patients use technology to shorten the rehabilitation process and improve its effectiveness [[7](#B7-sensors-22-03006)].

A large number of electronic devices used in sports and physical rehabilitation are classified into three groups using terminology in the field of electronics: consumer devices, high-end devices and systems and purpose-built devices and systems. *Consumer devices* include smart wristbands, heart rate monitors, smartwatches, smartphones, and many others. They usually contain various sensors, such as kinematic sensors to measure motion [[8](#B8-sensors-22-03006)] and sensors to measure physiological parameters of the user. Generally, users employ these devices to self-quantify their physical activity. Consumer devices are easy to use and predominantly provide some sort of statistical results, such as event counts, averages, progress, and the like. *High-end devices and systems* are primarily used for professional laboratory testing and research. They include optical tracking systems, force plate systems, video analysis systems, and others. They provide precise and accurate measurements of various activity parameters, such as movement patterns or force distribution, but their use is limited and restricted to specific tasks, environments and experts; not to mention their high acquisition and operating costs. *Purpose-built devices and systems* attempt to bridge the gap between consumer and high-end devices and systems. In most cases, they are designed to be task-specific and implemented (at least in part) as wearable devices. They are used to assess the kinetics and kinematics of movement or physiological parameters of the user, preferably without interfering with the performance of the activity. In general, their use is more complex than consumer devices, which typically do not require special setup, but less complex than high-end systems, which may require complicated setup and trained personnel. Purpose-built devices and systems using wearable technology enable task-specific acquisition of biomechanical and physiological parameters of activity. When compared to consumer or high-end devices, the task-specific data allows for targeted processing and analysis, resulting in higher quality results regarding the specific task. This ultimately increases rehabilitation benefits and training performance [[9](#B9-sensors-22-03006),[10](#B10-sensors-22-03006),[11](#B11-sensors-22-03006)].

One concept that leads to improved execution of activity and performance, and thus a competitive advantage in sports or a better rehabilitation process, is **biomechanical feedback (BMF) [[2](#B2-sensors-22-03006),[5](#B5-sensors-22-03006),[6](#B6-sensors-22-03006),[7](#B7-sensors-22-03006)]**. BMF is a treatment and body control method that uses sensors to measure a person’s physiological and physical body functions, parameters, and activities that cannot be perceived by the human senses. The data from the sensors are processed and the results are fed back to the person via one of the human senses. The person tries to respond to the received information in order to change the sensed functions, parameters and activities in the desired way, thus closing a feedback loop [[2](#B2-sensors-22-03006)]. BMF systems generally consist of at least four basic elements: a user, one or more sensors, a processing unit, and one or more actuators, as shown in [Figure 1](#sensors-22-03006-f001). There can be more than one instance of each element [[2](#B2-sensors-22-03006)].
