### 4.1 Enabling AI techniques in swimming

With this understanding of the research landscape, we now shift our focus to AI technologies that form the foundation for such recommendation systems. Although none of the studies reviewed has yet delivered a full AI-powered recommendation system, many employ techniques that show great promise. From traditional machine learning to advanced deep learning, these methods offer the accuracy, speed, and flexibility needed to process complex swimming data and generate meaningful insights. In this section, we explore these enabling AI techniques and how they can pave the way for the next generation of intelligent, swimmer-focused recommendation systems.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): CNNs are widely used for stroke recognition tasks. For instance, [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR12 "Costa J, Silva C, Santos M, Fernandes T, Faria S. Framework for intelligent swimming analytics with wearable sensors for stroke classification. Sensors (Basel). 2021. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/s21155162
                  
                .")] applied CNNs to classify swimming strokes using IMU data, achieving over 92% accuracy. [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR2 "Chen L, Hu D. An effective swimming stroke recognition system utilizing deep learning based on inertial measurement units. Adv Robot. 2022;37:1–13. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/01691864.2022.2160274
                  
                .")] enhanced CNNs with attention mechanisms to perform real-time, frame-wise stroke classification from video inputs. BiLSTM and RNNs: Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) and Recurrent Neural Net- works (RNNs) are particularly effective for modeling temporal patterns in swimming. [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR3 "Delhaye E, Bouvet A, Nicolas G, Vilas-Boas JP, Bideau B, Bideau N. Automatic swimming activity recognition and lap time assessment based on a single imu: a deep learning approach. Sensors (Basel). 2022. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/s22155786
                  
                .")] used BiLSTM networks to detect stroke transitions and lap turns, demonstrating the strength of sequential modeling. Classical Machine Learning Models: Algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs), Random Forests (RF), and Decision Trees (DTs) are frequently used for tasks like technique classification and turn detection. [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR13 "Fantozzi S, Coloretti V, Piacentini MF, Quagliarotti C, Bartolomei S, Gatta G, et al. Integrated timing of stroking, breathing, and kicking in front-crawl swimming: a novel stroke-by-stroke approach using wearable inertial sensors. Sensors (Basel). 2022;22:1419. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/s22041419
                  
                .")] found SVMs slightly outperformed RF in detecting turn timing with better precision-recall trade-offs. Hybrid Architectures: Some studies employed hybrid models that combine different techniques. For example, a CNN-RF pipeline for underwater gesture classification, combining deep feature extraction with tree-based interpretability, was developed. Autoencoders for Dimensionality Reduction: Autoencoders were used by [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR10 "Silva A, Costa A, Moura Oliveira P, Reis V, Saavedra J, Perl J, et al. The use of neural network technology to model swimming performance. J Sports Sci Med. 2007;6:117–25.")] to reduce high-dimensional sensor data for fatigue detection, maintaining performance while minimizing computational overhead.

Having explored the key AI techniques that provide the foundation for swimming analytics, we now turn to the specific domains within swimming where these methods have been applied. Understanding these application areas helps illustrate how different AI approaches contribute to improving swimmer performance, monitoring, and injury prevention. In the next section, we examine the swimming-related tasks addressed by AI, highlighting how these technologies are being used to tackle real-world challenges in the sport.

### 4.2 Swimming performance domains addressed by AI

AI has been applied in several key areas of swimming performance, especially those focused on technique optimization, workload monitoring, and real-time feedback. Stroke Classification: This remains one of the most studied applications. Deep learning models, especially CNNs paired with data from wearable sensors or video, can now recognize different swimming strokes with impressive speed and accuracy. [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR2 "Chen L, Hu D. An effective swimming stroke recognition system utilizing deep learning based on inertial measurement units. Adv Robot. 2022;37:1–13.

                  https://doi.org/10.3390/s21155162
                  
                .")].

Stroke Efficiency and Pacing Analysis: Ensemble machine learning models have been used to evaluate stroke length and rate, helping swimmers optimize pacing and manage energy distribution [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR41 "Koh C, Pagnier L, Chertkov M. Fatigue and Recovery Monitoring: [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR4 "Wang TY, Cui J, Fan Y. A wearable-based sports health monitoring system using cnn and lstm with self-attentions. PLOS ONE 2023;18(10):0292012.

Other studies used oxygen saturation and efficiency metrics from wearable biosensors to monitor physical strain [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR42 "Jeznach C, Olson SD. Dynamics of swimmers in fluids with resistance. Fluids. 2020.

Injury Risk Detection: [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR17 "Lin X, Liu X, Wang Y. Learning agile swimming: an end-to-end approach without cpgs. IEEE Robot Autom Lett. 2025;10(2):1992–9. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/lra.2025.3527757

From stroke classification to injury risk detection, the building blocks are clearly in place. Yet, there is still a missing piece: most of these systems stop at analysis. They tell us what is happening, but not necessarily what to do next.

### 4.3 Contextual and personalized analysis in swimming

Despite impressive sensing and analytics capabilities, very few systems take the next step: offering personalized recommendations in real-time that are tailored to the unique context of each swimmer. And that’s exactly what a true recommendation system should aim to deliver.

Session Contextualization: [[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR43 "Kheya TA, Bouadjenek MR, Aryal S. The Pursuit of Fairness in Artificial Intelligence Models: A Survey 2024. 
                  https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.17333
                  
                ")] integrated session-specific metadata, such as pool temperature and water conditions—into stroke prediction models. While accuracy improved, these enhancements did not translate into personalized training suggestions. Athlete Profiling: A limited number of studies incorporated historical performance or swimmer-specific data. [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR10 "Silva A, Costa A, Moura Oliveira P, Reis V, Saavedra J, Perl J, et al. The use of neural network technology to model swimming performance. J Sports Sci Med. 2007;6:117–25.")] built individualized fatigue models, yet these were not connected to adaptive or evolving recommendation logic. Skill-Level-Based Feedback: [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#ref-CR42 "Jeznach C, Olson SD. Dynamics of swimmers in fluids with resistance. Fluids. 2020. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/fluids5010014
                  
                .")] differentiated feedback thresholds for amateur and elite swimmers. However, the system lacked continuous learning and did not evolve with user behavior or performance. Bridging these gaps is essential to create truly adaptive AI recommendation systems that respond to evolving needs, goals, and context of each swimmer. With the right models and decision-making strategies, it’s possible to move from simply analyzing performance to actively shaping it.

### 4.4 Algorithmic comparisons and recommendation techniques

AI models used in swimming are no longer just tools for prediction—they are evolving into engines for intelligent decision making. By analyzing both historical trends and real-time data, these systems can recommend targeted actions, such as improving stroke, tailoring training plans, or optimal race strategies. The Table[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#Tab6) below offers a comparative analysis of the core algorithms used in artificial intelligence-powered swimming research. Table[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x#Tab6), which includes a dedicated ‘Recommendation Role’ column, highlights how methods such as ML, DL, CV, and IoT contribute differently (e.g., ML for classification, DL for automatic feature learning, CV for motion analysis, IoT for real-time monitoring). Classical ML models such as SVM and RF are interpretable and perform well on small datasets but tend to underperform on sequential, high-dimensional swimming data. Deep learning models, by contrast, can capture complex temporal and spatial dependencies but rely on large, multimodal datasets that are often unavailable in aquatic sports. This trade-off highlights the need for hybrid approaches that combine interpretability with scalability.

As the table shows, hybrid deep learning methods such as CNN-LSTM stand out for their ability to deliver fast, high-resolution feedback, essential for real-time coaching. That said, classical models still have a place, especially when transparency or limited data is a concern. But great algorithms are only as good as the data they receive. That’s where sensing technology comes in.

### 4.5 Wearable sensors for data acquisition

Wearable sensors provide high-quality real-time data that powers AI-driven recommendations. From biomechanics to physiological signals, these devices enable precise tracking and actionable feedback, bringing us closer to truly personalized coaching in the water.

This is a research article published in Discover Applied Sciences (Volume 8, article number 156, 2026) titled "AI for swimming recommendation systems exploring the current landscape and research opportunities" by Minal Patil, R. H. Goudar, and Geetabai S. Hukkeri. It is an open-access, peer-reviewed systematic review of 42 studies (2018–2024) examining AI applications in swimming.

The paper finds that while AI adoption in swimming is growing, it remains fragmented—most studies focus on isolated tasks such as stroke classification, turn detection, and fatigue monitoring, achieving 90–99% accuracy in stroke recognition using CNN-LSTM and BiLSTM architectures. However, none of the reviewed studies implemented full recommendation systems for swimmers, representing a clear research gap.

Swimming presents unique challenges for AI due to its aquatic environment, which disrupts sensors, causes IMU drift, and complicates motion capture. Unlike land-based sports, swimming involves complex three-dimensional movements across four distinct strokes (freestyle, butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke), each requiring specialized biomechanical models. The paper proposes a three-layer framework combining multimodal sensing, contextual awareness, and adaptive feedback for real-time, swimmer-centric recommendations.

Key findings from the review include: over 80% of studies focused on stroke classification, turn detection, or fatigue monitoring; most studies used small cohorts (n [less than] 30) with single-sensor setups in controlled environments; AI techniques used include CNNs, BiLSTM, RNNs, SVMs, Random Forests, and hybrid architectures; and wearable sensors (IMUs, accelerometers, sEMG, physiological sensors) are the primary data sources.

The paper outlines a structured roadmap for developing intelligent, evidence-driven recommendation systems for swimming, addressing challenges related to data quality, model interpretability, fairness/bias, scalability, and real-time feedback. It also includes a PRISMA methodology for literature selection, a classification framework, and comparisons with AI applications in other sports like basketball.

args.summary:
This is a podcast episode of "Inside with Brett Hawke" (posted January 9, 2025) featuring Jonty Skinner (legendary swim coach) and Kirk Grand (USA Swimming High Performance Specialist) discussing the potential of AI to revolutionize swimming performance. The conversation explores eight key areas where AI can impact the sport: training cataloging, biomechanics, coaching, anthropometry, recovery, physicality/physiology, race analysis, and athlete mindset.

Key discussion points include:
- **Current AI use**: Coaches are using AI to compile workouts and USA Swimming is developing an automated race analysis system.
- **Training cataloging**: The need to systematically catalog all training data (workouts, athlete responses) to feed AI systems, making them "smart."
- **Biomechanics**: Products like EOS Swim Better could have AI filters to simplify complex biomechanical data for coaches.
- **Recovery & Mindset**: AI could help monitor mood states, sleep, cortisol levels, and other recovery metrics, though this area is still underdeveloped.
- **Athlete-Coach Evolution**: The future will see athletes having more managerial control; coaches who are "my way or the highway" won't be successful in 2030. The relationship will be more collaborative.
- **Formula 1 comparison**: AI can help make every hundredth of a second count, similar to F1's approach.
- **Key ranking of performance elements** (Skinner): 1) Athlete Mindset, 2) Physiology, 3) Anthropometry, 4) Biomechanics, 5) Recovery, 6) Coaching, 7) Training, 8) Race Analysis.
- **NIL concerns**: Skinner warns that without a cap on NIL payments, Olympic sports programs will shrink to 10-12 fully funded teams, becoming training centers.
- **Decentralized challenge**: USA Swimming's decentralized nature makes it difficult to prepare for international competitions, but AI can help provide better data for coaches.
- **Wearable technology**: Coaches are increasingly using wearables to make decisions about athlete recovery and training intensity.
- **Age group concerns**: Parents are accessing AI-driven information, which can be both good and bad for youth swimming development.
- **Call to action**: The community needs to organize now to catalog and systematize data for AI integration over the next 5-10 years rather than waiting until it's too late.

# Advanced Machine Vision for Precision Swim Metric Analysis, 10-R6612

Principal Investigators

[Kase Saylor](/user/204/contact)

Omar Medjaouri

Inclusive Dates

04/28/2025 to 08/28/2025

## Background

There is a current initiative to develop an automated race analysis system to enhance performance insights through precise data collection and advanced analytics in competitive swimming. The objective is to create a system that provides high-accuracy, near real-time data for athletes, coaches, and analysts. In response to this initiative, our research focused on developing and validating a technical approach that accurately captures metrics such as stroke count and stroke rate from race videos.

![Graph showing capture stroke data for butterfly](https://www.swri.org/sites/default/files/106612-fig1-graph-stroke-detection-butterfly.jpg)

Figure 1: Stroke detection results for the butterfly stroke.

## Approach

The objective of our project was to create a system capable of automatically analyzing swimming race footage to provide detailed performance data. This system aims to give athletes, coaches, and analysts high-accuracy, near real-time insights into specific metrics like stroke count and stroke rate, thereby enhancing performance evaluation and training.

To achieve this, we developed algorithms for tracking swimmers and identifying individual strokes from race videos. We tracked swimmers in each video and identified their specific strokes using a spatio-temporal neural network based on a multi-scale vision transformer architecture, pretrained and then further trained with semi-supervised methods. Additionally, we created a calibration procedure to align video observations with the physical pool environment using known Olympic pool dimensions and landmarks, supported by a graphical interface to define key points and account for camera position variations. By leveraging pool lane floats as markers, we ensured accurate tracking, facilitating a virtual top-down view of the pool to refine swimmer tracking accuracy.

![Image of a pool on the left and graph of calibration on the right](https://www.swri.org/sites/default/files/106612-fig2-pool-calibration-projected-lanes.jpg)

Figure 2: Pool calibration with projected lanes.

## Accomplishments

The project successfully demonstrated the feasibility of an automated system for precision swim metrics. Our stroke detection algorithm achieved 89.2% accuracy in detecting all Olympic swimming strokes, with high precision and a low rate of false positives, essential for reliable stroke counting. Initially designed for a static camera setup, our calibration tool was adapted to handle moving camera data by estimating frame-to-frame transforms. Though panning and zooming errors presented challenges, using pool lane floats as reference features improved stability.

The stroke detection approach developed in this project can be adapted for various applications requiring automated event detection. The backbone feature extractor was trained on diverse human activity data and can be applied to domains such as manufacturing, health monitoring, and security. This versatility demonstrates that our technical advancements in stroke detection and calibration can extend beyond swimming to other fields, where precise movement identification and tracking are crucial for performance monitoring and analysis.

# **DIVE into Smarter Swimming: Why AI and Open Data Could Revolutionise the Pool**

![Vanessa Camilleri](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*u0BP9szRUd4BzLXOqEvK0A.jpeg)

--

Listen

Share

If you’ve ever watched a swimmer glide through the water and wondered what separates a great stroke from a merely good one, you’re not alone. Coaches, athletes, and scientists have wrestled with this question for decades. But while tools for analysing human performance have advanced in many sports, swimming, especially underwater, has remained notoriously hard to quantify.

![]()

That’s starting to change.

At the heart of this shift is **DIVE**: *Data-driven Intelligent Video Evaluation*. It’s a new research initiative that aims to make detailed swimming analysis available to more than just elite athletes with access to labs and specialists. Through AI and everyday video footage, DIVE seeks to offer coaches and swimmers real-time, objective feedback — and to contribute something the world of sports science desperately needs: a high-quality, publicly available dataset of swimming performance video, both above and below the waterline.

**Why Swimming Still Lacks Smart Tools**

Compared to running or cycling, swimming analysis is stuck in the slow lane. Movement is harder to capture because it’s partially or entirely submerged. Lighting, bubbles, water distortion, and angle of view all interfere with accurate tracking. Most coaches still rely on the naked eye, maybe aided by a few short video clips on a phone. And while motion capture systems exist, they’re expensive, often require wearing markers, and are confined to specialised labs.

The result? A serious gap between what’s needed and what’s accessible — not just for swimmers and coaches, but for researchers, too.

**What’s Missing: Data, Especially Underwater**

You might assume there’s a wealth of video datasets researchers can use to train AI systems in swimming biomechanics. That couldn’t be further from the truth.

Despite growing interest in sports technology, there is currently **no publicly available, real-world dataset of annotated swimming video** that includes both above- and underwater footage of swimmers in motion. Most existing data is either:

Only a handful of datasets (like SwimTrack or Politecnico di Milano’s SwimmerNet) even attempt underwater analysis, and none are fully open for public use. Some focus on bounding boxes; others offer static images or a few annotated frames, but not continuous stroke cycles or biomechanical key points.

This lack of data is a major bottleneck. Without diverse, annotated, high-quality footage of swimmers — from different angles, doing different strokes — AI systems can’t reliably detect technique, symmetry, or flaws. And without public data, researchers around the world can’t test, compare, or build on each other’s work.

**Enter** [**DIVE**](https://dive-project.eu/)

DIVE was born from a simple idea: what if you could analyse swimming performance using just a GoPro and a smart algorithm?

The [research team](https://dive-project.eu/#theteam) at DIVE are currently in early R&D, capturing footage with a **GoPro mounted on a stick** to maintain a stable view above and below the surface. Our system is being trained to extract **key points and body positions**, to analyse stroke rate, body alignment, symmetry, and turn performance.

Unlike closed systems, DIVE isn’t just a product — it’s a **hybrid tool** for both **coaching** and **research**. Our aim is twofold:

We’re collaborating with the **Aquatic Sports Association of Malta, ASA (https://asaofmalta.eu/),** and we plan to expand our dataset with diverse swimmers over time — different strokes, body types, and performance levels, all captured in real training environments.

**Why This Matters — Now**

AI is reshaping sports, from real-time analytics to personalised training, but swimming has lagged in one critical way: it’s incredibly difficult to measure what matters, especially underwater. The technology is evolving; wearable sensors are becoming more common, offering data on acceleration, force, and heart rate. We’re exploring just that through a related initiative: [**SWIM-360**](https://swim-360.eu/), a project focused on using **wearable tech to monitor physiological and biomechanical performance** in competitive swimmers.

But sensors tell only part of the story.

They can track what’s happening *inside* the body or offer raw motion metrics, but they often miss the *how*. That’s where video-based analysis shines. It captures visible form, technique, and subtle inefficiencies that even the best wearables can’t fully detect.

By pairing the data-rich approach of **SWIM-360** with the visual, AI-driven insights of **DIVE**, we see a powerful opportunity: an integrated view of swimming performance, both internal and external, quantifiable and observable.

More importantly, both projects share a commitment to **open research and practical impact**. We don’t want innovation to be locked behind institutional walls. Whether it’s physiological signals from a smartwatch or biomechanical feedback from a GoPro, the goal is the same — equip swimmers and coaches with tools that are effective, affordable, and grounded in real-world data.

That’s why DIVE matters. It’s not just about smarter feedback — it’s about bridging gaps between technologies, between athletes and researchers, and between raw data and real improvement.

***Project DIVE*** *is financed by Xjenza Malta through the Research Excellence Programme (REP)*.

**Further Reading & References**

**SwimXYZ: A Synthetic Dataset for Swimming Motion Analysis**  
 Ghouaiel, N., Amine, A., Bouakaz, S. (2023).  
 👉 <https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3623264.3624440>  
 A publicly available synthetic dataset simulating swimmers from multiple angles, used to overcome the lack of real annotated swimming video.

**MediaEval 2022 SwimTrack Challenge Overview**  
 LIRIS-CNRS.  
 👉 <https://multimediaeval.github.io/editions/2022/tasks/swimtrack/>  
 Describes an annotated dataset of race footage focused on swimmer tracking and stroke rate estimation. Access is restricted to challenge participants.

**Underwater Pose Estimation for Swimmers**  
 Cao, X., & Yan, W. Q. (2024). Multimedia Tools and Applications.  
 👉 <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11042-023-16618-w>  
 Introduces an underwater dataset of swimmer images with 14-point keypoint annotations for pose estimation research.

**SwimmerNET: Markerless Underwater 2D Pose Estimation**  
 Giulietti. N et al. (2023). Politecnico di Milano.  
 👉 <https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/23/4/2364>   
 Describes an internal dataset and AI model for underwater swimmer pose detection. The dataset is not open-source but provides useful benchmarks.

**Why Biomechanical Analysis in Swimming is Difficult but Crucial**  
Barbosa, T. M., et al. (2023). The role of the biomechanics analyst in swimming training and competition analysis. *Sports Biomechanics*, *22*(12), 1734–1751.  
 👉 <https://tinyurl.com/2vybhfrm>  
 A foundational paper on swimming biomechanics and why accurate, multi-angle data capture is vital for performance analysis.

**The Role of Wearable Technology in Competitive Swimming**  
 Morais, J. E., Oliveira, J. P., Sampaio, T., & Barbosa, T. M. (2022). Wearables in swimming for real-time feedback: A systematic review. *Sensors*, *22*(10), 3677.  
 👉 <https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/22/10/3677>  
 A useful introduction to wearable tech in aquatic environments and its limitations without complementary video analysis.

**OpenPose and Deep Learning-Based Keypoint Detection in Sports**  
 Cao, Z., Simon, T., Wei, S. E., & Sheikh, Y. (2017). IEEE CVPR.  
 👉 <https://github.com/CMU-Perceptual-Computing-Lab/openpose>  
 The most widely used open-source keypoint detection library, often used as a baseline in pose estimation research.

**Project DIVE & SWIM-360 (Department of AI, University of Malta)**  
 Ongoing interdisciplinary research projects combining AI, video analysis, and wearables to support athlete performance and open research in swimming.

args.summary:
The article discusses **DIVE** (Data-driven Intelligent Video Evaluation), a research initiative aimed at revolutionizing swimming analysis through AI and open data. Swimming has lagged in sports analytics due to the difficulty of capturing movement underwater—issues with lighting, bubbles, water distortion, and expensive motion capture systems. Currently, there is **no publicly available, real-world dataset of annotated swimming video** that includes both above- and underwater footage. Existing datasets (e.g., SwimTrack, SwimmerNet) are limited, restricted, or not fully open.

DIVE, led by Prof. Vanessa Camilleri at the University of Malta's Department of AI, uses a **GoPro mounted on a stick** to capture stable above- and underwater footage. The system trains AI to extract key points and body positions, analyzing stroke rate, body alignment, symmetry, and turn performance. It is designed as a **hybrid tool for coaching and research**, with plans to release an open dataset. The project collaborates with the **Aquatic Sports Association of Malta** and is funded by Xjenza Malta through the Research Excellence Programme.

A related initiative, **SWIM-360**, focuses on wearable tech for monitoring physiological and biomechanical performance. The article argues that pairing DIVE's video-based AI insights with SWIM-360's sensor data offers an integrated view of swimming performance. Both projects emphasize open research and practical, affordable tools for swimmers and coaches.

# Explainable quality assessment of effective aligned skeletal representations for martial arts movements by multi-machine learning decisions

* [Yiqun Pang](#auth-Yiqun-Pang-Aff1-Aff3)[1](#Aff1),[3](#Aff3)[na1](#na1),
* [Kaiqi Zhang](#auth-Kaiqi-Zhang-Aff2)[2](#Aff2)[na1](#na1) &

* 5229 Accesses
* 13 Citations
* [Metrics details](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4/metrics)

## Abstract

How to utilize modern technological means to provide both accurate scoring and objective feedback for martial arts movements has become an issue that needs to be addressed in the field of physical education. This study proposes an intelligent scoring method based on machine learning. Firstly, the key features are extracted by the feature alignment technique, which eliminates the influence of athletes’ movement speed, rhythm and duration on the scoring, thus reflecting the athletes’ skill level more realistically. Second, to further improve the objectivity and accuracy, an adaptive weighted multi-model decision-making strategy is proposed. In addition, this study is the first to use interpretable artificial intelligence to provide feedback for teaching and learning Wushu. Experimental results indicate that the integrated model using the weighted average strategy not only outperforms other algorithms after feature alignment (on the XSQ dataset MAE is 0.237, RMSE is 0.442, sMAPE is 8.569, R^{2} is 0.633, Pearson’s correlation is 0.807, ICC is 0.856. on the UMONS-Taichi dataset, MAE is 0.29, RMSE is 0.438, sMAPE is 10.01, R^{2} is 0.844, Pearson correlation is 0.921, and ICC is 0.954. on the PBB dataset, MAE is 0.261, RMSE is 0.351, sMAPE is 6.765, R^{2} is 0.557, Pearson correlation is 0.753, and ICC is 0.82), but is also close to the performance of human experts. In conclusion, this study not only achieves a performance of movement evaluation comparable to human experts, but also provides a technical framework for the rapid realizing of automatic scoring in other martial arts styles, which will promote the popularization and development of martial arts education.

## Introduction

As a treasure of traditional Chinese culture, Wushu (Chinese traditional martial arts) is popular among people all over the world for its deep cultural heritage and unique techniques. However, for a long time, the scoring of wushu movements has depended on the subjective judgment of coaches or referees, which to a certain extent limits the scientific nature of wushu training and the fairness of competitions. Therefore, how to utilize modern technical means, especially machine learning technology, to provide an objective and accurate scoring method for Wushu movements has become an urgent problem in the field of physical education.

The assessment of human behavior plays an important role in skills training, and meaningful feedback information can be provided to individuals and guide them to improve their skill level.[1](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#ref-CR1 "Lei, Q., Du, J.-X., Zhang, H.-B., Ye, S. & Chen, D.-S. A survey of vision-based human action evaluation methods. Sensors 19. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/s19194129
                  
                 (2019).") In recent years, with the rapid development of computer vision and machine learning technologies, more and more researchers have begun to try to apply these technologies to the assessment of movement quality in physical education and sports[2](#ref-CR2 "Patrona, F., Chatzitofis, A., Zarpalas, D. & Daras, P. Motion analysis: Action detection, recognition and evaluation based on motion capture data. Pattern Recogn. 76, 612–622. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2017.12.007
                  
                 (2018)."),[3](#ref-CR3 "Meng, M., Drira, H. & Boonaert, J. Distances evolution analysis for online and off-line human object interaction recognition. Image Vis. Comput. 70, 32–45. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.imavis.2017.12.003
                  
                 (2018)."),[4](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#ref-CR4 "Xu, C. et al. Learning to score figure skating sport videos. IEEE Trans. Circuits Syst. Video Technol. 30, 4578–4590. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/TCSVT.2019.2927118
                  
                 (2020)."). In the field of martial arts, there have been studies using these machine learning techniques to evaluate the actions of Tai Chi, Taekwondo, and Karate.[5](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#ref-CR5 "Pang, Y., Wang, Q., Zhang, C., Wang, M. & Wang, Y. Analysis of computer vision applied in martial arts. In 2022 2nd International Conference on Consumer Electronics and Computer Engineering (ICCECE), 191–196. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCECE54139.2022.9712803
                  
                 (2022)."),[6](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#ref-CR6 "Yuqing, Z., Mingliang, C., Haoyang, Z. & Yong, Z. Vr technology and application in martial arts. In 2021 IEEE 7th International Conference on Virtual Reality (ICVR), 240–245. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/ICVR51878.2021.9483700
                  
                 (2021).") The current methods of utilizing artificial intelligence for martial arts movement evaluation can be divided into rule determination method, similarity metric method and model-based method.

Generally speaking, the model-based method has a strong nonlinear fitting ability and is good at fitting the complex relationship between sports data and sports performance. Compared with similarity metrics, the model-based approach can be more accurate. However, due to the high complexity of AI models, the decision-making process is a “black box” , i.e., its decision-making process is not transparent and it is difficult to give any rationale for scoring. The “black box” property means that when the data fed to the model is biased, there will be misjudgment or omission of judgment, which greatly reduces the credibility of the evaluation results. Moreover, the “black box” property makes the model-based approach unable to provide specific suggestions for athletes and enthusiasts to improve their skills.

Moreover, in fact, the speed and rhythm of accomplishing the same movement may vary from one player to another. Even for the same competitor, there may be slight distortions in Wushu movements, possibly due to factors such as the competitor’s skill level, physical condition, or competitive status. These differences in rhythm and tempo can create potential challenges for movement assessment. In addition, the existing methods do not mimic the human scoring model well. In Wushu competitions, there are usually multiple judges forming a panel of judges who are responsible for judging the performance of the athletes. Each judge will rate the athlete’s technique, performance, and other aspects based on the athlete’s expertise and experience. These independent ratings will be aggregated, averaged, or combined using other methods to determine the final score. By combining the opinions of multiple judges, the impact of subjective bias or misjudgment of individual judges on the overall score can be reduced, thus improving the objectivity and fairness of the scoring. It can also reflect a more comprehensive evaluation as different judges may notice different details or aspects and by combining their views, a more comprehensive evaluation can be obtained. What’s more, considering the universality of the martial arts scoring system, the AI model should be able to do a good job of making an accurate assessment of martial arts movements with only a small number of samples.

Therefore, this study aims to propose an intelligent scoring method for martial arts routines based on feature alignment and multi-model decision-making, which is intended to solve the above problems and provide a framework for scientific training and objective evaluation of martial arts. The contributions of this study are:

* First, the undesirable interference on scoring due to the speed, rhythm, and duration of movements of different players is eliminated by the feature alignment method;
* Second, by simulating the scoring mechanism of real competition and combining the prediction results of multiple models to improve the robustness and accuracy of output scores;
* Moreover, an intelligent model of interpretable Wushu movement assessment is implemented for the first time by utilizing the SHaply interpreter;
* Last but not least, this study also provides a machine learning-based solution for scoring Wushu movements that can be applied to low sample size situations, providing strong support for the popularization and development of Wushu. The code of the program is available from the [GitHub link](https://github.com/pyqpyqpyqpyq789/Intelligent-Scoring-the-Long-Fist-Routine-Movements/)

## Literature review

### Motion capture in martial arts

Current motion capture techniques applied to martial arts are mainly infrared reflection-based[7](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#ref-CR7 "Burdack, J., Horst, F., Aragonés, D., Eekhoff, A. & Schöllhorn, W. Fatigue-related and timescale-dependent changes in individual movement patterns identified using support vector machine. Front. Psychol. 11, 2273. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.551548
                  
                 (2020)."),[8](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#ref-CR8 "Klempous, R. et al. Neural networks classification for training of five german longsword mastercuts - a novel application of motion capture: Analysis of performance of sword fencing in the historical european martial arts (hema) domain. In 2021 IEEE 21st International Symposium on Computational Intelligence and Informatics (CINTI), 000137–000142.

Monocular 3D human pose estimation is a group of techniques for predicting the 3D coordinates of the human skeleton from images or videos captured by a single camera. As an end-to-end deep learning framework consisting of a nonlinear shape space, a pose space deformation corrector, a skeleton joint center estimator, and a surface hybrid skinning function, GHUM reconstructs the 3D coordinates of human joints in real-time from a single image or video through nonlinear pose and shape optimization. Since the dataset used to train the BlazePose GHUM model contains a large number of fitness and yoga poses, the model learns about them during the training phase and may be more suitable for human pose estimation in sports scenarios.

Overview of the proposed method.

The overview of the proposed method is shown in Fig. [1](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#Fig1), which consists of the process of extracting the human skeleton representation from the video sequence and further learning the body pose features. Firstly, the video sequences containing martial arts actions are used as input; Secondly, the human skeleton data were extracted from the video sequence; Furthermore, based on these skeleton data, the features related to body posture are extracted to describe the posture and motion patterns of the human body at different time points; Then, a variety of machine learning algorithms are applied to process and analyze the extracted features; Then, a weighted average is calculated based on the output of the machine learning algorithm to obtain a comprehensive score; Ultimately, the relationships of main features and scores are analyzed from both global and local via the Shaply interpreter. Its whole set of movements covers the basic hand styles such as fist, palm and hook, and the basic steps such as bow stance, horse stance, servant stance, virtual stance and resting stance. The simple structure of Xingshen Quan’s routines, with its generous movements and flexible techniques, embodies the sport style of Chinese martial arts, which is characterized by the combination of form and spirit, and the unity of inside and outside.

To collect the movement data of Xingshen Quan, 60 volunteers of different levels were included in this study. ### Feature extraction

#### Extraction of human skeleton

The human pose estimation model built into MediaPipe was used to obtain the 3D skeleton coordinates of the participants from the XSQ and PBB videos. The minimum individual detection confidence of the model was set = 0.5, the minimum joint tracking confidence = 0.5, the coordinates were automatically smoothed to reduce jitter, the complexity of the skeleton detection model = 2 to improve the detection accuracy, and the coordinates were in meters. After the above operations, action sequences containing 33 joint coordinates are obtained, and the structure and order of the human skeleton are the same as the BlazePose[42](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#ref-CR42 "Xu, H. et al. Ghum & ghuml: Generative 3d human shape and articulated pose models. In 2020 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 6183–6192. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR42600.2020.00622
                  
                 (2020).").

#### Representation of body posture

To better characterize the relative positions and relationships of body parts and to avoid confusion due to the participants’ body types and shooting distances and directions, a total of 18 angles were defined in the present study (as shown in Table [1](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#Tab1), and the skeleton structures are provided in the supplementary materials Figs. [S1](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#MOESM1) and [S2](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#MOESM1)). The main body parts include: the upper limbs, lower limbs, and trunk. The angles representing the upper limbs include the shoulder joint angle, elbow joint angle, upper arm angle with vertical axis, and forearm angle with vertical axis; the lower limbs include the hip joint angle, knee joint angle, thigh angle with vertical axis and calf angle with vertical axis; and the trunk includes the shoulder-hip torsion angle and the head-hip torsion angle. In addition, symmetric vectors are included for each of the left and right sides of the upper and lower limbs, except for the trunk position. The body posture represented in this way encompasses tilt, rotation, and lateral inclination of the head; bending, twisting, and tilting of the torso; and flexion and extension of the limbs. Together, these angles define the position and posture of the body in space, thus helping to understand and describe a person’s body posture. The human skeletal coordinates in Figs. [S1](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#MOESM1) and [S2](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#MOESM1) are expressed in terms of angles and computed as shown in Eq. [1](/articles/s41598-024-83475-4#Equ1):

\begin{aligned} A\_i = \arccos \left( \frac{\mathbf {V\_1} \cdot \mathbf {V\_2}}{\left| \mathbf {V\_1} \right| \left| \mathbf {V\_2} \right| }\right) \cdot \frac{180}{\pi } \end{aligned}

(1)

where \mathbf {V\_1} \cdot \mathbf {V\_2} denotes the inner product of two skeletal segment vectors, \arccos is the inverse cosine function, and \pi is the circumference.

#### Feature alignment

In actuality, the speed and rhythm of accomplishing the same movement may vary from one participant to another. Even for the same participant, there may be some subtle distortions in the martial arts movements, which may be due to factors such as the skill level of the competitor, physical condition, or competition status. In the present study, we use a method that can deal with such time-scale variations by nonlinearly mapping the two time sequences so that the faster part of the time axis is “stretched” and the slower part is “compressed”, thus realizing the effective alignment of different rates of This enables efficient alignment of different rates of motion. The highest-scored action sequences in each dataset were sampled using 32 aliquots, which were defined as action templates. First, the highest scoring action sequence in each dataset is sampled using 32 equal points, which are defined as action templates. All other action sequences will be aligned to the 32 frames in the action template. * First, define an L1 \times L2 matrix *D*, where D\_{i,j} denotes the distance between the *i*th element in the sequence *X* and the *j*th element in sequence *Y*.
* Next, define an L1 \times L2 matrix *C*, where C\_{i,j} denotes the minimum distance from the start X\_1 to the end X\_i of the sequence *X*, and from the start Y\_1 to the end Y\_j of the sequence *Y*.
* Initialize the boundary conditions of the matrix *C*:

  \begin{aligned} & C\_{i,j}=D\_{i,j} \end{aligned}

  (2)

  \begin{aligned} & C\_{i,0} = C\_{i-1,0} + D\_{i,0} \quad \text {for } i = 1,2,\ldots ,L1 \end{aligned}

  (4)
* The rest of the matrix C is then filled by the following recursive formula:

  \begin{aligned} C\_{i,j} = D\_{i,j} + \min (C\_{i-1,j}, C\_{i,j-1}, C\_{i-1,j-1}) \quad \text {for } i = 1,2,\ldots ,L1 \quad and \quad \text {for } j = 1,2,\ldots ,L2 \end{aligned}

  where C\_{i-1,j}, C\_{i,j-1} and C\_{i-1,j-1} denote the three possible paths to reach the previous step of point *ij* respectively.
* Finally, the best matching path is obtained by finding the optimal path, i.e., the minimum path, from the upper left corner to the lower right corner of the matrix *C*.

#### Base regressors

Treating the assessment of Wushu movements as a regression task, linear regression (LR), lasso regression, support vector machine (SVM), k-nearest neighbor (KNN), decision tree (DT), random forest (RF), and bagging were used as the base regressors for fitting the relationship between the movement metrics and the scores.

### SHapley interpreter

The SHapley interpreter is a method for interpreting the prediction results of machine learning models. Based on the concept of Shapley values in cooperative game theory, the contribution of features can be metricized as a contribution to the prediction results to dissect the prediction process of the model.

The SHapley interpreter can provide both global and local interpretations for understanding the model’s prediction process on the whole and on individual samples. The global interpretation provides an understanding of the whole model, i.e., the extent of the model’s contribution and influences on different features. By calculating the SHapley values, it is possible to determine the extent to which each feature contributes to the model’s predictions as a whole. Global interpretation helps to understand the overall behavior of the model and can be used to compare the impact of different features on the model. Local interpretation, on the other hand, helps to understand the basis for scoring individual samples, i.e., the extent to which each feature in a particular sample influences the predictions, and thus explains why the model makes the predictions it does for that sample. Local interpretation helps to identify the key features in a single sample and the basis for the score in a particular action situation.

args.summary: This is a scientific article published in Scientific Reports (2025, volume 15, Article 323) titled "Explainable quality assessment of effective aligned skeletal representations for martial arts movements by multi-machine learning decisions." The study proposes an intelligent scoring method for martial arts movements using machine learning. Key methodological contributions include: (1) feature alignment using dynamic time warping (DTW) to eliminate the influence of movement speed, rhythm, and duration on scoring; (2) an adaptive weighted multi-model decision-making strategy that simulates real competition judging panels; and (3) the first use of interpretable AI (SHapley interpreter) to provide feedback for Wushu teaching and learning. Three datasets were used: Xingshen Quan (XSQ) with 180 video clips from 60 volunteers, Plum Blossom Boxing (PBB) with 105 video clips from 35 practitioners, and the open-access UMONS-Taichi dataset (1376 movement segments). Human skeleton data was extracted using MediaPipe's BlazePose, and 18 body angles were defined as features. The integrated model using weighted average strategy outperformed individual algorithms, achieving strong results: on XSQ dataset (MAE=0.237, RMSE=0.442, R²=0.633, Pearson=0.807, ICC=0.856), on UMONS-Taichi (MAE=0.29, RMSE=0.438, R²=0.844, Pearson=0.921, ICC=0.954), and on PBB (MAE=0.261, RMSE=0.351, R²=0.557, Pearson=0.753, ICC=0.82). The method achieved performance comparable to human experts and provides a technical framework for automatic scoring applicable to other martial arts styles.

# Transforming tennis with artificial intelligence: a bibliometric review

Tatiana Sampaio 1,2,3

João P. Oliveira 1,2,3

Daniel A. Marinho 1,2

Henrique P. Neiva 1,2

Jorge E. Morais 3,4\*

1. Department of Sports Sciences, University of Beira Interior, Covilhã, Portugal

## Abstract

The aim of this study was to conduct a scoping and bibliometric review of articles using artificial intelligence (AI) in tennis. The analysis covered various aspects of tennis, including performance, health, match results, physiological data, tennis expenditure, and prize amounts. Articles on AI in tennis published until 2024 were retrieved from the Web of Science database. A total of 389 records were screened, and 108 articles were retained for analysis. The analysis identified intermittent gaps in publication output during certain intervals, notably in the years 2007–2008 and 2012–2013. From 2012 onward, there was a clear upward trend in publications and citations, peaking in 2022. The theme was led by China, the United States, and Australia. These countries maintain their status as the top contributors in terms of publications. The analysis of author collaborations revealed multiple clusters, with notable contributions from researchers in China, Australia, Japan, and the United States. This bibliometric review has elucidated the evolution of AI research in tennis, highlighting the countries and authors that have significantly contributed to this field over the years. The prediction model suggests that the number of articles and citations on this topic will continue to increase over the next decade (until 2034).

## 1 Introduction

Tennis has experienced significant changes in recent decades (1). This globally practiced sport enjoyed both recreationally and competitively, requires players to continually develop and master essential technical skills for effective performance during matches. As the world's second most popular sport, trailing only soccer, tennis is played in 195 countries and boasts an estimated 87 million fans — individuals who have played tennis at least once — representing about 1.17% of the global population (2, 3).

Historically, tennis was primarily a technical sport, with a strong emphasis on specific skills such as stroke techniques. However, it has evolved into a more dynamic and explosive sport, characterized by increased serve and stroke velocities, and significantly higher physical demands (4, 5). The physical fitness levels of tennis players are now critical in determining match outcomes, particularly in competitions where players have closely matched skill levels (6, 7). To compete at the highest level, athletes now require a holistic combination of speed, agility, and power, coupled with moderate to high aerobic capacity (1). Supporting these physical demands are critical cognitive and psychological processes (8, 9). Players must exhibit exceptional reactive abilities, anticipation skills, and decision-making skills while maintaining mental fortitude to cope with fatigue, the pressure of high-stakes points, and the draw of significant extrinsic rewards like ranking and lucrative endorsements (10–12). The stop-and-start nature of tennis competitions further adds to the complexity (5).

Computational intelligence has developed into a powerful instrument in recent years for optimizing athletic performance in a variety of sports. With huge possibilities for future growth in the upcoming years, interest in AI and its subcategories is expanding at an exponential rate (13).

Applied scientists find machine learning (ML) to be an effective instrument in this dynamic and data-rich environment (14, 15). In terms of both research and practical application, the USA has been recognized as a leader in the application of AI in sports. Artificial intelligence has been utilized for player and game analysis for several years, mostly in baseball and American football (16).

AI and its subcategories, ML and deep learning have both seen significant growth in recent years. Therefore, the term AI is used even when referring to ML or deep learning in individual publications (17). The vast majority agree that AI is just a machine-implemented form of human intelligence. An approach to AI called ML describes computer systems that can learn from experiences or examples without explicit programming. In the domain of automatic feature discovery through representation learning, deep learning has also become a key methodology for ML implementation as an artificial neural network-based method (17).

The availability (i.e., quality and quantity) of data, which has a significant impact on the performance of AI models, has been one of the causes supporting the exponential growth of AI in recent years, as has the ongoing enhancement of the related techniques (18). Additionally, many people are finding it easier and more accessible to create ML models thanks to user-friendly open-source programming libraries like PyTorch (19) and scikit-learn (20). These factors have made it possible for AI to gradually make progress into sports contexts and applications, opening up an array of new possibilities (21, 22).

A significant bibliographic dataset has resulted from the research situation about AI technologies in sports, which makes manual examination unfeasible. To identify and justify new research necessities, the relevant research and structures must be thoroughly examined to uncover existing knowledge, challenges, and research shortcomings.

Bibliometric analysis is a promising method that is growing to become increasingly significant in many areas of research. For instance, bibliometric analyses are used to investigate the intellectual structures of specific fields based on their respective literature bases, as well as to identify new trends, collaborative features, and research aspects (23, 24). While traditional review approaches must concentrate on a reasonable amount of literature, bibliometric techniques (together with meta-analyses) are particularly promising and appropriate to assist in understanding of the massive quantity of material (25). Furthermore, although bibliometric analysis depends more on quantitative approaches than conventional systematic literature reviews, it can prevent or at least lessen the impact of scholarly interpretation bias (24).

Although AI has changed various aspects of sports science, a bibliometric review regarding the applications of AI in tennis remains an under-explored topic. While several systematic reviews have explored various applications of ML in tennis (26–31), no bibliometric review has specifically examined the applications of AI in tennis. Therefore, the aim of this study was to conduct a comprehensive scoping and bibliometric review of articles on AI in tennis. The objectives were to analyze the chronological distribution of publications and citations, to map the network of contributing countries/regions and institutions, and to identify the most influential journals and authors in this research domain. This review aims to provide a clearer understanding of the trends, collaborations, and key contributors in the field of AI applications in tennis.

## 2 Methods

### 2.1 Data source and search strategy

With over 250 fields covered, the Web of Science (WoS) incorporates reliable worldwide citation databases spanning all areas of research (32). For several journals chosen according to the index, the WoS list offers comprehensive details on definitions, coverage remarks, and the most significant impact factor score (32). Numerous bibliometric studies, particularly those on sports, have made extensive use of it (33, 34). For this reason, the database used in this bibliometric review is the WoS Core Collection (WoS by Clarivate Analytics).

The search spanned until June 1, 2024, and several strategies were developed to account for the recent emergence of the topic. Utilizing a comprehensive approach, the search strategy entailed combining the term “tennis” with various AI-related terminologies using the Boolean operator “AND/OR” (35). These terminologies encompassed “artificial intelligence”, “machine learning”, “deep learning”, “neural network”, “support vector machine”, “nearest neighbor”, “random forest”, “Bayesian logistic regression”, and “predictive modeling”. This search strategy aimed to capture all relevant studies investigating the application of AI and its subfields, including machine learning, within the domain of tennis.

### 2.2 Inclusion and exclusion criteria

The following inclusion criteria were applied: (i) written in English; (ii) articles involving tennis; (iii) articles with data analyzed with ML algorithms, deep learning, or other AI techniques; (iv) articles related to, but not limited to, performance, health, match results, physiological data and other relevant aspects; (v) articles focused on tennis players, including humans and robots. Exclusion criteria were: (i) articles written in languages other than English; (ii) articles lacking information on critical information to ascertain the use of AI techniques; (iii) articles focused on other sports (i.e., football, basketball, etc.).

### 2.3 Screening process

Two reviewers examined the titles and abstracts of the selected papers independently. When an article's eligibility was questionable, the entire text was obtained. The same two reviewers evaluated the eligibility requirements and checked through the articles published in the integral. These reviewers conducted two independent rounds of evaluation for each article. The article's complete content was assessed after the title and abstract were assessed. Disputes involving eligibility were settled by conversation and, if required, with the help of a third reviewer.

The WoS search yielded 389 records, of which 111 were duplicates and were therefore excluded. Additionally, 18 articles were excluded by automation tools (filtered to identify only articles written in English). The remaining 260 studies were then assessed by reading the relevant sections. 152 studies that did not meet the inclusion criteria (104 articles were focused on other sports, 36 articles used other statistical methods and 12 articles were in another language) were excluded. Finally, a total of 108 articles met the defined criteria and were included in the review. [Figure 1](#F1) shows the identification, screening, and inclusion of the articles from the WoS database for the review. When full-text publications were accessible, further information was retrieved for an in-depth study, including the approach and results.

### 2.4 Analytical methods and tools

The bibliometric data was extracted and analyzed using specialized software. The measurement program VOSviewer (<https://www.vosviewer.com>), created by Van Eck and Waltman, is based on Java and is intended for use in the creation and display of bibliometric networks (36). These networks can be built based on citation, bibliographic coupling, co-citation, or co-authorship links, and they comprise journals, researchers, or individual publications. As a result, in the cooperative network visualization and the co-sponsorship network visualization, distinct clusters were visually represented by different colors, and collaborative relationships were indicated by lines linking nodes. Specifically, the average publication year graph's colors designate distinct years, making temporal analysis easier. The various densities are also reflected in the color spectrum, especially on density graphs where denser locations are shown by redder colors.

The assessment of individuals (primarily authors, institutions, journals, and countries) based on bibliographic information is included in the first category. Scientific mapping, which is the second category, examines the connections across disciplines, fields, specializations, individual articles, and authors through a geographical visual representation of bibliometric networks. Therefore, by examining the earlier categories in the VOSviewer program, a comprehensive evaluation of the applications of ML in tennis was completed.

The number of years after a document was published has a substantial correlation with its citation count (37). A manuscript that was published earlier will often have had more time to gain citations than one that was released recently. Consequently, raw citation counts are not a valid indicator of publication impact. For this reason, the citation analysis in this study was normalized to take into consideration variations in the years of publication, enabling a more precise evaluation of the influence of academic publications. To reduce the bias brought on by variations in publication dates in citation practices, normalization is crucial in bibliometric analysis (38). As a result, each article's total number of citations was divided by the publication's age, which was determined by subtracting the present year from the year of publication. Additional information regarding the calculation of the metric can be found in (39).

Additionally, using Excel's exponential smoothing, the number of papers expected to be published in the next ten years (until 2034) was estimated based on historical publication trends using “=FORECAST.ETS” function (Microsoft, Microsoft 365, Washington, USA) (40). This makes it possible to evaluate time-series data and generate forecasts or predictions based on previous trends.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 Progression of publications by year

Between 2006 (the year of the first publication with ML in tennis) and 2024, the WoS database contained a total of 108 articles related to AI in tennis. [Figure 2A](#F2) shows the publication output regarding AI in tennis research during the period from 2006 to 2024. [Figure 2B](#F2) shows the citation output regarding AI in tennis research during the period from 2006 to 2024. The yearly publication trends reveal intermittent gaps in certain time intervals with no publications, particularly in the years 2007–2008 and 2012–2013. Despite these gaps, there is an overall upward trend in publications on the topic until 2022. After 2022, however, there is a noticeable decline in annual publications, with 24 records in 2022, 18 in 2023, and 5 in 2024. Notably, the largest number of articles was published in 2022, with 24 articles focusing on AI in tennis.

Publication output on AI in tennis by year and estimated number of articles for the next 10 years. The red solid line represents the estimate, and the red dashed lines represent the 95% confidence intervals **(A)**; Citation outputs related to AI in tennis research by year and the estimated number of citations for the next 10 years. The red solid line represents the estimate and the red dashed lines the 95% confidence intervals **(B).**

Regarding the yearly citation trends demonstrate intermittent gaps in certain time intervals with no citations, particularly in 2008. Despite these gaps, there is a clear upward trend in citations on the topic until 2023. After 2023, however, there is a marked decrease in annual citations, with 176 citations in 2023 and 54 in 2024. Notably, the largest number of citations was recorded in 2022, with 140 citations related to ML in tennis.

The exponential smoothing estimation model showed an average of 13.36 ± 2.74 articles per year (95% confidence intervals: −5.30; 32.01) that may be published between 2025 and 2034. For citations, the estimation model indicated an average of 139.14 ± 20.88 citations (95% confidence intervals: 69.47; 208.82) per year between the same time periods.

### 3.2 Web of science (WoS) categorization

The study field can be categorized, and potential interdisciplinary linkages might be found by examining the categories within the WoS. [Figure 3](#F3) presents the analysis of the WoS categories. ## 4 Discussion

### 4.1 Comprehensive analysis

The aim of this study was to conduct a comprehensive scoping and bibliometric review of articles using AI in tennis. From the bibliometric analysis of the use of AI in tennis, it is evident that there has been an unstable yet overall upward trend in research publications and citations. The analysis identified intermittent gaps in publication output during certain intervals, notably in the years 2007–2008 and 2012–2013, which reflects variability in research activity. Despite these gaps, the peak in publication numbers occurred in 2022 with 24 articles, while citation activity reached in 2023 176 citations. This suggests increased research interest and recognition of the importance of AI in tennis during these years. The subsequent decline in both publications and citations post 2022 indicates a potential change. However, the exponential smoothing estimation model predicts an average of 13.36 ± 2.74 articles per year and 139.14 ± 20.88 citations per year between 2025 and 2034, suggesting sustained interest in AI research in tennis in the coming years.

Additionally, the Web of Science categorization reveals that AI in tennis research spans multiple disciplines, with the most prominent fields being Engineering Electrical Electronic, Computer Science Artificial Intelligence, and Sports Sciences. This interdisciplinary approach underscores the comprehensive impact of AI technologies in various aspects of tennis, from performance analysis to equipment innovation.

Furthermore, a total of 34 countries have contributed to research, showcasing a global collaborative effort. Notably, China has emerged as a leading contributor, with significant input also from countries such as Australia, Japan, and the United States. This geographic distribution highlights the global recognition of the potential benefits of AI in enhancing tennis performance and strategy.

### 4.2 Keywords analysis and research hotspots

This bibliometric review offers critical insights into the evolving landscape of AI research in tennis, focusing on identifying emerging research hot spots through a comprehensive keyword analysis. The analysis identifies three primary clusters, each representing a significant concentration of research efforts and advancements in AI applications within tennis. These clusters not only map the current research landscape but also indicate promising directions for future studies, marking them as research hot spots.

#### 4.2.1 Performance analysis and optimization (cluster 1)

The first cluster is characterized by keywords such as classification, ML, neural network, performance, racquet sports, sport, and tennis. This cluster underscores the pivotal role of AI in performance analysis and optimization. Research in this area leverages sophisticated ML algorithms and neural networks to classify player movements, predict performance outcomes, and refine training regimens (46–48). The specific focus on tennis highlights the tailored application of these technologies to enhance athlete performance. Studies within this cluster emphasize the development of data-driven insights and personalized training strategies, essential for maintaining a competitive advantage in the sport (49, 50). The advancements in this area are crucial for developing more precise and effective performance enhancement techniques, enabling athletes and coaches to optimize training programs based on evidence and predictive analytics.

Recent developments in AI, particularly in ML and neural networks, have allowed for more detailed and accurate performance analysis (51–53). The ability to classify and analyze specific movements and techniques offers invaluable feedback for athletes, enabling them to refine their skills and strategies. Additionally, the predictive capabilities of AI can help anticipate performance trends and outcomes, allowing for proactive adjustments in training and competition strategies.

#### 4.2.2 Technological integration and innovation (cluster 2)

The second cluster is defined by keywords such as action recognition, computer vision, deep learning, support vector machine, and tracking. This cluster focuses on the integration of advanced AI technologies into tennis. Research aims to develop sophisticated systems for action recognition and tracking, employing techniques like support vector machines to improve accuracy and efficiency (54–[57](#B57)). These innovations enable real-time analysis of player movements and game dynamics, providing critical feedback for performance enhancement. The application of cutting-edge technologies such as computer vision and deep learning reflects the sport's adaptation to modern advancements, bridging traditional methods with progressive AI solutions.

In particular, computer vision technology has revolutionized the way player movements and game dynamics are analyzed. By processing video footage in real-time, these systems can track player positions, movements, and interactions with unprecedented precision. This capability not only enhances performance analysis but also facilitates the development of strategic insights that can be applied during matches. Deep learning algorithms further enhance these systems by improving the accuracy and reliability of action recognition and tracking ([58](#B58)–[60](#B60)). The integration of these technologies into training and competition settings represents a significant advancement in the sport, providing players and coaches with powerful tools to enhance performance and strategy.

#### 4.2.3 Biomechanics and wearable technology (cluster 3)

The third cluster is characterized by keywords such as biomechanics, sports, and wearable sensors. This cluster highlights the connection between biomechanics and wearable technology. Research in this area focuses on the use of wearable sensors to collect detailed biomechanical data, which is then analyzed to monitor player performance ([61](#B61), [62](#B62)). This cluster is particularly relevant for injury prevention and rehabilitation, as well as for optimizing training techniques based on biomechanical insights. The advancements in this field signify a move towards more comprehensive and real-time monitoring of athletes, enhancing both performance and safety.

Moreover, wearable technology has become increasingly sophisticated, with sensors capable of capturing a wide range of biomechanical data, including movement patterns, muscle activity, and joint angles ([63](#B63)). This data provides a detailed understanding of the physical demands and stresses placed on athletes during training and competition. By analyzing this information, researchers and trainers can identify potential injury risks and develop targeted interventions to prevent injuries and enhance recovery. This holistic approach to performance monitoring and injury prevention is essential for maintaining athlete health and longevity in the sport.

## 5 Implications for the future

The identification of these clusters through keyword analysis underscores the dynamic and evolving nature of AI applications in tennis. As the sport continues to bridge tradition with advancement, the insights from these clusters offer several key implications for the future.

First, the ongoing research in performance analysis and optimization will continue to provide athletes and coaches with valuable data-driven insights, fostering personalized and effective training methodologies. The advancements in ML and neural networks will enhance the ability to classify and predict performance, enabling more precise and effective training interventions. The integration of computer vision and deep learning technologies will pave the way for innovative solutions that enhance real-time performance monitoring and feedback, transforming traditional training and game analysis. These technologies will provide players and coaches with actionable insights that can be applied during matches, improving strategic decision-making and performance outcomes.

A continued exploration of these identified hot spots will further solidify the role of AI in tennis, supporting interdisciplinary collaborations and the development of novel applications in sport. The integration of AI technologies into tennis represents a significant advancement in the sport, offering new opportunities for research and innovation that align with the sport's history.

## 6 Conclusions

This bibliometric review allowed us to understand the evolution of articles published on the use of AI in tennis. Although the research activity has shown intermittent gaps, there has been a consistent increase in publications and citations, particularly peaking in 2022 and 2023. The prediction model indicates that the number of articles and citations on this topic will continue to grow until 2034. Three main research clusters were identified (Performance Analysis and Optimization, Technological Integration and Innovation, and Biomechanics and Wearable Technology). These clusters highlight AI's pivotal role in enhancing performance, integrating advanced technologies, and improving biomechanics. The ongoing research in these areas will continue to drive innovation and interdisciplinary collaboration in tennis.

This is a review article published in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living on December 23, 2024, titled "Transforming tennis with artificial intelligence: a bibliometric review" by Sampaio et al. The study conducted a scoping and bibliometric review of articles using artificial intelligence (AI) in tennis, covering performance, health, match results, physiological data, and prize amounts. A total of 389 records were screened from the Web of Science database, with 108 articles retained for analysis. The review identified intermittent publication gaps (notably 2007-2008 and 2012-2013), with an upward trend peaking in 2022. China, the United States, and Australia led contributions. The prediction model suggests continued growth in articles and citations until 2034.

**Methods:** Searched WoS Core Collection until June 1, 2024, using "tennis" combined with AI-related terms. Two reviewers screened independently. Data analyzed using VOSviewer for bibliometric networks and Excel exponential smoothing for forecasting.

**Key Findings:**
- 108 articles published between 2006-2024; peak in 2022 (24 articles)
- Citations peaked in 2023 (176 citations)
- Prediction: avg. 13.36 ± 2.74 articles/year and 139.14 ± 20.88 citations/year (2025-2034)
- Top WoS categories: Engineering Electrical Electronic (33), Computer Science AI (31), Sports Sciences (18)
- 34 countries contributed; top: China (46, 39%), Australia (11), Japan (8), England (6), USA (6)
- 310 researchers contributed; top authors: Reid M. (8), Gu SS, Kovalchik S., Powroznik P., Skublewska-paszkowska M. (3 each)
- Top cited article: Whiteside et al. (2017) "Monitoring Hitting Load in Tennis Using Inertial Sensors and Machine Learning" (citation index 8.43)

**Three Main Research Clusters Identified:**
1. **Performance Analysis and Optimization** - classification, ML, neural networks, performance analysis
2. **Technological Integration and Innovation** - action recognition, computer vision, deep learning, tracking
3. **Biomechanics and Wearable Technology** - wearable sensors, biomechanical data, injury prevention

**Conclusions:** AI research in tennis is interdisciplinary and growing. Three main clusters highlight AI's role in enhancing performance, integrating advanced technologies, and improving biomechanics. Research is expected to continue growing until 2034.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | Research on an intelligent tutoring system based on automatic construction of multimodal knowledge graphs and retrieval-augmented generation ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/computer-science/articles/10.3389/fcomp.2026.1777749/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Technology and Code article published in Frontiers in Computer Science (February 25, 2026) by Chao Deng and Bo Yuan from Guangdong University of Science and Technology, China. The paper presents a framework for an Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS) based on automatic construction of multimodal knowledge graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

**Key Contributions:**
1. A cross-modal knowledge fusion pipeline that aligns and merges entities from video transcripts (via FFmpeg/Whisper ASR) and textbook PDFs (via OCR and layout analysis)
2. A hybrid retrieval-augmented paradigm combining graph database queries (Neo4j) with vector similarity matching (HNSW index) to drive LLM-based Q&A
3. Direct processing of unstructured course videos as the application source

**System Architecture:**
- Knowledge Construction Layer: Processes multimodal inputs (video audio, textbook PDFs) through automatic speech recognition (Whisper), OCR (PaddleOCR), BERT-based entity recognition, relation extraction, entity disambiguation/fusion, and instructional context enrichment
- Dual Storage: Structured triples stored in Neo4j graph database; text chunks embedded as vectors in a vector database using HNSW indexing
- Q&A Layer: Hybrid retrieval (graph + vector) feeds into a RAG engine with streaming output via SSE

**Evaluation:**
- Case study used three videos (~45 min total) from a "Data Structures and Algorithms" course on "Stacks and Queues" plus corresponding textbook PDF
- Instructor review confirmed >90% of core syllabus concepts and prerequisite links were correctly identified
- Evaluation metrics included knowledge graph quality (Precision, Recall, F1), Q&A accuracy/relevance, and user satisfaction
- 50-question test set with blind evaluation by domain experts

**Key Innovations:**
- Cross-modal fusion mechanism integrating auditory knowledge (video explanations) with visual-textual knowledge (textbook content)
- Hybrid retrieval strategy balancing logical grounding (graph) and semantic flexibility (vectors)
- Human-in-the-loop maintenance via Knowledge Graph Review Interface and continuous feedback loop
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This study proposes a framework for an Intelligent Tutoring System based on the automatic construction of multimodal knowledge graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).", "The system integrates technologies such as FFmpeg, Whisper, OCR, and layout analysis to establish a pipeline for the fully automatic extraction and construction of knowledge graphs not only from course videos, but also from textbook PDFs.", "Our framework innovates by fusing precise relational queries from the graph database (Neo4j) with semantic similarity matching from the vector database.", "The instructor confirmed that over 90% of the core syllabus concepts and their fundamental prerequisite links were correctly identified and structured in the graph.", "Thus, this study provides a feasible and innovative path from multimodal resources to intelligent services for Intelligent Tutoring Systems, holding significant practical implications for advancing personalized learning."
</key_excerpts>
