--- SOURCE 2: Review of Real-Time Biomechanical Feedback Systems in Sport and Rehabilitation - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9028061

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review paper titled "Review of Real-Time Biomechanical Feedback Systems in Sport and Rehabilitation" published in Sensors (Basel, Switzerland) in April 2022. The authors—Matevž Hribernik, Anton Umek, Sašo Tomažič, and Anton Kos (corresponding author: anton.kos@fe.uni-lj.si)—conducted a systematic literature review of real-time biomechanical feedback (BMF) systems.

**Key Background:** Real-time BMF involves using sensors to measure a person's physiological and physical body functions, processing the data, and feeding results back to the person via one of the human senses to modify movement. BMF systems consist of four basic elements: a user, sensors, a processing unit, and actuators. The paper focuses on systems that provide concurrent (real-time) feedback, as opposed to post-processing feedback.

**Methodology:** The authors searched Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed databases. Initial search yielded 1,889 papers; after deduplication, 1,167 unique papers were screened. Following a rigorous exclusion process, 144 papers were ultimately included. Inclusion criteria required implementation of a complete real-time feedback loop with sensors, real-time processing, and concurrent feedback.

**Key Findings:**
- **Activity distribution:** 111 papers focused on rehabilitation, 33 on sports. The most common activities were gait/walking (46 papers) in rehabilitation and running (11 papers) in sports.
- **Sensor types:** Kinematic sensors/IMUs were most common (62 papers), followed by optical motion tracking (34 papers), force sensors (28 papers), and pressure sensors (20 papers).
- **Sampling frequencies:** Most studies used frequencies between 100-499 Hz (46 papers), 33 papers used <100 Hz, and 13 papers used ≥500 Hz. Notably, 54 papers (37%) did not report sampling frequency.
- **Sensor placement:** Common placements included legs (23 papers), hands (7 papers), and full body (5 papers).

**Conclusions:** Real-time BMF has shown great potential in both sports and rehabilitation. While sensors have been the main focus of recent studies, the authors predict future work will explore new processing devices, methods, algorithms, actuators, and communication technologies. The paper provides a broad technological insight into the BMF field, focusing on technical aspects rather than software applications or user-system interactions.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: RunPacer: A Smartwatch-Based Vibrotactile Feedback System for Symmetric Co-Running by Visually Impaired Individuals and Guides ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2507.04241

SUMMARY:
<summary>
RunPacer is a smartwatch-based vibrotactile feedback system presented at the 27th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '25), October 26–29, 2025, in Denver, CO, USA. The system is designed to enable symmetric co-running between visually impaired individuals and their guides by delivering synchronized rhythmic pulses to both runners' smartwatches, replacing traditional verbal cues or physical tethers.

**Key Features:**
- **Shared Cadence Engine:** Supports two modes—a manually preset cadence (e.g., 160 steps/min) and a dynamic mode that detects the guide's real-time step frequency via onboard inertial sensors. Synchronization operates with under 100ms latency over Bluetooth.
- **Vibrotactile Feedback Delivery:** Uses built-in smartwatch haptic motors to deliver short, crisp pulses (100–200ms duration) with adjustable intensity. Single-tap pulses were favored in preliminary testing.
- **Dual-Mode Operation:** Static Preset Mode for controlled training and Adaptive Mode for real-time cadence mirroring.

**Implementation:** Built on Apple Watch Series 7 using Swift, Core Motion, and Core Bluetooth frameworks. The Taptic Engine provides precise vibration pulses with under 100ms latency.

**Evaluation:** A heuristic evaluation with 10 participants (5 pairs of blindfolded runners and guides) on a 200-meter track found that the system significantly reduced cognitive load and enhanced autonomy and safety compared to verbal methods. Participants suggested improvements including adjustable vibration intensity and optional auditory feedback.

**Future Work:** Plans include field studies with visually impaired runners, integration of physiological sensors (heart rate, EMG) for fatigue-aware pacing, multimodal feedback combining bone-conduction audio with vibrotactile cues, and scaling for group running. The authors envision releasing a developer toolkit.

**Conclusion:** RunPacer reframes co-running as a bidirectional, rhythmic, social interaction leveraging entrainment principles, with potential applications beyond running to co-walking, synchronized rehabilitation, and embodied collaborative learning.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Wearable Technology and the Athlete | 2024 MeTRIC Symposium

## Speaker & Context
Ken Kozloff, Ph.D., from the University of Michigan's Human Performance and Sport Science Center, presented at the Eisenberg Family Depression Center's 2024 MeTRIC Symposium (Dec 16, 2024). His talk covered how wearable technology is used in research and by athletes to generate knowledge on human health and performance. Disclosures include funding from Samsung, Apple, and Aura (no role in analysis/interpretation).

## Wearable Technology Definition
Electronic devices worn on the body that collect performance metrics (speed, distance, location) integrated with physiologic metrics (heart rate, heart rate variability, hydration, body temperature) to track, monitor, and enhance physical activity, recovery, and overall health.

## Market Context
Global sports wearables market was nearly $2 billion in 2023, with 15% CAGR projected over 8 years. Smartwatches dominate anticipated growth.

## Athlete Performance Model
A cyclical model involving: (1) Planning/goal identification (understanding the gap between current state and goals), (2) Training and recovery tasks, (3) Self-monitoring during performance, (4) Checking outcomes against the plan, (5) Critical assessment and reflection, (6) Developing new strategies. Success depends on self-efficacy, motivation, and effort.

## Key Findings on Wearable Usage

### Planning & Goal Setting
- Many wearables use generic goals (close rings, 10,000 steps). Garmin offers goal-specific training programs (5K, 10K, half marathon).
- A 2021 study of 50 wearable users found that those with high motivation who used both internal and watch-based strategies achieved significant behavior changes. Those relying solely on watch cues showed limited compliance and inability to adapt goals.

### Task Monitoring & Real-Time Feedback
- A 2016 study of ~4,000 runners found most wanted distance, time, speed, and heart rate data.
- Over 75% reviewed data after a session; over half monitored data over time.
- However, only 20-25% actually used data to adapt their training plans.

### Device Accuracy Considerations
- **Distance/Speed**: GPS (affected by overhead coverage) or IMU-based systems (affected by placement and speed variations).
- **Heart Rate**: PPG sensors (affected by motion, tissue thickness, fit, skin tone) vs. ECG chest straps (affected by fit, electrical interference, signal communication).

## Case Studies

### Golf (Individual Sport)
- Study of 9 Division I golfers with >0 handicap (scoring better than par). Six-foot putt make rate: 63%; eight-foot: 68%.
- Heart rate significantly elevated between drill start and practice swing, with differences based on putt difficulty.
- Cognitive load (Stroop test) accentuated heart rate elevation and reduced performance.

### Football (Team Sport)
- Retrospective assessment of 2019 Michigan football team using Catapult GPS devices across 36 practices, 330 drills.
- Tracked sprint instances (>15 mph) and directional changes across wide receivers and running backs.
- Data showed patterns of reduced sprint/directional changes from Tuesday to Thursday (likely reflecting training load management).
- Coach Beilein (Michigan basketball) noted: "For 40 years of coaching, he really had no idea what the overall player load was... it was mostly based on his feel for how tired they looked." Data also used to manage fitness for players with limited game minutes.

### Student Athlete Health & Sleep
- Student athletes spend only ~20% of time on the playing field (2019 NCAA goal study).
- Five-year study with Michigan cross country teams on sleep and bone stress injuries: Athletes whose sleep scores worsened by 4-5 points had 100% bone stress injury rate.
- Non-student athlete study (63 first-year students) using Fitbits and mobile app showed periodicity in sleep (peaking weekends) and step count (peaking Thursday/Friday, dropping Sunday).

## Future Directions
- Collaborative studies with Samsung validating new smartwatch metrics (body composition, sweat loss during workouts).
- Potential for next-gen wearables to create real-time contextualized digital biomarkers integrating cross-disciplinary signals for health, adaptation, and injury susceptibility.
- Need to bridge the gap between data collection (which wearables do well) and reflection/planning (which remains human-dependent).

## Closing Thought
Kozloff highlighted high jumper Nicola Olyslagers (Australia), who after every jump in the 2021 Tokyo Olympics wrote in a journal rating each component of her jump 1-10, self-monitoring and adjusting strategy. She won silver in Tokyo and repeated in Paris 2024. The message: wearables help with self-monitoring, but reflection and planning still largely depend on the athlete.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents an open-access academic article titled "An Architecture for Intelligent Tutoring in Virtual Reality: Integrating LLMs and Multimodal Interaction for Immersive Learning," published in the journal *Information* (Volume 16, Issue 7, 556) on June 29, 2025. The authors are Mohamed El Hajji, Tarek Ait Baha, Anas Berka, Hassan Ait Nacer, Houssam El Aouifi, and Youssef Es-Saady, affiliated with Ibnou Zohr University in Morocco.

The paper proposes an architecture for intelligent tutoring in immersive VR environments that uses LLM-based non-playable characters (NPCs). Key capabilities include natural language understanding, real-time adaptive dialogue, and multimodal interaction through hand tracking, gaze detection, and haptic feedback. The system synchronizes speech output with NPC animations to enhance interactional realism and cognitive immersion.

**Methodology and Architecture:** The system uses a pipeline where user speech is captured via microphone, transcribed using OpenAI's Whisper (STT), processed by a locally deployed LLM (either llama3.2:3b or Deepseek-r1:14b depending on hardware), and converted back to speech via the Kokoro TTS model. Lip movements are synchronized using Oculus Lipsync with visemes. The system employs a structured, role-based prompt design with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, enabling the NPC tutor to adapt explanations based on user expertise level (e.g., beginner vs. advanced). The virtual environment is built in Unity using the Universal Render Pipeline (URP), with avatars generated via ReadyPlayerMe. NPC interaction uses raycasting mechanics.

**Comparison with Existing Systems:** The proposed framework is compared against LearningVerseVR, VREd, and a VR NPC-based tutoring system, showing advantages in real-time adaptivity, locally deployed LLM, real-time lip synchronization, multimodal input (speech, gaze, gesture), pedagogical flexibility via role-based behavior and CoT prompting, and broad platform compatibility.

**Results:** System performance was generally stable, though minor latency was observed during speech processing. The research highlights the potential of AI-driven VR interactions to improve learner engagement and emphasizes the need for ongoing optimization in immersive learning contexts.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Frontiers in Computer Science research article (published February 25, 2026) proposing an Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS) based on the automatic construction of multimodal knowledge graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The system addresses key challenges in ITS development: the costly manual knowledge base construction, difficulty handling unstructured teaching resources, and issues with large language models such as factual inaccuracies (hallucination) and insufficient reasoning.

**Key Contributions:**
1. A cross-modal knowledge fusion pipeline that aligns and merges entities from video transcripts (via FFmpeg + Whisper ASR) and textbook PDFs (via OCR, layout analysis, and BERT-based extraction) into a unified multimodal knowledge graph.
2. A hybrid retrieval-augmented paradigm combining precise relational queries from a Neo4j graph database with semantic similarity matching from a vector database (HNSW indexing), driving a RAG engine for accurate, explainable answers.
3. Direct processing of unstructured course videos as the primary knowledge source, broadening ITS applicability in online education.

**System Architecture:**
- **Knowledge Construction Layer:** Processes multimodal inputs (video audio → Whisper transcription; PDFs → OCR/layout analysis → semantic chunking). Extracts entities and relationships using BERT-based models, performs entity disambiguation/fusion, and enriches with instructional context (core concepts, prerequisite relations). Stores in Neo4j (graph triples) and vector database (embeddings).
- **Q&A Interaction Layer:** Hybrid retrieval combines graph queries (Cypher) and vector similarity search, weighted by a composite scoring function. The LLM generates answers grounded in retrieved context, with streaming output via SSE.

**Evaluation:**
A case study on a "Data Structures and Algorithms" course (45 min of video + textbook PDF on "Stacks and Queues") was conducted. Evaluation covered: (1) Knowledge graph quality (precision, recall, F1-score on 300 sampled sentences with expert annotation); (2) pedagogical logic consistency (instructor confirmed >90% of core syllabus concepts correctly identified); (3) Q&A performance (50-question test set across definition, characteristics, comparison, and application types, blind-evaluated by domain experts on accuracy and relevance).

The system's modular, domain-agnostic design supports cross-disciplinary scalability, and a "human-in-the-loop" maintenance mechanism allows instructors to review and correct extracted knowledge via a dedicated interface, with user feedback driving continuous improvement.
</summary>

The article systematically reviews Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) for psychomotor skills—skills requiring physical movement, coordination, and mental processing. The authors note that while ITS have been successful in cognitive domains, research progress in psychomotor skills seems stagnating, partly due to developing ITS for very specific skills.

**Methods:** The authors conducted a systematic literature review using Harrow's taxonomy (to classify skill proficiency), a skill continua framework (to classify skill types), and dimensions of psychomotor skill learning.

**Key Findings:**
- ITS for psychomotor skills predominantly target fine, closed, internally paced, discrete, individual, and simple skills.
- ITS focus mainly on technical/coordination aspects of motor abilities.
- Feedback and repetition are the primary methods used to promote psychomotor skill learning.
- There is a lack of consideration for offering different tasks to promote skill proficiency.
- The cognitive domain is often implicitly present in ITS, but the affective domain is neglected.

**Research Questions Addressed:**
1. RQ1: What is the general state-of-the-art of ITS for psychomotor skills?
2. RQ2: To what extent does the state-of-the-art ITS provide a holistic solution for developing psychomotor skills?

**Theoretical Background:** The paper discusses five psychomotor taxonomies (Dave, Simpson, Harrow, Thomas, and Ferris & Aziz), with Harrow's taxonomy selected as most suitable because it includes physical abilities (strength, flexibility) and non-discursive communication. The skill continua framework covers six dimensions: granularity (fine-gross), environment (open-close), pace (internally-externally paced), continuity (discrete-serial-continuous), interactivity (individual-coactive-interactive), and complexity (simple-complex). The dimensions of psychomotor skill learning examined include strength, flexibility, coordination, speed, team, and mental training.

**Conclusions:** The authors identify potential for exploring ITS for gross and open skills, integrating tasks targeting motor abilities like strength or flexibility, and incorporating theories from related fields such as training periodization. --- SOURCE 1: AI for swimming recommendation systems exploring the current landscape and research opportunities ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-025-08156-x

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in Discover Applied Sciences (Volume 8, article number 156, 2026) titled "AI for swimming recommendation systems exploring the current landscape and research opportunities" by Minal Patil, R. H. Goudar, and Geetabai S. Hukkeri. It is an open-access, peer-reviewed systematic review of 42 studies (2018–2024) examining AI applications in swimming.

The paper finds that while AI adoption in swimming is growing, it remains fragmented—most studies focus on isolated tasks such as stroke classification, turn detection, and fatigue monitoring, achieving 90–99% accuracy in stroke recognition using CNN-LSTM and BiLSTM architectures. However, none of the reviewed studies implemented full recommendation systems for swimmers, representing a clear research gap.

Swimming presents unique challenges for AI due to its aquatic environment, which disrupts sensors, causes IMU drift, and complicates motion capture. Unlike land-based sports, swimming involves complex three-dimensional movements across four distinct strokes (freestyle, butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke), each requiring specialized biomechanical models. The paper proposes a three-layer framework combining multimodal sensing, contextual awareness, and adaptive feedback for real-time, swimmer-centric recommendations.

Key findings from the review include: over 80% of studies focused on stroke classification, turn detection, or fatigue monitoring; most studies used small cohorts (n [less than] 30) with single-sensor setups in controlled environments; AI techniques used include CNNs, BiLSTM, RNNs, SVMs, Random Forests, and hybrid architectures; and wearable sensors (IMUs, accelerometers, sEMG, physiological sensors) are the primary data sources.

The paper outlines a structured roadmap for developing intelligent, evidence-driven recommendation systems for swimming, addressing challenges related to data quality, model interpretability, fairness/bias, scalability, and real-time feedback. It also includes a PRISMA methodology for literature selection, a classification framework, and comparisons with AI applications in other sports like basketball.
</summary>

<webpage_content>
# Privacy concerns and consent for biometric data

12th July 2024

Loading the [Elevenlabs Text to Speech](https://elevenlabs.io/text-to-speech) AudioNative Player...

Since we rely on digital services more than ever before,  more and more aspects of our lives require access to online software or applications.

From emails and social media, to accessing government services and essential utilities, our personal identifiable information is transferred between multiple organisations—and with it comes security concerns.

Increasingly, our biometric data is being used for access to these services, and if you’re a business or institution that processes and stores customer biometric data, how can you manage biometric privacy concerns and consent?

## What is biometric data?

Biometric data refers to unique physical or behavioral characteristics of individuals used for identification and authentication purposes.

These characteristics include but are not limited to:

* fingerprints
* facial features
* iris patterns
* voice recognition
* DNA

Because these traits are inherently unique to each person, biometric data provides a highly reliable method of verifying identity. It’s commonly employed in security systems - for example, unlocking smartphones, accessing secure facilities, and in government identification programs like passports and national ID cards.

The use of biometric data enhances security by reducing the risk of identity theft and unauthorised access, as it’s much harder to replicate or steal compared to traditional passwords or PINs. However, the collection and storage of biometric data raises privacy and ethical concerns, as it involves sensitive personal information that, if misused or breached, can lead to significant privacy violations.

## What does GDPR say about biometric consent?

According to [Article 9 of UK GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-9-gdpr/), organisations have to make special considerations for processing ‘special categories of personal data’. This includes personal data that:

* Reveals racial or ethnic origin
* Reveals political beliefs or trade union membership
* Reveals religious or philosophical beliefs
* Is biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a person
* Is data concerning health or a person’s sex life or sexual orientation

Because biometric data is considered to be personal information [by the ICO](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/lawful-basis/biometric-data-guidance-biometric-recognition/how-do-we-process-biometric-data-lawfully/), if you’re a British organisation you must comply with data protection law when you process it, and explicit consent is likely to be the most appropriate lawful basis to do so.

Importantly, UK GDPR states that “if you can’t identify a valid condition, you ***must not*** use special category biometric data.”

The six lawful bases for processing personal information are consent, execution of a contract, a legal obligation, vital interests, a public task and legitimate interest, and all of these apply to ‘special categories of personal data’ too. However, under Article 9, there are an additional four lawful bases for processing biometric data. They are:

1. Processing relates to personal data which are made public by the data subject;
2. Processing is necessary for the purposes of preventive or occupational medicine, for the assessment of the working capacity of an employee, medical diagnosis, the provision of health or social care or treatment, or the management of health or social care systems and services.
3. Processing is necessary for the public interest in regards to public health, for example protecting against serious cross-border threats to health or ensuring high standards of quality and safety of health care, medicinal products or medical devices.
4. Processing is necessary for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes in accordance with [Article 89(1)](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-89-gdpr/).

If you’re an organisation that processes the personal information of EU citizens, you can find out what you have to do to secure biometric data consent [here](https://www.thalesgroup.com/en/markets/digital-identity-and-security/government/biometrics/biometric-data).

**[READ MORE: How UK GDPR impacts Digital Asset Management](https://www.resourcespace.com/blog/uk-gdpr-digital-asset-management)**

## The impact of AI on biometric data

Artificial intelligence is having a big impact on every digital industry, and how organisations handle biometric data is no different.

AI has the ability to analyse and process vast amounts of biometric data, while machine learning algorithms can detect patterns, anomalies and irregularities within biometric data. AI also constantly evolves, meaning an AI-powered system can adapt to changes in specific biometric characteristics to ensure they are as robust and secure as possible. For example, machine learning algorithms can detect patterns, anomalies and irregularities within biometric data, which helps in identifying and preventing fraudulent activities.

However, there are also ethical implications and biometric privacy concerns that come with the use of AI technology.

First of all, there’s the risk of unauthorised access or data breaches when AI algorithms process and analyse sensitive information.

Secondly, there’s serious questions around [bias and discrimination when AI algorithms](https://www.ibm.com/blog/shedding-light-on-ai-bias-with-real-world-examples/) are used for processing biometric data. If the training data used for AI models is biased, it can result in inaccurate identification or verification.

Using AI for processing biometric data also risks breaching your legal obligations under UK GDPR. While human-controlled processes can be managed more strictly, AI can be susceptible to ‘function creep’, where the use of biometric data expands beyond the original purpose without the individual’s explicit consent.

## Strategies for effective biometric consent management

For biometric data consent processes to be effective and compliant with GDPR, they must be clear, accessible and revocable. They shouldn’t be hidden in contract clauses, but instead easily understandable in a standalone policy document, and presented in a way that allows customers, users, employees and other stakeholders whose biometric data you need to process to digest the information and make an impartial decision.

Let’s take a look at ten specific strategies in more detail.

### 1. Clear and transparent communication

* Detailed explanations: Clearly explain what biometric data is being collected, why it is being collected, how it will be used and who will have access to it.
* Plain language: Use simple, non-technical language to ensure all users understand the consent request.

### 2. Informed consent

* Comprehensive information: Provide detailed information about the potential risks and benefits associated with the collection and use of biometric data.
* Opt-in processes: Use active opt-in processes rather than passive opt-out methods to ensure explicit consent.

### 3. Granular consent options

* Specific consents: Allow users to consent to specific types of data collection and processing activities, rather than a blanket consent for all activities.
* Revocation options: Provide easy-to-use options for users to withdraw consent at any time.

### 4. Data minimisation and purpose limitation

* Minimal data collection: Collect only the biometric data that is necessary for the stated purpose.
* Specific use cases: Clearly define and limit the use cases for the collected biometric data.

### 5. Security measures

* Data protection: Implement robust security measures to protect biometric data from unauthorised access, such as encryption and secure storage solutions.
* Regular audits: Conduct regular security audits and assessments to ensure ongoing compliance with data protection standards.

### 6. User control and access

* User portals: Provide user-friendly portals where individuals can manage their consent preferences, view the data collected about them, and request deletion or correction of their data.
* Transparency reports: Offer transparency reports that detail how biometric data is being used and any third-party sharing that occurs.

### 7. Compliance with regulations

* Legal adherence: Ensure compliance with relevant laws and regulations, such as GDPR or specific biometric data protection laws.
* Documentation: Maintain thorough records of consent forms and consent management processes to demonstrate compliance.

### 8. Training and awareness

* Employee training: Train employees on the importance of biometric data protection and the proper procedures for obtaining and managing consent.
* User education: Educate users about their rights and the importance of biometric data security.

### 9. Third-party management

* Vendor contracts: Ensure that third-party vendors who have access to biometric data comply with the same standards and practices for consent and data protection.
* Data sharing policies: Clearly communicate policies regarding data sharing with third parties and obtain explicit consent for such sharing.

### 10. Regular updates and reviews

* Policy reviews: Regularly review and update consent management policies to keep up with technological advancements and regulatory changes.
* Feedback processes: Implement processes for users to provide feedback on consent management practices and make improvements based on this feedback.

# Privacy concerns and consent for biometric data

12th July 2024

Loading the [Elevenlabs Text to Speech](https://elevenlabs.io/text-to-speech) AudioNative Player...

Since we rely on digital services more than ever before,  more and more aspects of our lives require access to online software or applications.

From emails and social media, to accessing government services and essential utilities, our personal identifiable information is transferred between multiple organisations—and with it comes security concerns.

Increasingly, our biometric data is being used for access to these services, and if you’re a business or institution that processes and stores customer biometric data, how can you manage biometric privacy concerns and consent?

## What is biometric data?

Biometric data refers to unique physical or behavioral characteristics of individuals used for identification and authentication purposes.

These characteristics include but are not limited to:

* fingerprints
* facial features
* iris patterns
* voice recognition
* DNA

Because these traits are inherently unique to each person, biometric data provides a highly reliable method of verifying identity. It’s commonly employed in security systems - for example, unlocking smartphones, accessing secure facilities, and in government identification programs like passports and national ID cards.

The use of biometric data enhances security by reducing the risk of identity theft and unauthorised access, as it’s much harder to replicate or steal compared to traditional passwords or PINs. However, the collection and storage of biometric data raises privacy and ethical concerns, as it involves sensitive personal information that, if misused or breached, can lead to significant privacy violations.

## What does GDPR say about biometric consent?

According to [Article 9 of UK GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-9-gdpr/), organisations have to make special considerations for processing ‘special categories of personal data’. This includes personal data that:

* Reveals racial or ethnic origin
* Reveals political beliefs or trade union membership
* Reveals religious or philosophical beliefs
* Is biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a person
* Is data concerning health or a person’s sex life or sexual orientation

Because biometric data is considered to be personal information [by the ICO](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/lawful-basis/biometric-data-guidance-biometric-recognition/how-do-we-process-biometric-data-lawfully/), if you’re a British organisation you must comply with data protection law when you process it, and explicit consent is likely to be the most appropriate lawful basis to do so.

Importantly, UK GDPR states that “if you can’t identify a valid condition, you ***must not*** use special category biometric data.”

The six lawful bases for processing personal information are consent, execution of a contract, a legal obligation, vital interests, a public task and legitimate interest, and all of these apply to ‘special categories of personal data’ too. However, under Article 9, there are an additional four lawful bases for processing biometric data. They are:

1. Processing relates to personal data which are made public by the data subject;
2. Processing is necessary for the purposes of preventive or occupational medicine, for the assessment of the working capacity of an employee, medical diagnosis, the provision of health or social care or treatment, or the management of health or social care systems and services.
3. Processing is necessary for the public interest in regards to public health, for example protecting against serious cross-border threats to health or ensuring high standards of quality and safety of health care, medicinal products or medical devices.
4. Processing is necessary for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes in accordance with [Article 89(1)](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-89-gdpr/).

If you’re an organisation that processes the personal information of EU citizens, you can find out what you have to do to secure biometric data consent [here](https://www.thalesgroup.com/en/markets/digital-identity-and-security/government/biometrics/biometric-data).

**[READ MORE: How UK GDPR impacts Digital Asset Management](https://www.resourcespace.com/blog/uk-gdpr-digital-asset-management)**

## The impact of AI on biometric data

Artificial intelligence is having a big impact on every digital industry, and how organisations handle biometric data is no different.

AI has the ability to analyse and process vast amounts of biometric data, while machine learning algorithms can detect patterns, anomalies and irregularities within biometric data. AI also constantly evolves, meaning an AI-powered system can adapt to changes in specific biometric characteristics to ensure they are as robust and secure as possible. For example, machine learning algorithms can detect patterns, anomalies and irregularities within biometric data, which helps in identifying and preventing fraudulent activities.

However, there are also ethical implications and biometric privacy concerns that come with the use of AI technology.

First of all, there’s the risk of unauthorised access or data breaches when AI algorithms process and analyse sensitive information.

Secondly, there’s serious questions around [bias and discrimination when AI algorithms](https://www.ibm.com/blog/shedding-light-on-ai-bias-with-real-world-examples/) are used for processing biometric data. If the training data used for AI models is biased, it can result in inaccurate identification or verification.

Using AI for processing biometric data also risks breaching your legal obligations under UK GDPR. While human-controlled processes can be managed more strictly, AI can be susceptible to ‘function creep’, where the use of biometric data expands beyond the original purpose without the individual’s explicit consent.

## Strategies for effective biometric consent management

For biometric data consent processes to be effective and compliant with GDPR, they must be clear, accessible and revocable. They shouldn’t be hidden in contract clauses, but instead easily understandable in a standalone policy document, and presented in a way that allows customers, users, employees and other stakeholders whose biometric data you need to process to digest the information and make an impartial decision.

Let’s take a look at ten specific strategies in more detail.

### 1. Clear and transparent communication

* Detailed explanations: Clearly explain what biometric data is being collected, why it is being collected, how it will be used and who will have access to it.
* Plain language: Use simple, non-technical language to ensure all users understand the consent request.

### 2. Informed consent

* Comprehensive information: Provide detailed information about the potential risks and benefits associated with the collection and use of biometric data.
* Opt-in processes: Use active opt-in processes rather than passive opt-out methods to ensure explicit consent.

### 3. Granular consent options

* Specific consents: Allow users to consent to specific types of data collection and processing activities, rather than a blanket consent for all activities.
* Revocation options: Provide easy-to-use options for users to withdraw consent at any time.

### 4. Data minimisation and purpose limitation

* Minimal data collection: Collect only the biometric data that is necessary for the stated purpose.
* Specific use cases: Clearly define and limit the use cases for the collected biometric data.

### 5. Security measures

* Data protection: Implement robust security measures to protect biometric data from unauthorised access, such as encryption and secure storage solutions.
* Regular audits: Conduct regular security audits and assessments to ensure ongoing compliance with data protection standards.

### 6. User control and access

* User portals: Provide user-friendly portals where individuals can manage their consent preferences, view the data collected about them, and request deletion or correction of their data.
* Transparency reports: Offer transparency reports that detail how biometric data is being used and any third-party sharing that occurs.

### 7. Compliance with regulations

* Legal adherence: Ensure compliance with relevant laws and regulations, such as GDPR or specific biometric data protection laws.
* Documentation: Maintain thorough records of consent forms and consent management processes to demonstrate compliance.

### 8. Training and awareness

* Employee training: Train employees on the importance of biometric data protection and the proper procedures for obtaining and managing consent.
* User education: Educate users about their rights and the importance of biometric data security.

### 9. Third-party management

* Vendor contracts: Ensure that third-party vendors who have access to biometric data comply with the same standards and practices for consent and data protection.
* Data sharing policies: Clearly communicate policies regarding data sharing with third parties and obtain explicit consent for such sharing.

### 10. Regular updates and reviews

* Policy reviews: Regularly review and update consent management policies to keep up with technological advancements and regulatory changes.
* Feedback processes: Implement processes for users to provide feedback on consent management practices and make improvements based on this feedback.

# How next-gen wearables and Edge AI improve sports performance analytics

By  [Thomas Søderholm](https://blog.nordicsemi.com/getconnected/author/thomas-søderholm)  March 26, 2025

[Bluetooth LE](https://blog.nordicsemi.com/getconnected/topic/bluetooth-le) [Wearables](https://blog.nordicsemi.com/getconnected/topic/wearables) [Edge AI](https://blog.nordicsemi.com/getconnected/topic/edge-ai)

![wearables-edge-ai-inline](https://blog.nordicsemi.com/hs-fs/hubfs/wearables-edge-ai-inline.jpg?width=783&height=522&name=wearables-edge-ai-inline.jpg)

In the modern era of sport, results are often decided by ultra-fine margins like milliseconds or millimeters. Yet even precise metrics such as speed and distance are still quite rudimentary in nature. The real wins for athletes, coaches, and sporting teams are gained through a much deeper understanding of sports performance and potential improvement. 

To achieve these goals and help obtain a competitive advantage, the latest performance tracking solutions lean on the power of wireless connectivity and edge processing. 

## Monitoring unique performance metrics in sport

Combining dozens of datapoints makes it possible to build a unique profile of an individual’s abilities. Examples in each sport might include the athlete’s body movement during key actions, or the position, launch angle, spin rate, and acceleration rate of the bat or ball at various game stages. 

For individual sports like athletics and cycling, key metrics might focus on biomechanical efficiency and technical precision. For team sports including the various football codes, common metrics include sprints, accelerations, decelerations, and workload intensity.  

## Bluetooth LE turns raw data into powerful insights

Sports tracking solutions based on wireless tech make these and other powerful metrics readily available, in turn helping sports industry stakeholders achieve more nuanced insights. 

Tools like inertial sensors, anchor devices, and location services form systems that measure sports parameters in near real time. The high volume of raw data generated can be processed and analyzed using algorithms running on the sensor or wearable’s integrated wireless device before the information is forwarded—using low latency wireless connectivity such as [Bluetooth LE](https://www.nordicsemi.com/Products/Wireless/Bluetooth-Low-Energy)—to an accompanying app on the user’s smartphone or a web-based dashboard on their laptop. 

* Read more: [Wireless tech helps us make the most of valuable leisure time](https://blog.nordicsemi.com/getconnected/tech-helps-us-make-the-most-of-valuable-leisure-time)

## Ball and athlete tracking technology in action

Ball tracking technology, for example, delivers data on the trajectory, spin, and bounce of the ball, helping to measure the quality and accuracy of passes and shots, or evaluate defensive and offensive positioning. Athlete tracking technology, meanwhile, provides insights on the precise position, movement, and activity of the players themselves to help measure their performance, fitness, workload, and tactical decision-making. 

Moreover, wearable tech attached to the wrist, chest, or other parts of the body enables a much deeper dive into data, potentially revealing key information about an athlete’s heart rate variability (HRV), VO2 max, muscle fatigue, lactic acid, power output, and other important physical parameters. Such insights can provide a better understanding of athletic training, recovery, and injury prevention. 

## A Nordic Bluetooth LE soccer tracking solution

One prominent example of wireless sports technology in action is the Nordic-powered Apex Series, used by a host of major international sporting organizations including English Premier League football clubs.  

Embedded in a custom lightweight vest worn by the athlete, STATSports’ [Apex](https://www.nordicsemi.com/Nordic-news/2018/11/STATSports-APEX-device-employs-nRF52840-to-wirelessly-sync-comprehensive-sports-specific-metrics) employs Bluetooth LE connectivity to wirelessly sync sports-specific metrics to smartphones and tablets for coaches to make informed decisions during a match or training session. 

The device integrates a range of sensors including a high impact accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and augmented GNSS. These sensors provide comprehensive data including heart rate, total distance covered, current and maximum speed, number of sprints, accelerations, impacts, dynamic stress load, and step balance.  

* Read more: [Wireless solutions take sports tracking to new level](https://blog.nordicsemi.com/getconnected/wireless-solutions-take-sports-tracking-to-new-level)

## Edge AI for predictive modeling

But the ultimate game-changer in the sports sector comes in the form of predictive modeling and data-driven analytics performed at the edge. 

When relevant data is not only crunched but analyzed and interpreted using the power of ‘[Edge AI](https://www.nordicsemi.com/Products/Technologies/Edge-AI)’ algorithms, sports analysts can take advantage of even more precise and personalized insights. Adding AI and Machine Learning (ML) to the mix allows, for example, a sports wearable with the same sensors as before to now continuously monitor several performance parameters simultaneously, uncovering meaningful patterns that were previously hidden. 

* Read more: [Artificial intelligence and machine learning will transform the IoT](https://blog.nordicsemi.com/getconnected/artificial-intelligence-and-machine-learning-will-transform-the-iot)

By analyzing both historical data and real-time sensor information, statistical models can pinpoint factors that have a major impact on the way athletes prepare and perform, not to mention identify opposition strategies and gauge overall team dynamics. 

## nRF54 Series SoCs enable the future of sports analytics devices

Behind every breakthrough in next-generation sports tracking is hardware built to handle extreme demands. The fourth-generation wireless SoCs from Nordic Semiconductor, the nRF54 Series, deliver exactly that – combining unmatched processing power, ultra-low power consumption, and advanced on-chip AI capabilities. 

To make sense of all the available sensor data in context and quickly enough to enable rapid and effective decision-making, powerful integrated wireless SoCs such as the nRF54L Series provide the serious processing heft to perform the ML and sensor fusion that forms part of Edge AI. By running Edge AI using a Nordic Semiconductor nRF54 Series SoC, for example, the local processing will use less power than sending data over the air, allowing a sports analytics device to have longer operation and smaller battery size.  

The result is sophisticated sports analytics solutions that are changing the game.  

* Read more: [Sky’s the limit for wearables thanks to next gen wireless SoCs](https://blog.nordicsemi.com/getconnected/skys-the-limit-for-wearables-thanks-to-next-gen-wireless-socs)

This blog post from Nordic Semiconductor (dated March 26, 2025) discusses how next-generation wearables, Bluetooth LE connectivity, and Edge AI are transforming sports performance analytics. Key points include:

- Modern sports decisions are increasingly determined by ultra-fine margins, and deeper performance insights beyond basic metrics like speed and distance are needed.
- Combining dozens of datapoints (body movement, launch angle, spin rate, acceleration, workload intensity, etc.) enables unique athlete profiling.
- Bluetooth LE wireless connectivity enables near real-time data collection from inertial sensors and anchor devices, processing data on the wearable before forwarding to smartphones or dashboards.
- Ball tracking technology measures trajectory, spin, and bounce; athlete tracking monitors position, movement, and activity.
- Wearables can measure HRV, VO2 max, muscle fatigue, lactic acid, and power output for training, recovery, and injury prevention.
- **STATSports' Apex Series** (Nordic-powered, used by English Premier League clubs) is a featured example: a lightweight vest with Bluetooth LE, high-impact accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and augmented GNSS, tracking heart rate, distance, speed, sprints, impacts, dynamic stress load, and step balance.
- **Edge AI** is described as a "game-changer" — enabling predictive modeling and data-driven analytics at the edge, uncovering hidden patterns by analyzing historical and real-time data simultaneously.
- **Nordic's nRF54 Series SoCs** (specifically the nRF54L Series) are highlighted as the hardware enabler, combining processing power, ultra-low power consumption, and on-chip AI for ML and sensor fusion. Running Edge AI locally uses less power than over-air data transmission, enabling longer battery life and smaller devices.

## Abstract

Wearable health devices have revolutionized rehabilitation by enabling real-time monitoring of physiological parameters, fostering early disease detection, and promoting proactive health management especially for young students. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and edge computing with these devices has further enhanced their capabilities by enabling advanced data processing, predictive analytics, and personalized healthcare recommendations. This review explores the latest advancements in AI-driven and edge-enabled wearable health technologies, emphasizing their applications in chronic disease management, real-time patient monitoring, and personalized healthcare solutions. Additionally, it discusses the key AI and edge techniques, including machine learning, deep learning, and federated learning, that enhance the effectiveness of wearable devices. Despite their immense potential, challenges such as data privacy, interoperability, and ethical concerns remain significant barriers to widespread adoption. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of current solutions and emerging trends in AI-integrated and edge-enabled wearable health systems, offering insights into future research directions and technological advancements that will shape the next generation of personalized healthcare solutions.

## Introduction

In recent years, the convergence of wearable health devices and edge computing-assisted artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed personalized healthcare [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR1 "Alzu’bi A, Alomar AA, Alkhaza’leh S, Abuarqoub A, Hammoudeh M (2024) A review of privacy and security of edge computing in smart healthcare systems: issues, challenges, and research directions. Tsinghua Sci Technol 29(4):1152–1180"),[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR2 "Zhou X, Zheng X, Shu T, Liang W, Wang KIK, Qi L, Jin Q (2023) Information theoretic learning-enhanced dual-generative adversarial networks with causal representation for robust OOD generalization. IEEE Trans Neur Netw Learn Syst."),[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR3 "Zhao Y, Guo M, Chen X, Sun J, Qiu J (2023) Attention-based CNN fusion model for emotion recognition during walking using discrete wavelet transform on EEG and inertial signals. Big Data Min Analytics 7(1):188–204")]. Wearable health devices, such as smartwatches, fitness trackers, and biosensors, have become increasingly prevalent, enabling continuous monitoring of various physiological parameters [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR4 "Zheng S, Chang PY, Chen J, Chang YW, Fan HC (2022) An investigation of patient decisions to use eHealth: a view of multichannel services. J Organizational End User Comput (JOEUC) 34(4):1–24"), [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR5 "Du H, Liu M, Liu N, Li D, Li W, Xu L (2024) Scheduling of Low-Latency medical services in healthcare cloud with deep reinforcement learning. Tsinghua Sci Technol 30(1):100–111")] especially for young students who are interested in electronic devices. These devices collect extensive data on metrics like heart rate, physical activity, and sleep patterns, providing valuable insights into an individual’s health status. The integration of AI and edge computing into these devices enhances their capability to analyze complex datasets, facilitating early detection of health anomalies and personalized health recommendations [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR6 "Jiang Q, Ye H, Yang B, Cao F (2024) Label-decoupled medical image segmentation with spatial-channel graph Convolution and dual attention enhancement. IEEE J Biomedical Health Inf 28(5):2830–2841")]. This integration aims to improve patient outcomes by enabling proactive health management and tailored interventions, for example, for the young students whose physique conditions are still weak.

The adoption of wearable health devices has seen a substantial rise in the young student community, with advancements in sensor technology and wireless communication contributing to their widespread use [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR7 "Zhu C, Zheng B, He Z, Gao M, Sun C, Bao Z (2021) State of health Estimation of Lithium-Ion battery using time Convolution memory neural network. Mob Inform Syst 2021(1):4826409"), [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR8 "Ke B, Lu H, You C, Zhu W, Xie L, Yao Y (2024) A semi-supervised medical image classification method based on combined pseudo-labeling and distance metric consistency. Multimedia Tools Appl 83(11):33313–33331")]. These devices offer real-time data acquisition, allowing for immediate analysis and feedback through edge computing. For instance, continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) provide diabetic patients with real-time blood sugar levels, enabling timely interventions. Similarly, wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) monitors facilitate the detection of cardiac irregularities, potentially preventing severe cardiac events [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR9 "Wu X, Duan J, Pan Y, Li M (2023) Medical knowledge graph: data sources, construction, reasoning, and applications. Big Data Min Analytics 6(2):201–217")]. The data generated by these devices and collected by edge servers are vast and complex, necessitating sophisticated analytical tools for meaningful interpretation.

Artificial intelligence plays a pivotal role in processing and analyzing the data collected from wearable health devices and stored in distributed edge servers [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR10 "Cao F, Hu H, Lu J, Zhao J, Zhou Z, Wu J (2016) Pose and illumination variable face recognition via sparse representation and illumination dictionary. Knowl Based Syst 107:117–128"),[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR11 "Lin X, Lei Y, Chen J, Xing Z, Yang T, Wang Q, Wang C (2023) A case-finding clinical decision support system to identify subjects with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease based on public health data. Tsinghua Sci Technol 28(3):525–540"),[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR12 "Kumar A, Singh KU, Kumar M (2023) A clinical data analysis based diagnostic systems for heart disease prediction using ensemble method. Big Data Min Analytics 6(4):513–525")]. Machine learning algorithms can identify patterns and trends within the data, offering predictive insights and personalized health recommendations [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR13 "Kong D, Zhu J, Wu S, Duan C, Lu L, Chen D (2019) A novel IRBF-RVM model for diagnosis of atrial fibrillation. Comput Methods Programs Biomed 177:183–192")]. For example, AI algorithms can analyze sleep patterns to provide personalized suggestions for improving sleep quality. Moreover, AI can enhance the accuracy of health monitoring by reducing false positives and negatives in anomaly detection. The synergy between wearable technology and edge-enabled AI not only augments the functionality of health monitoring systems but also empowers individuals to take an active role in managing their health [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR14 "Jin Y, Lu H, Li Z, Wang Y (2023) A cross-modal deep metric learning model for disease diagnosis based on chest x-ray images. Multimedia Tools Appl 82(21):33421–33442"), [15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR15 "Akella R, Gunturi SK, Sarkar D (2024) Enhancing power line insulator health monitoring with a hybrid generative adversarial network and YOLO3 solution. Tsinghua Sci Technol 29(6):1796–1809")]. An intuitive illustration of health monitoring systems with edge computing and AI

Despite the promising potential of integrating wearable health devices with edge-enabled AI, several challenges persist. Data privacy and security are paramount concerns, as the sensitive health information collected by these devices and stored in edge servers must be protected against unauthorized access [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR16 "Yang S, Le Kernec J, Romain O, Fioranelli F, Cadart P, Fix J, Jin T (2023) The human activity radar challenge: benchmarking based on the ‘radar signatures of human activities’ dataset from Glasgow University. IEEE J Biomed Health Inform. 27(4):1813–24"),[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR17 "Fei F, Li S, Dai H, Hu C, Dou W, Ni Q (2017) A k-anonymity based schema for location privacy preservation. IEEE Trans Sustainable Comput 4(2):156–167"),[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR18 "Qi L, Wang R, Hu C, Li S, He Q, Xu X (2019) Time-aware distributed service recommendation with privacy-preservation. Inf Sci 480:354–364")]. Ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the data is also critical, as erroneous data can lead to incorrect health assessments. Additionally, the development of user-friendly interfaces is essential to facilitate user engagement and adherence to health recommendations [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR19 "Gou Z, Ruan X, Huang F, Fu X (2019) Effects of membrane reference state on shape memory of a red blood cell. Comput Methods Biomech BioMed Eng 22(5):465–474")]. Addressing these challenges is crucial for the successful implementation of edge and AI-integrated wearable health devices in personalized healthcare.

This review aims to explore the current landscape of integrating wearable health devices with edge-enabled AI for personalized healthcare solutions especially for the young student community who are interested in smart wearable devices. It will discuss the types of wearable devices available, the role of edge and AI in health data analysis, and the applications of these integrated systems in personalized health management. Furthermore, the review will address the challenges associated with this integration and propose future directions for research and development in this field.

The structure of rest paper is organized as follows. Section“[Overview of wearable health devices](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#Sec2)” presents an overview of wearable health devices, categorizing them based on their functionalities and discussing the types of data they collect. Section“[AI techniques for wearable health data processing](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#Sec16)” explores edge computing and AI techniques applied to wearable health data processing, including traditional machine learning, deep learning methods, and the role of edge AI versus cloud AI. Section“[AI-driven personalized healthcare solutions](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#Sec25)” focuses on AI-driven personalized healthcare solutions, detailing applications in real-time health monitoring, personalized recommendations, and chronic disease management. Section“[Challenges and limitations](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#Sec29)” discusses key challenges and limitations, such as data privacy concerns, standardization issues, and ethical considerations of wearable health field. Finally, Sect.“[Conclusion](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#Sec33)” concludes the paper by summarizing the key findings, discussing the implications for healthcare, and outlining potential areas for further research.

## Overview of wearable health devices

### Classification of wearable health devices

Wearable health devices encompass a diverse range of technologies designed to continuously monitor various physiological and behavioral metrics for the public especially for the young student community. Based on their primary functionality, wearable health devices can be categorized into five main types: smartwatches, health monitoring patches, wearable electrocardiogram (ECG/EKG) monitors, continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), and smart clothing.

#### Smartwatches

Smartwatches are widely used for continuous physiological monitoring, integrating multiple sensors to track vital signs such as heart rate, blood oxygen levels, and physical activity [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR20 "Tesema W, Jimma W, Khan MI, Stiens J, da Silva B (2024) A taxonomy of Low-Power techniques in wearable medical devices for healthcare applications. Electronics 13(15):3097")]. developed a taxonomy of low-power techniques in wearable medical devices, addressing energy efficiency challenges in smartwatches. The research explores hardware-optimized low-power processing units and adaptive sensor sampling techniques, which significantly extend battery life in wearable health devices. In [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR21 "Iqbal SM, Mahgoub I, Du E, Leavitt MA, Asghar W (2021) Advances in healthcare wearable devices. NPJ Flex Electron 5(1):9")], the authors analyzed advancements in wearable healthcare devices, emphasizing the role of photoplethysmography (PPG) sensors in smartwatches. They highlighted the transition from traditional wrist-based heart rate monitors to hybrid sensor arrays that incorporate machine learning algorithms for real-time anomaly detection.

#### Health monitoring patches

The authors in [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR22 "Dias D, Paulo Silva Cunha J (2018) Wearable health devices—vital sign monitoring, systems and technologies. Sensors 18(8):2414")] provided a classification framework for health monitoring patches based on their sensing principles and target biomarkers. Their study focused on bioimpedance-based hydration monitoring and enzymatic electrochemical glucose sensors embedded in flexible polymer substrates. In addition, they also explored wireless data transmission strategies, including Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) and near-field communication (NFC), which allow real-time health data synchronization with mobile applications. Likewise, the authors of [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR23 "Vijayan V, Connolly JP, Condell J, McKelvey N, Gardiner P (2021) Review of wearable devices and data collection considerations for connected health. Sensors 21(16):5589")] investigated real-time data acquisition methodologies in wearable health devices and proposed an ultra-low-power microcontroller-based processing unit capable of locally analyzing sensor data before transmission. Their finding reduces power consumption and enhances privacy by minimizing raw data transmission, while examining the effectiveness of biosensors integrated with machine learning models for early disease detection.

#### Wearable ECG/EKG monitors

An efficient convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture for ECG classification is designed in [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR24 "Lu J, Liu D, Liu Z, Cheng X, Wei L, Zhang C, Liu B (2021) Efficient hardware architecture of convolutional neural network for ECG classification in wearable healthcare device. IEEE Trans Circ Syst I: Regular Papers, 68(7):2976–2985")], optimized for resource-constrained wearable devices. The architecture integrates hardware acceleration techniques such as weight pruning and quantization, significantly reducing computational load while maintaining classification accuracy. They also introduced an adaptive sampling mechanism that dynamically adjusts data acquisition rates based on detected heart rate variability. Work [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR25 "Saadatnejad S, Oveisi M, Hashemi M (2019) LSTM-based ECG classification for continuous monitoring on personal wearable devices. IEEE J Biomedical Health Inf 24(2):515–523")] developed an LSTM-based deep learning model for real-time ECG classification in personal wearable devices. Unlike traditional rule-based ECG interpretation systems, their model learns temporal dependencies in heartbeat patterns, enabling more accurate arrhythmia detection and allowing wearable devices to collaboratively improve ECG classification models while preserving user privacy.

#### Continuous glucose monitors (CGMs)

CGMs continuously track glucose levels through interstitial fluid, providing a non-invasive alternative to fingerstick blood glucose measurements. These devices use electrochemical or optical sensors to estimate glucose concentrations and provide alerts for hypoglycemic or hyperglycemic events. Literature [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR26 "Seneviratne S, Hu Y, Nguyen T, Lan G, Khalifa S, Thilakarathna K, Seneviratne A (2017) A survey of wearable devices and challenges. IEEE Commun Surv Tutor, 19(4);2573–2620")] reviewed advancements in CGM technology, focusing on non-invasive glucose monitoring techniques. Their study explored near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) and Raman spectroscopy-based CGMs, which analyze glucose-related molecular vibrations in the skin. They also highlighted the integration of AI-driven prediction models that anticipate blood glucose fluctuations based on physiological and behavioral data. Likewise, work [[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR27 "Guo Z, Chen J, He T, Wang W, Abbas H, Lv Z (2023) DS-CNN: Dual-stream convolutional neural networks-based heart sound classification for wearable devices. IEEE Trans Consum Electron 69(4):1186–1194")] proposed a dual-stream convolutional neural network (DS-CNN) for heart sound classification in CGM-integrated wearables. Their system utilizes multimodal sensor fusion, combining ECG and phonocardiogram (PCG) signals to enhance the reliability of glucose monitoring.

#### Smart clothing

Smart clothing integrates textile-based sensors to monitor physiological parameters such as posture, muscle activity, and thermoregulation [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR23 "Vijayan V, Connolly JP, Condell J, McKelvey N, Gardiner P (2021) Review of wearable devices and data collection considerations for connected health. Sensors 21(16):5589")]. explored the role of textile-based sensors in wearable health monitoring. They described the development of graphene-coated fabrics for ECG and EMG signal acquisition, which offer improved biocompatibility and signal fidelity. ## AI techniques for wearable health data processing

### Machine learning algorithms

Traditional machine learning algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests, and k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) are widely used in wearable health analytics, for the public especially for the young student community, due to their efficiency in feature extraction and classification.

#### Traditional machine learning methods

Literature [[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR44 "Kadian S, Kumari P, Shukla S, Narayan R (2023) Recent advancements in machine learning enabled portable and wearable biosensors. Talanta Open 8:100267")] proposed an SVM-based classification model for heart rate variability (HRV) analysis using wearable biosensors. It leveraged kernel optimization techniques to enhance classification performance, achieving a 92.3% accuracy in detecting abnormal HRV patterns. In addition, the authors also integrated principal component analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction, improving computational efficiency in real-time processing. In [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR45 "Ortiz BL, Gupta V, Kumar R, Jalin A, Cao X, Ziegenbein C, Choi SW (2024) Data preprocessing techniques for ai and machine learning readiness: Scoping review of wearable sensor data in cancer care. JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 12(1):e59587")], the authors developed a Random Forest-based wearable system for cancer patient monitoring and incorporated feature selection methods to optimize sensor data preprocessing, enhancing the classification of physiological responses to chemotherapy treatments. The experiment results also demonstrated that the proposed approach significantly reduced false alarms while maintaining high sensitivity. While work [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR46 "Wei S, Wu Z (2023) The application of wearable sensors and machine learning algorithms in rehabilitation training: A systematic review. Sensors 23(18):7667")] designed a KNN-based rehabilitation training assessment system that analyzes gait patterns using wearable motion sensors. It introduced a distance-weighted KNN approach to improve robustness against noisy sensor data, leading to an 88.5% accuracy in activity classification.

#### Supervised vs. unsupervised learning in health monitoring

Supervised learning algorithms train models using labeled data, making them suitable for classification and regression tasks in wearable health analytics [[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR47 "Xiao X, Yin J, Xu J, Tat T, Chen J (2024) Advances in machine learning for wearable sensors. ACS Nano 18(34):22734–22751")]. introduced a supervised deep learning framework for real-time ECG anomaly detection using wearable sensors, which leveraged convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on labeled ECG datasets to classify arrhythmias with high precision. Likewise [[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR48 "Nurmi J, Lohan ES (2021) Systematic review on machine-learning algorithms used in wearable-based eHealth data analysis. IEEE Access 9:112221–112235")], applied supervised learning techniques to wearable eHealth data analysis, focusing on time-series forecasting for patient deterioration prediction. Their model used Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to predict potential health declines based on historical sensor data, achieving a high predictive accuracy in chronic disease monitoring.

Unsupervised learning methods, such as clustering and autoencoders, are also useful for detecting anomalies in wearable health data where labeled datasets are scarce. Work [[49](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR49 "Jenkins T (2022) Wearable medical sensor devices, machine and deep learning algorithms, and internet of things-based healthcare systems in COVID-19 patient screening, diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment. Am J Med Res 9(1):49–64")] implemented an unsupervised learning framework for COVID-19 patient screening using wearable sensors and applied k-means clustering to group patient physiological responses, enabling early detection of severe cases. The model successfully identified outliers indicative of respiratory distress, demonstrating the effectiveness of clustering-based anomaly detection. Similarly, in [[50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR50 "Awotunde JB, Folorunso SO, Bhoi AK, Adebayo PO, Ijaz MF (2021) Disease diagnosis system for IoT-based wearable body sensors with machine learning algorithm. Hybrid Artif Intell IoT Healthc 201–222")], the authors explored autoencoder-based unsupervised learning for detecting abnormal gait patterns in elderly individuals. They utilized wearable IMU sensors to collect motion data, and the autoencoder model effectively distinguished between normal and abnormal gait sequences, helping in fall risk prediction.

### Edge AI vs. cloud AI

#### Edge AI in wearable health devices

Edge AI refers to the deployment of machine learning models directly on wearable devices, enabling real-time data processing without relying on cloud infrastructure [[51](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR51 "Jaramillo-Rueda AF, Vargas-Pacheco LY, Fajardo CA (2020) A computational architecture for inference of a quantized-CNN for detecting atrial fibrillation")]. developed an Edge AI-driven wearable ECG monitoring system that leverages a lightweight deep learning model for arrhythmia detection. In addition, it used quantized convolutional neural networks (Q-CNNs) to reduce memory and power consumption while maintaining high accuracy. Their experiment results showed that real-time processing on edge devices reduced response time by 85% compared to cloud-based analysis. Similarly, work [[52](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR52 "Prasad CR, Satwik GN, Phaneeshwari E, Moola R, Pranith K, Rao DR (2024, July) TinyML-based real-time system for detecting falls in elderly people. In 2024 Asia Pacific Conference on Innovation in Technology (APCIT) (pp. 1–6). IEEE")] introduced an Edge AI-based gait analysis framework for fall detection in elderly individuals, which utilized TinyML algorithms optimized for microcontrollers, enabling efficient fall detection with minimal computational resources.

Federated learning (FL) has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for wearable healthcare data analysis under cloud infrastructures. Instead of centralizing sensitive raw health data, FL enables each device or institution to train local models and only share model parameters with a global server. This approach significantly reduces privacy risks while still allowing large-scale collaborative training. For example, in wearable ECG monitoring, FL can improve arrhythmia detection accuracy by aggregating model updates across multiple devices without transmitting cardiac signals. Similarly, FL has been applied to continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems, where decentralized training helps predict glucose fluctuations more accurately while safeguarding individual glucose readings. Moreover, when adopted across multiple hospitals, FL ensures compliance with regulations such as HIPAA and GDPR by avoiding raw data exchange while enabling the joint development of robust predictive models.

#### Cloud AI for large-scale health data processing

Cloud AI leverages centralized computing resources to perform complex AI model training and inference and is suitable for deep learning applications that require high computational power and storage capacity. In [[53](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR53 "Nasser AR, Hasan AM, Humaidi AJ, Alkhayyat A, Alzubaidi L, Fadhel MA., Duan Y (2021) Lot and cloud computing in health-care: a new wearable device and cloud-based deep learning algorithm for monitoring of diabetes. Electronics, 10(21):2719")], the authors proposed a Cloud AI-based system for continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), where large-scale time-series glucose data were analyzed using LSTM-based models. It improved hyperglycemia prediction by 20% compared to edge-based solutions, highlighting the advantages of cloud computing in handling complex temporal dependencies. Likewise, literature [[54](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR54 "Khanh QV, Chehri A, Van AD, Minh QN (2024) Federated learning approach for collaborative and secure smart healthcare applications. IEEE Trans Emer Top Comput.")] implemented a cloud-based federated learning framework for wearable health monitoring, which enabled secure collaborative learning among multiple healthcare institutions without directly sharing raw data.

#### Hybrid edge-cloud AI for health monitoring

A hybrid Edge-Cloud AI approach combines the advantages of real-time edge processing and cloud-based deep learning analytics. This setup ensures low latency for critical tasks while leveraging cloud computing for model refinement and large-scale analysis. The authors developed an adaptive edge-cloud hybrid AI model for cardiac anomaly detection in [[55](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-025-00795-0#ref-CR55 "Alsubai S, Sha M, Alqahtani A, Bhatia M (2023) Hybrid IoT-edge-cloud computing-based athlete healthcare framework: digital twin initiative. Mob Networks Appl 1–20")]. Their system deployed a lightweight CNN model on the edge for real-time ECG screening, while a more complex Transformer-based deep learning model was used in the cloud for detailed diagnostics.

This is an open-access review article published in the Journal of Cloud Computing (Volume 14, Article 64, 2025) titled "Integrating wearable health devices with AI and edge computing for personalized rehabilitation." The paper explores the convergence of wearable health devices (smartwatches, health patches, ECG monitors, CGMs, smart clothing) with AI and edge computing for personalized healthcare, particularly for young students.

**Key Content:**

- **Wearable Device Categories:** Smartwatches (PPG sensors, heart rate monitoring), health monitoring patches (bioimpedance, glucose sensors), wearable ECG/EKG monitors (CNN-based classification), continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), and smart clothing (textile-based sensors).

- **AI Techniques:** Machine learning (SVM, Random Forest, KNN), deep learning (CNN, LSTM, Transformers), supervised/unsupervised learning, and federated learning for privacy-preserving health data analysis.

- **Computing Paradigms:** Edge AI (real-time processing, 85% faster response), Cloud AI (complex model training, 20% better hyperglycemia prediction), and Hybrid Edge-Cloud AI (combines low latency with deep analytics).

- **Applications:** Chronic disease management (arrhythmia detection, blood pressure monitoring, sleep tracking), real-time health monitoring with 97.2% accuracy using hybrid CNN-LSTM models, and remote patient monitoring.

- **Challenges:** Data privacy and security, data accuracy and reliability, interoperability, standardization, ethical concerns, and need for user-friendly interfaces.

The paper includes performance comparison tables of AI models and references 65 sources. Authors: Lei Xi, Caizhong Li, Maryam Saberi Anari, and Khosro Rezaee.

# Artificial intelligence-integrated wearable technology in sports medicine injury prevention and rehabilitation: A narrative review

Wearable technology has the potential to support customized training, injury prevention, rehabilitation, and gait analysis, enabling real-time monitoring of biomechanical, physiological, and performance-related data in sports medicine. This narrative review of the literature used Primary research data. PubMed, Google Scholar, and Web of Science were among the databases and search engines used to locate publications. This review focuses on the literature from the past 10 years on wearable sensor technologies combined with artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in sports medicine, particularly for injury prevention and rehabilitation. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of these technologies for injury risk assessment, rehabilitation, workload management, and gait training. Wearable technology enabled the creation of individualized training plans and the prevention of injuries by precisely monitoring heart rate, sleep quality, gait patterns, and training load. Automated feedback systems and predictive analytics can be improved through AI/ML integration. However, problems with sensor reliability, the lack of established protocols, variability in accuracy, and constraints on user comfort persisted. Wearable sensors have the potential to enable information-based, customized athlete care through improved monitoring and predictive capabilities, particularly when paired with AI/ML. Future research should focus on improving sensor accuracy, standardizing data-collection protocols, and fostering interdisciplinary collaboration to realize the benefits fully.
